title: Greek cities in present-day West Asia
cyprus_note: The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.

cities.site: Ruins between Agios Tychonas and Limassol, Limassol district
cities.greek_from_text: Greek beside Eteocypriot by the 4th c. BC: bilingual royal and civic inscriptions and the Greek-named king Androkles, who sailed with Alexander at Tyre (Arrian 2.22.2). Euboean and other Greek pottery from the 10th c. BC shows trade, not speech. A Greek city after the end of the kingdom, c. 300 BC
cities.until_text: Eteocypriot disappears c. 300 BC; Amathus was a Greek city and see (Tychon, 5th c.; Heliodorus at Chalcedon, 451; Theodore after 614; Alexander at Nicaea, 787). The town was refortified in the 7th c., then shrank as its people moved to Neapolis/Nemesos (Limassol), 10 km west; it was almost deserted when Richard I took Cyprus in 1191.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions to late antiquity; basilicas; the site was largely abandoned by the 8th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: decline after Mu'awiya's raids on Cyprus, 649 and 653/654 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140, 6146; the Soloi basilica inscriptions record the captives); the people moved to Limassol. Later accounts say Richard I destroyed what was left in 1191.
cities.pre_greek_note: Founded c. 1050 BC by a non-Greek (Eteocypriot) community; its Eteocypriot name is not known. Amathus is missing from Esarhaddon's list of 673/672 BC unless Assyrian Nuria (usually taken as Marion) or Qartihadasti is Amathus, as a minority holds.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Eteocypriot inscriptions in the Cypriot syllabary (6th-4th c. BC); bilingual Eteocypriot and Greek inscriptions of the 4th c. BC, among them the pedestals of statues dedicated by the last king, Androkles, and an honorific inscription of the city; Ps.-Skylax 103 calls the Amathusians autochthonous
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Amathus (Hdt. 5.104-114, Onesilos' siege); IACP Cyprus chapter; Ptolemaic and Roman city; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Bilingual (Eteocypriot and Greek) until c. 300 BC, then a Greek city; the bilingual period is recorded. Greek speech in the town may be older than the 4th c. BC.

cities.other_names: Arsinoe (Ptolemaic name, Strabo 14.6.3; the identification is probable, not certain); Famagosta (Italian); Famagouste (French); Magusa, Gazimagusa (Turkish); Varosha (the suburb where Greeks lived after 1571)
cities.site: Walled city of Famagusta and the suburb of Varosha, Famagusta district
cities.greek_from_text: Probably the Ptolemaic Arsinoe, 'a city and harbour' after Salamis (Strabo 14.6.3), named after Arsinoe II and so founded or renamed under Ptolemy II, c. 270s BC. As Ammochostos it grew after the decline of Constantia (Salamis) in the later 7th c., and it became a major port after Christian refugees from Acre arrived in 1291.
cities.until_text: Greek community through the Lusignan, Genoese (1373-1464) and Venetian (1489-1571) periods, beside Latins, Syrians, Armenians and Jews (St George of the Greeks, 14th c.). After the Ottoman conquest of 1571 Christians were barred from the walled city and lived in Varosha. Greek-speaking until 1974.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek cathedral of St George (14th c.); Varosha the Greek quarter from 1571; about 39,000 inhabitants of Varosha fled in August 1974; the suburb was fenced off, and part of it was reopened by the Turkish Cypriot authorities in 2020, contrary to UN Security Council resolutions 550 (1984) and 789 (1992).
cities.ended_by: Turkish invasion of 1974: the landing west of Kyrenia on 20 July and the second offensive of 14-16 August. The Greek Cypriots of Famagusta and Varosha fled before the advancing Turkish army or were expelled (as the Turkish army entered the town on 15-16 August 1974; Varosha was then fenced off). At the third round of the Vienna talks (2 August 1975) it was agreed that Turkish Cypriots in the south could move north and that Greek Cypriots in the north could stay or move south; in the following years most of those who had stayed in the north left or were moved south, except the enclaved of the Karpas. Their homes were given to Turkish Cypriots displaced from the south and to settlers from Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights has held Turkey responsible for the continuing denial of the displaced owners' access to their homes (Loizidou v. Turkey, 1996, a Kyrenia property; Cyprus v. Turkey, 2001). Earlier: Lala Mustafa Pasha's siege of 1570-1571 ended with the surrender of 1 August 1571 and the execution of Marcantonio Bragadin. The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.refounded_by: Grew into the chief port of eastern Cyprus after the later 7th c.; Lusignan port city from 1291
cities.status_evidence: Latin see from 1196; seat of a Greek bishop (resident at Karpasia from 1260); chief port of Lusignan Cyprus
cities.note: The Ptolemaic Arsinoe of Strabo is usually placed here, but no Hellenistic town has been excavated under Famagusta, so the early phase rests on the identification. The town is not documented between Strabo and the 7th c.
sources: Edbury, The Kingdom of Cyprus and the Crusades (1991)
Walsh, Coureas & Edbury, Medieval and Renaissance Famagusta (2012)

cities.site: Ruins near Liastrika, Akanthou (Tatlısu), Famagusta district
cities.greek_from_text: A town with a Greek name on the north coast, attested by Strabo (14.6.3) and Ptolemy (5.14.4); the remains are Hellenistic to late antique
cities.until_text: Flourished from the Hellenistic period to late antiquity; declined and was abandoned after the first Arab raids of the mid-7th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Late antique remains; no see.
cities.ended_by: No named act: abandoned after Mu'awiya's raids on Cyprus, 649 and 653/654 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140, 6146; the Soloi basilica inscriptions record the captives).
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 14.6.3 (as a place on the north coast, not called a city); Ptolemy 5.14.4 (coastal list); remains of a Hellenistic-Roman settlement
cities.note: Strabo names Aphrodisium only as the point where the island is narrowest; its rank as a town rests on Ptolemy's list and the remains, and it may have been a dependency of Salamis. The Hellenistic start date is an estimate.

cities.site: Ruins at Agios Philon on the north coast, 2-3 km north of Rizokarpaso (Dipkarpaz), Famagusta district
cities.greek_from_text: City of Cyprus in Ps.-Skylax 103 (c. 340s BC); stormed by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 306 BC (Diod. 20.47.2)
cities.until_text: Not ended. A Roman town and see (Philon, ordained by Epiphanius c. 400; Hermolaus at Chalcedon, 451); the coastal town was abandoned after the Arab raids of the 7th c. and its people moved inland to Rizokarpaso; from 1260 the seat of the Greek bishop of Famagusta. Rizokarpaso is the largest village of the enclaved Greek Cypriots in the north. The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.fade_evidence: Basilica of Agios Philon (5th-6th c.); Greek bishop at Karpasia under the Latins (Bulla Cypria, 1260); 343 enclaved Greek Cypriots in the north in 2014, most of them in Rizokarpaso.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. The coastal town declined after Mu'awiya's raids on Cyprus, 649 and 653/654 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140, 6146), and its people moved inland to Rizokarpaso. In August 1974 the Karpas came under Turkish control; its Greek Cypriots were cut off and could not flee. Most left or were moved south in the following years. A few hundred remain enclaved, most of them elderly, and UNFICYP supplies them. The European Court of Human Rights found that their living conditions were degrading treatment and violated their rights to private and family life, religion, expression, education and property (Cyprus v. Turkey, Grand Chamber, 10 May 2001).
cities.pre_greek_note: A Phoenician founder (Pygmalion) appears in Greek tradition only.
cities.status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 103; Diod. 20.47.2; IACP Cyprus chapter; Pliny NH 5.130; see (Hierocles 707)
cities.note: Kept open because the community moved 3 km inland to Rizokarpaso (Ριζοκάρπασο, Turkish Dipkarpaz), whose name continues Karpasia and where Greek Cypriots still live. Archaeology dates the town from the 7th c. BC (town_from); the first Greek text is later.

cities.site: Kyrenia town (harbour and castle area), Kyrenia district
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a city of Cyprus by Ps.-Skylax 103 (c. 340s BC) and taken by Ptolemy I in 312 BC (Diod. 19.79.4); earlier Iron Age tombs
cities.until_text: Greek city, Roman town and see; a Lusignan and Venetian fortress town; surrendered to the Ottomans in 1570. Greek-speaking until 1974.
cities.fade_evidence: Kyrenia had a Greek Cypriot majority in the 1960 census; the few Greek Cypriots who stayed after July 1974 left or were moved south in 1975-76.
cities.ended_by: Turkish invasion of 1974: the landing west of Kyrenia on 20 July and the second offensive of 14-16 August. The Greek Cypriots of Kyrenia fled before the advancing Turkish army or were expelled (the Turkish landing at Pente Mili, west of the town, on 20 July 1974; the town was taken in the following days). At the third round of the Vienna talks (2 August 1975) it was agreed that Turkish Cypriots in the south could move north and that Greek Cypriots in the north could stay or move south; in the following years most of those who had stayed in the north left or were moved south, except the enclaved of the Karpas. Their homes were given to Turkish Cypriots displaced from the south and to settlers from Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights has held Turkey responsible for the continuing denial of the displaced owners' access to their homes (Loizidou v. Turkey, 1996, a Kyrenia property; Cyprus v. Turkey, 2001). The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 103; Diod. 19.79.4; IACP Cyprus chapter; Ptolemy 5.14.4; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: The legend of Achaean settlers (from Keryneia in Achaea) is a note. The town was probably Greek-speaking before the 4th c. BC, but no earlier text names it.

cities.other_names: Kitrusi (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Chythroi; Kythrea (medieval and modern)
cities.site: Kythrea (Değirmenlik), at the springs below the Pentadaktylos range, Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: King Pilagura (Philagoras, a Greek name) of Kitrusi in Esarhaddon's list of 673/672 BC
cities.until_text: Under Salamis in the Classical period; a Roman town and see (Hierocles); the medieval town of Kythrea with its water mills; Greek-speaking until 1974.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Chytroi; Kythrea had a Greek Cypriot majority in the 1960 census.
cities.ended_by: Turkish invasion of 1974: the landing west of Kyrenia on 20 July and the second offensive of 14-16 August. The Greek Cypriots of Kythrea fled before the advancing Turkish army or were expelled (in the second Turkish offensive, 14-16 August 1974). At the third round of the Vienna talks (2 August 1975) it was agreed that Turkish Cypriots in the south could move north and that Greek Cypriots in the north could stay or move south; in the following years most of those who had stayed in the north left or were moved south, except the enclaved of the Karpas. Their homes were given to Turkish Cypriots displaced from the south and to settlers from Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights has held Turkey responsible for the continuing denial of the displaced owners' access to their homes (Loizidou v. Turkey, 1996, a Kyrenia property; Cyprus v. Turkey, 2001). The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom (Esarhaddon 673/672 BC); IACP Cyprus chapter; Pliny NH 5.130; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Kythrea had a Turkish Cypriot minority quarter. Founding legends (Chytros, grandson of Akamas) are notes only.

cities.other_names: Kty (Phoenician); Kittim (Hebrew Bible); Qartihadasti? (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC; disputed); Salines/Le Salines (Frankish); Larnaka (from the medieval period)
cities.site: Larnaca town (Kathari, Bamboula and the acropolis), Larnaca district
cities.greek_from_text: Greek speakers among the residents by the 4th c. BC beside the Phoenician majority: Greek inscriptions and Zeno of Kition (born c. 334 BC). Greek city after Ptolemy I ended the Phoenician kingdom and killed Pumiyathon, 312 BC (Diod. 19.79.4)
cities.until_text: Not ended. Phoenician speech faded in the 3rd c. BC; Kition was then a Greek city, a see (Hierocles), and as Larnaca a Greek-speaking town to the present.
cities.fade_evidence: Last Phoenician inscriptions at Kition, 3rd c. BC; Greek inscriptions from the Hellenistic period on; bishops of Kition; Larnaca Greek-speaking to the present.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Ptolemy I ended the Phoenician dynasty, 312 BC. Arab raids from 649 (Mu'awiya); Ottoman conquest, 1570.
cities.pre_greek_note: Late Bronze Age town from the 13th c. BC; rebuilt c. 1200 BC in ashlar, which Karageorghis linked to Aegean settlers, but no Greek text supports this. Phoenician town from c. 800 BC. The Assyrian Qartihadasti ('new town') is Kition for many, Amathus or Limassol for others.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Phoenician kingdom from c. 800 BC to 312 BC (royal Phoenician inscriptions and coins, Baalmilk I to Pumiyathon); Greek inscriptions and Greek-educated citizens in the 4th c. BC (Zeno, born at Kition c. 334 BC); Phoenician inscriptions end in the 3rd c. BC
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Kition (Phoenician kings, coins); IACP Cyprus chapter; city of the Ptolemaic and Roman period; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Bilingual start date is an estimate from 4th-c. evidence; the Greek majority dates from the 3rd c. BC. Cimon died besieging Kition in 450/449 BC.

cities.other_names: Kuri (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Episkopi (the medieval and modern village, from the bishop's seat)
cities.site: Kourion archaeological site on the bluff above Episkopi Bay, within the Western (Akrotiri) Sovereign Base Area, Limassol district; Episkopi village 2 km north-east
cities.greek_from_text: Aegean-type tombs of the 11th c. BC at Kaloriziki (tomb 40, with the gold sceptre); Greek-named king Damasos (Damasu) of Kuri in 673/672 BC; Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions from the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates (Archaic period). Herodotus (5.113) calls the Kourians Argive colonists
cities.until_text: The city was ruined by the earthquakes of 365-370, rebuilt with a basilica and bishop's palace (5th c.), and abandoned in the 7th c. after the Arab raids; the bishop and people moved to Episkopi, which is Greek-speaking today.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Zeno of Kourion at the Council of Ephesus, 431; the acropolis was destroyed in the Arab raids of 649 and the bishop's seat moved to Episkopi; Episkopi village Greek-speaking to the present.
cities.ended_by: Not ended for the community. The site: earthquakes of 365-370 (no named act); abandoned in the 7th c. after Mu'awiya's raids on Cyprus, 649 and 653/654 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140, 6146; the Soloi basilica inscriptions record the captives).
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.pre_greek_note: The Late Bronze Age town of Episkopi-Bamboula nearby was abandoned c. 1050 BC.
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Kourion (Stasanor, Hdt. 5.113; Esarhaddon 673/672 BC); IACP Cyprus chapter; Roman city; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: The 11th-c. date rests on archaeology, not on a text; the first Greek text from Kourion is later. Phase left open because the community moved to Episkopi, which kept the see.

cities.site: Agios Fotios hill north-west of Athienou, Larnaca district
cities.greek_from_text: Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions and Greek-style sculpture from the sanctuaries of Golgoi, from the 6th c. BC
cities.until_text: Named as a town by Pliny (NH 5.130, AD 77) and Stephanus; not a see. The sanctuary finds run into the Roman period; the town's end is not documented, and the area's Greek speech continued at Athienou nearby.
cities.fade_evidence: Roman-period finds; no late antique city or bishop.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town is last attested in the early Roman period.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.130 (Golgi); Stephanus s.v. Golgoi; Theocritus and Catullus (Aphrodite of Golgoi); syllabic inscriptions
cities.note: Not a kingdom; probably under Idalion or Kition. The tradition of a founder Golgos from Sikyon is a note. Athienou and the site lie inside the UN buffer zone, farmed under the Republic's administration.

cities.other_names: Edi'il (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); 'dyl (Phoenician); Dali (modern village)
cities.site: Ambelleri and Moutti tou Arvili hills at Dali, Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: King Ekishtura (Akestor, a Greek name) of Edi'il in Esarhaddon's list of 673/672 BC; the Idalion bronze tablet (c. 478-470 BC), a contract of king Stasikypros and 'the polis' with the physician Onasilos in Greek (Cypro-syllabic)
cities.until_text: Not ended. The kingdom fell to Kition c. 450 BC and had a Phoenician-speaking administration and community until the end of the 4th c. BC; it declined in the Hellenistic and Roman periods and survives as the village of Dali, which is Greek-speaking.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek syllabic and alphabetic inscriptions; Dali village Greek-speaking today.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Loss of independence: conquered by Kition, c. 450 BC; Kition's kingdom ended by Ptolemy I, 312 BC.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.pre_greek_note: Late Cypriot fortified settlement on Ambelleri (13th-12th c. BC); its name before the Greeks is not attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Kition took Idalion c. 450 BC; Phoenician administrative archive of ostraca (5th-4th c. BC) and the Phoenician-Greek syllabic bilingual of 388 BC (dedication to Reshef-Mikal/Apollo Amyklaios)
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom (Esarhaddon 673/672 BC); the Idalion tablet names the polis; IACP Cyprus chapter
cities.note: Not a city in Hierocles; after the Classical period Idalion was a small town. Kept open-ended because Dali continues the community.

cities.other_names: Lpš (Phoenician); Lapathos (Strabo); Lambousa (the late antique coastal town); Lapithos (medieval and modern)
cities.site: Ancient town at Lambousa on the coast below Lapithos (Lapta), Kyrenia district
cities.greek_from_text: Greek-named kings beside Phoenician ones: Demonikos (coins, c. 388 BC) and Praxippos (coins with Greek letters; Diod. 19.79.4). Strabo (14.6.3) calls it a foundation of Laconians and Praxander
cities.until_text: Greek city from the Hellenistic period; a see (Hierocles); Lambousa was a rich port in the 7th c. (the Lambousa treasure of silver plates). Lapithos remained a Greek-speaking town until 1974.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and the see in late antiquity; Lapithos had a Greek Cypriot majority in the 1960 census.
cities.ended_by: Turkish invasion of 1974: the landing west of Kyrenia on 20 July and the second offensive of 14-16 August. The Greek Cypriots of Lapithos fled before the advancing Turkish army or were expelled (the town was taken as the Turkish bridgehead was widened westwards in late July and early August 1974). At the third round of the Vienna talks (2 August 1975) it was agreed that Turkish Cypriots in the south could move north and that Greek Cypriots in the north could stay or move south; in the following years most of those who had stayed in the north left or were moved south, except the enclaved of the Karpas. Their homes were given to Turkish Cypriots displaced from the south and to settlers from Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights has held Turkey responsible for the continuing denial of the displaced owners' access to their homes (Loizidou v. Turkey, 1996, a Kyrenia property; Cyprus v. Turkey, 2001). Earlier: the Arab raids on Cyprus of 649 and 653/654. The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.pre_greek_note: Tombs of the 11th c. BC at Kastros are of Aegean type, so the town may have been Greek-speaking before its Phoenician dynasty; no early text survives. The Phoenician name Lpš renders the same name.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Phoenician kings and coin legends (Sidqmelek, c. 450-425 BC); king Demonikos (Greek name) with the Semitic legend 'Dmnks king of Lpš' (c. 388 BC); Phoenician inscriptions to 275 BC (Lapethos 3, under Ptolemy II); Ps.-Skylax 103 calls Lapethos Phoenician; the last king, Praxippos (c. 330-312 BC), struck coins with Greek letters
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Lapethos (Phoenician coins; Diod. 19.79.4); IACP Cyprus chapter; Ps.-Skylax 103; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Bilingual (Phoenician and Greek) in the 5th-4th c. BC, a Greek city afterwards. The start date is a cautious first attestation; Greek speech there may be older. The ruins at Lambousa lie on the coast about 3 km north of the present village of Lapithos (Λάπηθος, Turkish Lapta), which continues the name.

cities.other_names: Lidir (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Ledroi, Ledra; Leukousia, Leukosia (from the 4th-7th c.); Nicosie (Frankish); Lefkoşa (Turkish)
cities.site: Old Nicosia within the Venetian walls and the hills of Agios Georgios and Ambelokipi, Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: King Unasagusu (Onasagoras, a Greek name) of Lidir in Esarhaddon's list of 673/672 BC
cities.until_text: Not ended. A small town in antiquity and a see (Triphyllios, 4th c.); capital of Cyprus from the late 10th or 11th c., of the Lusignan kingdom and of Venetian Cyprus; taken by the Ottomans in 1570. Greek-speaking to the present.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Ledra/Leukosia; the Greek community under Latin and Ottoman rule; Greek-speaking city today.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Stormed by Lala Mustafa Pasha's army on 9 September 1570, with the killing of much of the garrison and population. The city has been divided by the Green Line since the intercommunal fighting of 1963-64; its northern part has been under Turkish control since 1974, and the Greek Cypriots still living there left in 1974.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom (Esarhaddon 673/672 BC); IACP Cyprus chapter; see (Hierocles 707, Leukousia); capital from the 11th c.
cities.note: The ancient centre lies in the southern part of the divided city. Bronze Age sites lie under and around the city, but continuity with the Iron Age town is not shown.

cities.site: Probably near Limnitis (Yeşilırmak), west of Soloi, Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: Named by Strabo (14.6.3) as 'a city Limenia' inland above Soloi; Strabo wrote c. AD 20, probably from Hellenistic sources
cities.until_text: Known only from Strabo (14.6.3, c. AD 20), who names 'a city Limenia' inland above Soloi; Ptolemy's list of the inland towns of Cyprus (5.14.6) names only Chytroi, Tremithous and Tamassos, and no later source names it. Its later history is unknown.
cities.fade_evidence: No later attestation; not a see.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town is not attested after Strabo.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 14.6.3 (polis)
cities.note: A single mention and an uncertain site; the link with the village of Limnitis (Λιμνίτης, Turkish Yeşilırmak) rests on the name only. Limnitis was a Turkish Cypriot village before 1974. The Barrington Atlas places it, with a query, south-east of the islet of Petra tou Limniti.

cities.other_names: Arsinoe (Ptolemaic refoundation, c. 270 BC); Nuria (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC; usual identification, king Bususu); Polis tis Chrysochous (medieval and modern)
cities.site: Polis Chrysochous town (Marion to the north, Arsinoe under the town), Paphos district
cities.greek_from_text: Many Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions from the tombs of Marion, from the 6th c. BC; Ps.-Skylax 103 lists Marion as Greek
cities.until_text: Not ended. Ptolemy I razed Marion in 312 BC and moved its people to Paphos (Diod. 19.79.4); Ptolemy II refounded it as Arsinoe c. 270 BC. Arsinoe was a see; from 1260 it was the seat of the Greek bishop of Paphos. Polis is a Greek-speaking town today.
cities.fade_evidence: Hellenistic and Roman inscriptions of Arsinoe; bishops of Arsinoe; Greek bishop of Paphos at Arsinoe 1260-1571; Polis Greek-speaking to the present.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Interrupted: razed by Ptolemy I, 312 BC, its people moved to Paphos (Diod. 19.79.4); refounded by Ptolemy II, c. 270 BC.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Marion (kings Stasioikos I and II; coins); IACP Cyprus chapter; Ps.-Skylax 103; Arsinoe a city and see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Marion had a king with a non-Greek name (Sasmas, 5th c. BC) and Phoenician finds, but no clear Phoenician-speaking community. Arsinoe lies on the same site, so the two are one entry with two phases.
sources: Childs, Smith & Padgett, City of Gold (2012)

cities.other_names: Paphos; Sebaste Claudia Flavia Paphos (Roman titles); Augusta (title after the earthquake of 15 BC); Baffo (Venetian); Baf (Ottoman Turkish); Kato Paphos and Ktima (medieval and modern quarters)
cities.site: Kato Paphos, Paphos town, Paphos district (archaeological park)
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Nikokles, last king of Paphos, c. 320 BC as the new royal seat
cities.until_text: Not ended. Capital of Ptolemaic and Roman Cyprus until the 4th c. AD; a see; damaged by the earthquakes of 332 and 342 and raided by the Arabs in the 7th c.; Latin see from 1196; taken by the Ottomans in 1570. Paphos is a Greek-speaking town today.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the Ptolemaic and Roman capital; bishops of Paphos (Cyril at Nicaea, 325); Greek bishops of Paphos relegated to Arsinoe under the Latins (Bulla Cypria, 1260); Greek-speaking town to the present.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Interruptions: earthquakes of 332 and 342 (no named act); Arab raids from 649 (Mu'awiya); Ottoman conquest, 1570 (Lala Mustafa Pasha's campaign).
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemaic and Roman capital (strategos; koinon of the Cypriots); city coins; see (bishop at Nicaea 325); Hierocles 706-707
cities.note: Founded by Nikokles, a Cypriot Greek king of Paphos, not by an outside power. A separate entry from Palaepaphos: a refoundation on a new site 16 km away.

cities.other_names: Theodosias/Theodosiana (5th c.); Nemesos; Lemesos (by the 10th c.); Limisso (Venetian); Leymosun (Turkish)
cities.site: Old Limassol around the castle, Limassol district
cities.greek_from_text: Became a town and see in the 5th c. as Theodosias or Neapolis, probably around the time of the Council of Chalcedon (451); bishop Leontius of Neapolis wrote in Greek in the 7th c.
cities.until_text: Not ended. Took over from Amathus in the 7th c.; Richard I landed here in 1191; seat of the Templars and Hospitallers; raided by the Genoese (1373) and the Mamluks (1424-1426); taken by the Ottomans in July 1570. Greek-speaking to the present.
cities.fade_evidence: Leontius of Neapolis (7th c.); bishop at the Council of 787; from 1260 the Greek bishop of Limassol resided at Lefkara.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Arab raids from 649 (Mu'awiya); Mamluk raids under Sultan Barsbay, 1424-1426; Ottoman conquest, July 1570.
cities.status_evidence: See (Theodosias/Neapolis, 5th c.; Leontius, 7th c.); Georgius Cyprius
cities.note: The date of the see's founding is not secure; the name Theodosias suggests Theodosius II (408-450).

cities.other_names: Paphos (until c. 320 BC); Palaipaphos (Hellenistic and Roman); Pappa (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Kouklia (medieval and modern)
cities.site: Kouklia village, Paphos district (sanctuary of Aphrodite and the hills of Marcello and Hadjiabdoullah)
cities.greek_from_text: Bronze spit (obelos) inscribed o-pe-le-ta-u, 'of Opheltas', in Greek of the Arcado-Cypriot type, from tomb 49 at Palaepaphos-Skales, Cypro-Geometric I (c. 1050-950 BC): the earliest Greek text from Cyprus
cities.until_text: Not ended. The kings of Paphos ruled here until Nikokles moved the capital to Nea Paphos c. 320 BC; Old Paphos remained a Greek town around the sanctuary of Aphrodite through Roman times, and Kouklia on the site is still a Greek-speaking village.
cities.fade_evidence: Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions of the kings of Paphos (6th-4th c. BC); Greek inscriptions of the sanctuary to the Roman period; Kouklia is a Greek Cypriot village today.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Loss of rank: Nikokles moved the royal seat to Nea Paphos, c. 320 BC. Kouklia was a mixed village; its Turkish Cypriots moved north in 1975 and its Greek Cypriots remain.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.founder: Aegean (Greek-speaking) settlers on a Late Bronze Age town
cities.pre_greek_note: Paphos was a Late Cypriot town and sanctuary from c. 1600 BC; its name in non-Greek sources before the Greeks is not known. Assyrian Pappa (673/672 BC) renders the Greek-period name.
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Paphos (Esarhaddon 673/672 BC: king Ituandar = Eteandros; Cypro-syllabic royal inscriptions and coins); IACP Cyprus chapter (Paphos)
cities.note: The legend of Agapenor of Tegea as founder (Paus. 8.5.2) is a note, not a date. The Opheltas spit is the key evidence for Greek speakers by the 11th c. BC.

cities.other_names: Constantia (Κωνσταντία, from c. 346, after Constantius II); Sillu(w)a? (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC)
cities.site: Ruins near Agios Sergios (Yeni Boğaziçi), north of Famagusta, Famagusta district
cities.greek_from_text: New town on the coast c. 1075-1050 BC, when nearby Enkomi was abandoned, with Aegean-type material; Greek kingship clear from the 6th c. BC (king Euelthon's coins with Cypro-syllabic Greek legends, c. 560-525 BC; Hdt. 4.162, 5.104)
cities.until_text: The city, renamed Constantia and made metropolis of Cyprus after the earthquakes of 332 and 342, was sacked in the first Arab raid of 649 and hit again in 653/654; it shrank in the later 7th c. and its people moved to Ammochostos (Famagusta) nearby. Administration: the see kept the name Constantia. Speech: the Greek community continued at Famagusta.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Epiphanius (367-403); 7th-c. rebuilding and coin finds; the city was largely abandoned by the 8th c.
cities.ended_by: Sacked in Mu'awiya's raid, 649 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140); second raid 653/654. In 691 Justinian II moved part of the Cypriot population to Nea Ioustinianoupolis on the Hellespont; they returned in 698/699. No single act of abandonment is recorded.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.pre_greek_note: The predecessor, Enkomi (2 km west), was a Late Bronze Age town abandoned c. 1050 BC; its ancient name is not known (Alashiya is disputed). Assyrian Sillu(w)a is identified with Salamis by most, with Soloi by some.
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Salamis (Hdt. 5.104, 8.11; Evagoras I, Isocrates); royal coins with Greek legends; IACP Cyprus chapter; metropolis of Cyprus (Constantia); Hierocles 706
cities.note: The Teucer foundation legend is a note, not a date. Since 1974 the site lies in the north; the Greek Cypriots of the surrounding villages fled in August 1974.

cities.other_names: Silli (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Aipeia (legendary earlier town, Plut. Solon 26)
cities.site: Ruins at Potamos tou Kampou (Yedidalga), west of Lefka (Lefke), Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: Greek-named kings: Philokypros, host of Solon (early 6th c. BC; Hdt. 5.113; Plut. Solon 26), and his son Aristokypros, killed in 498/497 BC; Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions
cities.until_text: A Greek city and see (Auxibius) into the 7th c.; the basilica was destroyed and the town abandoned after the Arab raids. Under the Latins (1260) the Greek bishop of Soloi was moved to Solea.
cities.fade_evidence: Two Greek inscriptions in the basilica of Soloi record the Arab raids and the captives taken; no later town on the site.
cities.ended_by: Mu'awiya's raids on Cyprus, 649 and 653/654 (al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6140, 6146; the Soloi basilica inscriptions record the captives): the basilica was burnt and the town declined and was abandoned.
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom of Soloi (Hdt. 5.113-115, five-month Persian siege); IACP Cyprus chapter; Roman city; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: Assyrian Silli is usually taken as Soloi. The stories of a foundation by Akamas or Phaleros of Athens, and of Solon advising King Philokypros to move the town into the plain (Plut. Solon 26), are traditions, not evidence of a colony. The Greek Cypriots of the Morphou and Lefka area fled or were expelled in 1974.

cities.other_names: Tamesi (Assyrian, Esarhaddon's prism (Nineveh A), 673/672 BC); Temese? (Homer, Od. 1.184, disputed); Politiko (modern village)
cities.site: Politiko village (royal tombs and sanctuary), Nicosia district
cities.greek_from_text: King Admesu (Admetos, a Greek name) of Tamesi in Esarhaddon's list of 673/672 BC; Cypro-syllabic Greek inscriptions
cities.until_text: Not ended. Under Kition's kings in the 4th c. BC (bilingual period); Alexander gave it to Pnytagoras of Salamis; a Roman town and see (Herakleidios, by tradition its first bishop); later the village of Politiko, Greek-speaking today.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Tamassos (Hierocles lists the city); the monastery of Agios Herakleidios at Politiko; Greek-speaking village.
cities.ended_by: Not ended. Loss of independence: sold by Pasikypros to Pumiyathon of Kition (4th c. BC); Arab raids from 649 (Mu'awiya).
cities.origin: Greek settlement of the migration era
cities.pre_greek_note: Homer's Temese, where copper was traded, may be Tamassos; it is a Greek text and gives no pre-Greek name.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Phoenician and Greek (syllabic) bilingual dedications to Reshef/Apollo, 375 and 362 BC, under the kings of Kition; king Pasikypros sold the kingdom to Pumiyathon of Kition for 50 talents (Duris in Athen. 4.167c)
cities.status_evidence: Kingdom (Esarhaddon 673/672 BC; Duris); royal tombs; IACP Cyprus chapter; see (Hierocles 706)
cities.note: The Greek date is the first text; the town is older (Cypro-Geometric). Whether its first Iron Age people spoke Greek is not known.

cities.site: Tremetousia (Erdemli), Larnaca district
cities.greek_from_text: First listed as an inland city of Cyprus by Ptolemy (5.14.6), 2nd c. AD; its bishop Spyridon (early 4th c.) is said by Rufinus, Socrates and Sozomen to have attended the Council of Nicaea, 325, though his name is not in the surviving signature lists
cities.until_text: A see from the 4th c. (Spyridon; bishops in 381, 681 and 787); Richard I defeated Isaac Komnenos here in 1191 and the town declined to a village. Greek-speaking until 1974.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Trimithous to the 11th c.; the church of Agios Spyridon in the village.
cities.ended_by: Turkish invasion of 1974: the landing west of Kyrenia on 20 July and the second offensive of 14-16 August. The Greek Cypriots of Tremetousia fled before the advancing Turkish army or were expelled (in the second Turkish offensive, August 1974). At the third round of the Vienna talks (2 August 1975) it was agreed that Turkish Cypriots in the south could move north and that Greek Cypriots in the north could stay or move south; in the following years most of those who had stayed in the north left or were moved south, except the enclaved of the Karpas. Their homes were given to Turkish Cypriots displaced from the south and to settlers from Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights has held Turkey responsible for the continuing denial of the displaced owners' access to their homes (Loizidou v. Turkey, 1996, a Kyrenia property; Cyprus v. Turkey, 2001). Tremetousia is one of the few villages of the Larnaca district under Turkish control. The north of Cyprus has been under Turkish military occupation ever since, an occupation illegal under international law: the UN General Assembly demanded 'the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces from the Republic of Cyprus' (Res. 37/253, 1983), and the Security Council declared the secession of the north 'legally invalid' and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus (Res. 541, 1983); only Turkey recognises the breakaway state.
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.14.6; see (bishop Spyridon, early 4th c.: Rufinus, HE 10.5; Socrates 1.12; Sozomen 1.11); Hierocles 707; Georgius Cyprius
cities.note: The town may be older than its first mention. Its pre-1974 Greek Cypriot population is inferred from the village's history; the village had 169 inhabitants in 2011.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Tartus (old town), Tartus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The mainland town of the Aradian state; Greek civic life of Aradus from the 2nd c. BC; Antaradus is named as a separate town by Ptolemy and Pliny and as a see from the 4th c.; Constantius II refounded it as Constantia in 346.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, c. 636; al-Baladhuri says the inhabitants evacuated it, and Mu'awiya later rebuilt it, settled soldiers and gave them fiefs. Speech: the Greek-speaking population left with the conquest; later Christians spoke Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: Refounded by Constantius II, 346; bishops Cymatius (under Constantine, shared with Aradus), Musaeus, Alexander, Paulus, Atticus, Theodorus (d. 518), Asyncretius (553); Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena; flight of the inhabitants at the conquest (al-Baladhuri).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, c. 636; the inhabitants evacuated it and Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan resettled it with soldiers (al-Baladhuri).
cities.other_language: Phoenician (as part of the Aradian state)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Mainland town of Aradus; Phoenician until the Hellenistic period.
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena; bishops from the 4th c.; Ptolemy 5.15
cities.note: The earliest separate civic evidence for Antaradus is late; the start date follows the Greek civic life of the Aradian state.
sources: Jones, Cities of the Eastern Roman Provinces

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Arwad island, Tartus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Aradus received autonomy and began a civic era in 259 BC; Greek civic institutions (boule, demos) and city coins with the Greek legend ΑΡΑΔΙΩΝ are attested in the 2nd c. BC, alongside Phoenician.
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together. Mu'awiya's first assault (winter 649) failed, and the islanders arrested his envoy, the bishop Thomarichos; at the second (spring 650) they surrendered for safe passage. Some left for Roman territory and some for Syria; the island was emptied, its walls destroyed and the town razed so that it could not serve the Roman fleet (Theophanes; Syriac chronicles).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 2nd c. BC to the Roman period; bishops Cymatius (under Constantine), Mocimus (381), Paulus (451), Atticus (458), Asyncretius (553); Hierocles (Phoenice); evacuation in 650.
cities.ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria for Caliph Uthman, spring 650; the inhabitants were made to leave and the town was razed (Theophanes; Syriac chronicles).
cities.pre_greek_name: Arwad (Phoenician ʾrwd; Akkadian Arwada; Hebrew Bible Arvad)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Coins with Greek legend ΑΡΑΔΙΩΝ but Phoenician letters and dates in the 2nd c. BC; Greek civic decrees of boule and demos.
cities.status_evidence: Civic era 259 BC (Antiochus II); city coins with Greek legends (2nd c. BC on); Greek decrees of boule and demos; bishops from Constantine's reign; Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Phoenician survived beside Greek through the late Hellenistic period; the date of the end of Phoenician is uncertain.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Caesarea ad Libanum / Καισάρεια ἡ ἐν τῷ Λιβάνῳ (Roman); Colonia Caesarea Libani (Severan); Arqa (Arabic)
cities.site: Tell Arqa, Akkar Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with the Greek legend 'of the Caesareans in the Lebanon', dated year 461 of the Seleucid era (AD 149/150) under Antoninus Pius; the Caesar name implies an earlier Roman (re)foundation.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Mu'awiya c. 636 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the Roman inhabitants largely fled; Christians who stayed came to speak Arabic. Crusaders besieged Arqa in 1099. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Birthplace of Severus Alexander (208); colony under the Severans; bishops in the 5th-6th c.; Hierocles (Phoenice); Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan with Mu'awiya, c. 636; most Roman inhabitants fled (al-Baladhuri).
cities.refounded_by: renamed Caesarea under Roman rule (date unknown); colonia under Elagabalus or Severus Alexander
cities.other_language: Aramaic/Phoenician (the native town of the Ituraean period)
cities.bilingual_evidence: An Ituraean-ruled native town in the 1st c. BC; Greek civic coinage only from the Roman period.
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Antoninus Pius on); Roman colony; bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Earlier coins may exist; the first Greek civic evidence could be older than AD 149.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Leucas / Claudia Leucas (Roman coins); Bulunyas, Baniyas (Arabic); Valania (Crusader)
cities.site: Baniyas, Tartus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: First city coins with the Greek legend ΒΑΛΑΝΕΩΤΩΝ, dated year 1 (37/36 BC) under Mark Antony (RPC I 4456); later issues under Augustus and, as 'Claudian Leucadians', under Claudius. Strabo (16.2.12) lists Balanaia among the Aradian towns.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit in 637/638; on the emperors' side by the treaty of 969/970 and taken by John Tzimiskes in 975, the seat of a strategos; the date of its loss is not recorded (the Muslims built al-Marqab above it in 1062; probably lost with Gabala c. 1081); held by soldiers from Cyprus c. 1102-1104; Crusader 1109-1188 (the Latin bishop lived at Margat); Saladin 1188. Speech: shift to Arabic by the 9th c.; under the emperors only officials and soldiers are attested. The end is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop at Nicaea 325 and three more to the 6th c.; Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai). Under the emperors (969/975 to c. 1081): the seal of Veken, strategos of Balaneus (DO Seals 5, 15.1); 'the soldiers of Eumathios' from Cyprus, c. 1102-1104 (Anna Komnene XI).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). Later rulers: the emperors in Constantinople, 969/975 to c. 1081; the Crusaders, 1109; Saladin, 1188.
cities.other_language: Phoenician (an Aradian town before the Roman period)
cities.bilingual_evidence: An Aradian dependency (Strabo 16.2.12) before Roman times.
cities.status_evidence: City coins (from 37/36 BC, Mark Antony, to the 1st c. AD; as Claudia Leucas from Claudius); bishop at Nicaea 325 (Euphration); Hierocles (Syria Secunda); Notitia Antiochena; Theodorias 528
cities.note: The coins name the Balaneotai and, from Claudius, the Claudian Leucadians, so Leucas and Balanea are one city (RPC I lists them together). Under the emperors (969/975 to c. 1081) only officials and soldiers are attested, so no second phase is counted (earlier versions of this set had one, 969-1081).
sources: Nesbitt et al., Catalogue of Seals at Dumbarton Oaks 5 (2005), 15.1

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Laodicea in Phoenicia / Λαοδίκεια ἡ ἐν Φοινίκῃ (Seleucid); Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Berytus (Roman); Bayrut (Arabic)
cities.site: Beirut (downtown), Beirut Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Renamed Laodicea in Phoenicia under Antiochus IV; its city coins with Greek and Phoenician legends date from 175-164 BC; Berytian merchants formed a Greek-speaking association (the Poseidoniasts) on Delos in the 2nd c. BC.
cities.until_text: Administration: the earthquake of 551 and the fire of 560 ruined the city and its law school moved to Sidon; Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Mu'awiya took it c. 636 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: most Roman inhabitants fled; the Christians who stayed shifted to Arabic. John Tzimiskes held the town briefly in 975. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Law school teaching in Greek in the 5th-6th c.; bishops from the 4th c.; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena (metropolis after 451); the 551 earthquake (Malalas, Agathias); Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Destroyed by Diodotus Tryphon, c. 140 BC (Strabo 16.2.19); refounded by Agrippa as a colony, 15/14 BC; ruined by the earthquake of 551; taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan with Mu'awiya, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri).
cities.founder: Antiochus IV (renaming); Augustus and Agrippa (colonia, 15/14 BC)
cities.refounded_by: Agrippa for Augustus, colonia with veterans of legions V Macedonica and VIII Augusta, 15/14 BC
cities.other_language: Phoenician (Hellenistic period); Latin (the Roman colony, 1st-3rd c. AD)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Seleucid coins of Laodicea in Phoenicia with Greek and Phoenician legends; the Roman colony used Latin in its public life and law school until Greek took over in the 4th-5th c.
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid city coins; Roman colony; law school; bishops from 325; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: The Roman colony of 15/14 BC is the same site and keeps one entry; Latin was the language of the colony's public life for about three centuries while Greek remained the language of much of the population.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Batroun, North Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with the Greek legend ΒΟΤΡΥΗΝΩΝ dated year 28 (37/36 BC) of a civic era starting 64/63 BC, the year of Pompey's settlement (RPC I 4523).
cities.until_text: Administration: the town was badly hit by the earthquake of 551 (a landslide at Theouprosopon blocked the harbour) and passed to the Arabs with the Lebanese coast, c. 636. Speech: gradual shift to Arabic. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: City coins to the 3rd c.; bishops in the 5th-6th c.; Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena; the 551 earthquake (Malalas, Agathias); Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: No named act recorded for Botrys itself: it passed to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Mu'awiya with the neighbouring coast, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Phoenician town founded by Ithobaal of Tyre (Menander in Josephus, AJ 8.324); Greek civic coins only from the 1st c. BC.
cities.status_evidence: City coins (37/36 BC to the 3rd c. AD); bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Botrys was founded as a Phoenician town by Ithobaal I of Tyre (Menander in Josephus, AJ 8.324).

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Jbeil, Keserwan-Jbeil Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Municipal coins of Antiochus IV (175-164 BC) with Greek and Phoenician legends; Greek inscriptions follow; Philo of Byblos wrote in Greek in the late 1st-2nd c. AD.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Mu'awiya c. 636 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the Roman elite fled; the Christians who stayed shifted to Arabic by the 9th c. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Philo of Byblos (c. 64-141); city coins to the 3rd c.; bishops from the 4th c.; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena; damaged in 551; Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan with Mu'awiya, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri).
cities.pre_greek_name: Gubla (Phoenician gbl; Akkadian Gubla; Hebrew Bible Gebal)
cities.other_language: Phoenician (until about the 1st c. BC/1st c. AD)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Municipal coins of Antiochus IV with Greek and Phoenician legends ('of holy Byblos' / lgbl qdšt); Phoenician inscriptions into the late Hellenistic period.
cities.status_evidence: Municipal coins of Antiochus IV; city coins of the Roman period; Philo of Byblos; bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Jableh (Roman theatre), Latakia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The city counted a civic era from 47/46 BC (Caesar's grant of autonomy); its city coins with the Greek legend ΓΑΒΑΛΕΩΝ are dated by that era from year 16 (31/30 BC; RPC I 4449) and continue under Augustus (e.g. AD 13/14, RPC I 4452).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit in 637/638 (Mu'awiya built a new fort beside the Roman town); ruled from Constantinople from 968 (Yaqut) and the seat of a strategos ('Zebel') from 975 until 1080/81, when the qadi Ibn Sulayha expelled the Romans with the help of the Banu Ammar of Tripoli; Crusader from 23 July 1109 (Tancred with the Genoese); Saladin 1188. Speech: the Greek-speaking population shifted to Arabic by the 9th c. Under the emperors the only Greek speakers recorded are the officials and the garrison, the 'Rum' who left for Tripoli in 1080/81 (Yaqut); the townspeople were Muslims with their own qadi and Arabic-speaking Orthodox, and a local Arab, Abdellas, was the imperial judge. The end is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Severian of Gabala, Greek preacher and bishop (fl. c. 400); bishops to the 6th c.; Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai). Under the emperors (968/975-1080/81): the seal of the strategos Eustratios Botaneiates (DO Seals 5, 13.1); Abdellas, judge of Zebel; the qadi Mansur, 'ra'is Jabala', and his son Ibn Sulayha (Sato 1991); 'those of the Rum who were in it moved to Tripoli' (Yaqut, s.v. Jabala, 473 AH).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). Later rulers: the emperors in Constantinople, 968-1080/81 (expelled by the qadi Ibn Sulayha with the Banu Ammar of Tripoli); Tancred, 1109; Saladin, 1188.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Bronze and Iron Age town of Gibʿala is usually placed at Tell Tweini, 1.5 km from the Roman town.
cities.other_language: Phoenician/Aramaic (the native town of the Aradian coast, before the Roman period)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A native coastal town in the Aradian sphere before the Roman period; no Greek civic evidence before the 1st c. BC.
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Augustus to the 3rd c.); Roman theatre; bishop Severian (c. 400); Hierocles (Syria Prima); Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Under the emperors (968/975-1080/81) Gabala was the seat of a strategos, but the only Greek speakers attested there are officials and the garrison, so no second phase is counted (earlier versions of this set had one, 969-1081).
sources: Nesbitt et al., Catalogue of Seals at Dumbarton Oaks 5 (2005), 13.1
Sato, 'Qadis in the Syrian Coastal Towns of Tripoli and Jabala', Bulletin of the Society for Near Eastern Studies in Japan 34.2 (1991)

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Ras Ibn Hani, north of Latakia, Latakia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A new fortified Hellenistic town was laid out on the cape in the mid-3rd c. BC, probably by Ptolemy III in the Third Syrian War (246-241 BC; large finds of Ptolemaic bronzes); civic weights of the 'Herakleotai by the sea' are dated 108/107 and 103/102 BC.
cities.until_text: The Hellenistic town on the cape shrank in the late Hellenistic period; Strabo (16.2.12) still lists Heraclea near Laodicea, but no later civic evidence is known. Laodicea absorbed the area.
cities.fade_evidence: Civic weights dated 108/107 and 103/102 BC (legend ΗΡΑΚΛΕΩΤΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΘΑΛΑΣΣΗΙ); Strabo 16.2.12 (c. AD 20).
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town faded into the territory of Laodicea; the date is uncertain.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Late Bronze Age palace town on the cape belonged to Ugarit; the Ugaritic/Akkadian name is not securely identified.
cities.status_evidence: Civic lead weights with the ethnic of the Herakleotai by the sea (SE 205 and 210); Strabo 16.2.12; Hellenistic town plan at Ras Ibn Hani
cities.note: The identification of Heraclea with Ras Ibn Hani is the usual one but not certain. The founder is inferred from coin finds; Seleucid foundation is also possible.
sources: Bounni and Lagarce, Ras Ibn Hani

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Laodicea in Syria; Iulia Laodicea (after 47 BC); Septimia Aurelia Laodicea (colonia, AD 198); al-Ladhiqiyya (Arabic); La Liche (Crusader)
cities.site: Latakia (old city), Latakia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Seleucus I c. 300 BC as one of the four cities of the Syrian tetrapolis and named after his mother Laodice (Strabo 16.2.4; Appian, Syr. 57).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit for Abu Ubayda, c. 637; ruled again from Constantinople from 968/970 to c. 1082, when the Banu Munqidh held it; Seljuk from 1086/87; held by imperial garrisons in 1099-1103 and 1104-1108; Principality of Antioch to 1188; Saladin 1188; Mamluks 1287. Speech: the Greek-speaking city lost its elite at the conquest and its Christians shifted to Arabic by the 9th c. Under the emperors Laodicea had governors, garrisons and a metropolitan with a Greek seal, but no resident Greek-speaking community is recorded: Ibn Butlan (c. 1050) describes Muslims with their own qadi and Friday mosque beside Orthodox Christians ('Rum') who rang their bells against the call to prayer, and the only Greek speakers he mentions are 'strangers from the Rum' lodging in the port's inns. The end is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai). Under the emperors (968/970 to c. 1082): governors, garrisons, the Muslim townspeople deported in 992 after a revolt, and the seal of Theodore, metropolitan of 'Laodikeia the Great' (DO Seals 5, 12.1); Ibn Butlan's letter of c. 1050 (Yaqut, s.v. al-Ladhiqiyya). The Antiochene Melkites read Arabic: 'Abdallah ibn al-Fadl translated the Greek Fathers for them (c. 1050).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, c. 637 (al-Baladhuri). Later rulers: the emperors in Constantinople, 968/970 to c. 1082; the Banu Munqidh; the Seljuks, 1086/87; the Principality of Antioch, 1108-1188; Saladin, 23 July 1188; the Mamluk sultan Qalawun, 20 April 1287.
cities.refounded_by: Julius Caesar (Iulia, 47 BC); Septimius Severus (colonia, 198); Justinian (metropolis of Theodorias, 528)
cities.pre_greek_note: Greek writers give the earlier names Ramitha and Leuke Akte (Philo of Byblos in Stephanus); Pleiades also lists Mazabda. No securely identified name in a non-Greek source.
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid foundation; city coins with Greek legends from the 2nd c. BC; bishop at Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Syria Prima); Notitia Antiochena (metropolis of Theodorias)
cities.note: Ruled again from Constantinople c. 968-1082, and held by imperial garrisons in 1099-1103 and 1104-1108, Laodicea had governors, soldiers and a metropolitan with a Greek seal, but no source shows a resident Greek-speaking community, so no second phase is counted (earlier versions of this set had one, 970-1086).
sources: Yaqut, Mu'jam al-buldan, s.v. al-Ladhiqiyya (Ibn Butlan's letter, c. 1050)
Nesbitt et al., Catalogue of Seals at Dumbarton Oaks 5 (2005), 12.1
Holmes, Basil II and the Governance of Empire (2005)
Anna Komnene, Alexiad XI and XIII

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Amrit, south of Tartus, Tartus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Civic tetradrachms with the Greek legend ΜΑΡΑΘΗΝΩΝ dated year 37 of the city's era (223/222 BC), with a Semitic numeral; the civic era began in 259 BC, as at Aradus.
cities.until_text: Destroyed by its rival Aradus in the reign of Alexander Balas (c. 148 BC); Strabo (16.2.12) says it lay in ruins and the Aradians had divided its land.
cities.fade_evidence: Diodorus 33.5 (the Aradians kill the Marathene envoys and plan to take the city); Strabo 16.2.12.
cities.ended_by: Destroyed by the Aradians, c. 148 BC (Diodorus 33.5; Strabo 16.2.12).
cities.pre_greek_note: The Phoenician name is assumed to survive in Amrit, but no secure pre-Greek attestation is known to me.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Civic coins of the late 3rd and early 2nd c. BC with the Greek legend ΜΑΡΑΘΗΝΩΝ and Semitic (Phoenician/Aramaic) numerals; the city sent envoys to the Seleucid king (Diodorus 33.5).
cities.status_evidence: Civic coins with Greek legends; Diodorus 33.5; Strabo 16.2.12; temple of Amrit (Persian period)
cities.note: Marathus was a Phoenician town with Greek civic coinage for about 70 years; Greek speech among its citizens is likely but its extent is uncertain.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Ard Artousi, by the mouth of the Nahr al-Bared, North Governorate (Minieh-Danniyeh)
cities.greek_from_text: Civic bronze coins with the Greek city name, late 2nd or early 1st c. BC (BMC Phoenicia 136-137; SNG Copenhagen), assigned by some to the reigns of Antiochus VIII and IX; the town existed by 138 BC, when Tryphon fled there (1 Macc 15:37); later civic coins are dated by the Pompeian era (RPC I 4503, 29/28 BC).
cities.until_text: The earthquake and tsunami of 9 July 551 destroyed the Roman town; the see is still recorded in 553, but the town then vanishes from the record. Speech ended with the town, before or at the Arab conquest of the Tripolis coast.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops Phosphorus (451), Nilus (536) and Stephen (553); city coins to Elagabalus; remains exposed in 2007 at the Nahr al-Bared camp.
cities.ended_by: No named act: destroyed by the earthquake and tsunami of 551; any survivors came under the Arabs with the Tripolis coast, c. 636-644.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Bronze Age port of Ullaza is often linked with Orthosias, but the identification is not secure.
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid and Roman city coins; 1 Macc 15:37; Strabo 16.2.12; Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena; bishops 451-553
cities.note: The Greek name (after Artemis Orthosia) and the civic coins show a Greek town. No founder, settlers or new layout are attested, so it is counted as a Greek town grown into a city. The local name Ard Artousi continues Orthosia.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Arab al-Mulk (Balda), south of Jableh, Latakia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Strabo (16.2.12) lists Paltos as a town of the Aradian coast; the first positive Greek civic evidence is the city coinage with the legend ΠΑΛΤΗΝΩΝ under Severus Alexander (222-235); bishops follow from the 4th c.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit in 637/638 (al-Baladhuri names Balda); the see survived in the Notitia of Anastasius and in the 10th c. Speech: no evidence for Greek-speaking residents after the conquest; the Christians shifted to Arabic. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops: Cymatius (4th c.), Severus 381, Sabbas 451, John 518; autocephalous see under Antioch in the Notitia of Anastasius (c. 570) and still in the 10th c. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Ubada ibn al-Samit, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri); no later named act.
cities.other_language: Phoenician (an Aradian town before the Roman period)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Founded from Aradus (Strabo 16.2.12); no Greek civic evidence before the Roman period.
cities.status_evidence: City coins of Severus Alexander (RPC VI); bishops 4th c. to 518; Hierocles (Syria Prima); Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Greek speech is surely older than the first city coins, but no earlier civic Greek evidence is known. Paltos was founded by Aradus as a Phoenician town.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Paneion (the sanctuary of Pan); Neronias (under Agrippa II); Caesarea Paneas; Baniyas (Arabic)
cities.site: Banias, Golan Heights
cities.admin1: Golan Heights (Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967)
cities.greek_from_text: Philip the Tetrarch founded the city of Caesarea at the spring and sanctuary of Pan, 3/2 BC (city era of 3 BC; Josephus AJ 18.28); the Greek sanctuary of Pan existed from the 3rd century BC (battle of Panion, 200 BC)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs in 635-636 with the Damascus region. Speech: no evidence for a Greek-speaking community after the conquest; the medieval town of Baniyas was Arabic-speaking. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: City coins from Philip to Elagabalus; the statue said to show Christ and the woman healed of bleeding (Eusebius HE 7.18), removed under Julian (Sozomen); bishops to the 6th century. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town passed to the Arabs in the conquest of 635-636; no later Greek evidence.
cities.pre_greek_note: The identification with biblical Baal-gad or Baal-hermon is speculative.
cities.status_evidence: City coins with Greek legends (Philip to Elagabalus); Josephus AJ 18.28, BJ 2.168; bishop at Nicaea 325; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena (under Tyre)
cities.note: The site is in the Golan Heights, at the foot of Mount Hermon. Herod built a temple of Augustus at the Paneion in 20 BC before Philip founded the city.
sources: Wilson, Caesarea Philippi: Banias, the Lost City of Pan (2004)

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Jiyeh, Chouf District, Mount Lebanon Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: First attested as a bishop's see: bishop Thomas at Chalcedon, 451; the town at Jiyeh had a large church of the 4th-5th c.
cities.until_text: The see appears in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570) but not in the 10th-c. list. The town at Jiyeh was abandoned in the second half of the 7th c., without a destruction layer (Polish-Lebanese excavations).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops Thomas (451), Alexander (late 5th c.), Theodore (518), Christophorus (536), Paul (late 6th c.) (Le Quien); 7th-c. coins and pottery are the last at Jiyeh.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town was left in the later 7th c., after the Arab conquest of the coast (c. 636).
cities.status_evidence: Bishops 451-6th c.; Notitia Antiochena (suffragan of Tyre); Polybius 5.69 (the place, 218 BC)
cities.note: Le Quien placed the see at Haifa, which some still follow; most now place it at Jiyeh, north of Sidon. The town grew from a Phoenician and Hellenistic settlement.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Ras al-Bassit, Latakia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Archaeology places the Greek settlement in the 7th c. BC (Courbin's excavations, with Greek pottery from the late 8th c.); Herodotus 3.91 calls Posideion a polis on the Cilician-Syrian border.
cities.until_text: The town was destroyed in the 5th or 4th c. BC and rebuilt with a fortified acropolis under Seleucus I after 312 BC; it thrived in the late Roman period (larger harbour, villas, a 6th-c. church complex). The site was largely abandoned after the Arab conquest of the 630s; a Crusader chapel of the 12th-13th c. and later Venetian shipping do not show a continuing Greek town.
cities.fade_evidence: Hellenistic, Roman and late Roman levels at Ras al-Bassit (Courbin); 6th-c. church complex; abandonment after the 630s.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the coast north of Laodicea passed to the Arabs in the campaign of Ubada ibn al-Samit for Abu Ubayda, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri names Laodicea and Gabala, not Posideion); the town was then largely abandoned.
cities.founder: Greek traders (legend: Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus, Hdt. 3.91)
cities.status_evidence: Herodotus 3.91 (polis); Greek pottery and houses from the 8th-6th c. BC; Strabo 16.2.12
cities.note: Herodotus names the hero Amphilochus as founder; this is legend. The mother city is unknown; the first Greeks were probably Euboean and East Greek traders, as at Al Mina. Whether the early Greek presence was a self-governing polis or a trading community in a native town is debated, and some doubt that Herodotus' Posideion is Ras al-Bassit.
sources: Courbin, Fouilles de Ras el Bassit

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Ake (Greek); Antiochia Ptolemais (Seleucid coins, 2nd c. BC); Colonia Claudii Caesaris Ptolemais (Claudius); Akka (Arabic); Acre, Saint-Jean d'Acre (Crusader)
cities.site: Tel Akko (Tell el-Fukhkhar) and the Old City of Akko, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Ptolemy II refounded Phoenician Akko as Ptolemais in the 260s BC; the Zenon papyri of 259 BC already use the new name
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended when the Arab armies took the coast, c. 636-638. Speech: the Greek-speaking élite of the coastal cities left or was replaced; Baladhuri says Mu'awiya settled Muslims, including Persians, in the coastal towns of al-Urdunn and built a shipyard at Akka. No Greek-speaking community is attested here after the 7th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops of Ptolemais to the 6th c.; Mu'awiya's resettlement and naval base (Baladhuri); later Christians of Akka are Arabic-speaking Melkites
cities.ended_by: Taken by the Arab armies, c. 636-638; Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan resettled the coastal towns with Muslims and made Akka a naval base (Baladhuri)
cities.refounded_by: Antiochus IV (Antiochia Ptolemais, c. 170 BC); Claudius (Roman colonia, AD 51-54)
cities.pre_greek_name: ʿAkko (Phoenician; Hebrew Bible, Judges 1:31); Akkû (Akkadian); ʿk (Egyptian)
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemaic refoundation; Greek civic coins (Seleucid and Roman); Roman colonia; bishops from the 2nd c.; Aeneas at Nicaea 325
cities.note: The Hellenistic city spread from the old tell to the peninsula, a new layout, which is why it is counted as a royal foundation. Greek mercenaries gathered here for the Persian campaigns against Egypt in the 4th c. BC, before the Greek city.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.site: Ras al-Qantara by Sarafand, South Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a see under Tyre in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570); the Piacenza pilgrim (c. 570) calls it a small and very Christian town. Greek-speaking Sareptans are attested abroad from the 1st c. AD, but the town was then a dependency of Sidon.
cities.until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs with Sidon, c. 636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Notitia Antiochena and the Piacenza pilgrim (c. 570) are the last evidence of the Christian town before the conquest. Regional markers: Greek stayed in the caliphate's registers until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the dated Greek inscriptions of Syria nearly stop in the early 7th c.; the Melkites of Syria wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra).
cities.ended_by: No named act: it passed to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and Mu'awiya with Sidon, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri).
cities.pre_greek_name: Ṣarepta (Phoenician ṣrpt; Akkadian Ṣariptu; Hebrew Bible Ṣārǝpat)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Phoenician town of the territory of Sidon; Sareptans abroad wrote Greek (their dedication to the 'Holy God' of Sarepta at Puteoli, AD 79); a see of the Greek-speaking church c. 570.
cities.status_evidence: A see under Tyre in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570); no bishop is known by name (Latin titular bishops only from the 14th c.). The Madaba map calls the place 'the long village' (Makra Kome); the Piacenza pilgrim calls it a small town.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see rests on the Notitia Antiochena alone and may have been short-lived; Sareptans who wrote Greek are known only abroad (Puteoli, AD 79).

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Colonia Aurelia Pia Sidon (Elagabalus); Ṣayda (Arabic); Sagette (Crusader)
cities.site: Saida, South Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The Greek epigram for the Sidonian Diotimos, victor in the chariot race at Nemea, set up in Sidon c. 200 BC, speaks for a Greek-speaking civic elite; municipal coins of Antiochus IV with the Greek legend ΣΙΔΩΝΙΩΝ follow (175-164 BC).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan with Mu'awiya, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: most Roman inhabitants fled; the Christians who stayed shifted to Arabic by the 9th c. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop at Nicaea 325; the Berytus law school moved here after 551; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena; Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan with Mu'awiya, c. 636 (al-Baladhuri).
cities.pre_greek_name: Ṣīdūn (Phoenician ṣdn; Akkadian Ṣiduna; Hebrew Bible Ṣīdōn)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Phoenician and Greek on the civic coins of the 2nd-1st c. BC; Greek-Phoenician bilingual inscriptions; Sidonians abroad wrote both.
cities.status_evidence: Diotimos inscription; civic coins from Antiochus IV; era of autonomy 111 BC; Roman colony; bishops from 325; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Greek was spoken at the royal court of Sidon from the 4th c. BC (the 'philhellene' king Abdashtart I); that alone does not date the city's Greek community.
sources: Bickerman, Sur une inscription grecque de Sidon (Diotimos)

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Tripolis of Phoenicia; Ṭarābulus al-Sham (Arabic); Tripoli
cities.site: Tripoli (al-Mina peninsula), North Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Civic coinage with the Greek legend ΤΡΙΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ from 112/111 BC; autonomy from Antiochus IX (c. 105/104 BC), with tetradrachms inscribed ΤΡΙΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΤΗΣ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΥΤΟΝΟΜΟΥ. The Phoenician joint settlement existed by the 4th c. BC (Diodorus 16.41 for 351 BC).
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: Mu'awiya's general Sufyan ibn Mujib al-Azdi besieged the town and its Roman inhabitants escaped by sea in imperial ships; Mu'awiya settled Jews and later garrisons there (al-Baladhuri). Christians who stayed came to speak Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Hellanicus at Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Phoenice); Notitia Antiochena; damaged in the 551 earthquake; the flight by sea at the conquest (al-Baladhuri).
cities.ended_by: Besieged by Sufyan ibn Mujib al-Azdi for Mu'awiya; the inhabitants fled by sea in imperial ships, and under Uthman (644-656) Mu'awiya settled Jews there (al-Baladhuri). Other accounts date the conquest to 635.
cities.pre_greek_note: A Phoenician name Athar is often given in modern works, but I know no secure ancient attestation; the Greek name describes its three quarters.
cities.bilingual_evidence: The federal town of Aradus, Sidon and Tyre (Diodorus 16.41; Strabo 16.2.15); Phoenician the language of its founders; Greek on the civic coinage from 112/111 BC.
cities.status_evidence: Civic coins (from 112/111 BC; autonomy under Antiochus IX, c. 105/104 BC; Pompeian era 64/63 BC; Roman city coins to the 3rd c. AD); bishop at Nicaea 325; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: The date of the Arab conquest of Tripolis is given variously between 636 and the 640s. Tripolis began as a joint Phoenician settlement of Aradus, Sidon and Tyre (Diodorus 16.41).

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Tyrus; Colonia Septimia Severa Tyrus (Septimius Severus); Ṣur (Arabic); Sur
cities.site: Sour (al-Mina and al-Bass), South Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Municipal coins of Antiochus IV (175-164 BC) with Greek and Phoenician legends; a Greek decree of the association of Tyrian Herakleistai, merchants and shipowners, on Delos, c. 150 BC (I.Délos 1519); Greek writers from Tyre follow (Antipater of Tyre, Stoic, 1st c. BC).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs c. 636-640; Mu'awiya settled Persian and other Muslim garrisons in Tyre and the coast towns (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the Greek-speaking elite emigrated; the Christians who stayed shifted to Arabic by the 9th c. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek writers (Antipater, Maximus, Porphyry, Marinus); metropolitan see of Phoenice; Greek tomb inscriptions of al-Bass to the 6th-7th c.; Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Taken by the army of Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, c. 636-640; Mu'awiya resettled the coast towns (al-Baladhuri).
cities.refounded_by: Septimius Severus (colonia, c. 198); Alexander's siege and resettlement, 332 BC
cities.pre_greek_name: Ṣur (Phoenician ṣr; Akkadian Ṣurru; Hebrew Bible Ṣōr)
cities.other_language: Phoenician (until about the 1st c. BC/1st c. AD)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Civic coins with Greek and Phoenician legends ('of the Tyrians' / lṣr) under Antiochus IV and after autonomy (126/125 BC); Tyrian Heracleists on Delos wrote Greek (153 BC).
cities.status_evidence: Civic coins from Antiochus IV; era of autonomy 126/125 BC; Greek writers; Roman colony; metropolitan see; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Alexander took Tyre in 332 BC and sold or killed much of its population, but the city was resettled and stayed Phoenician-speaking for at least another century.

cities.list_group: Phoenicia and the north Syrian coast
cities.other_names: Rachlea, Raclea (Notitia Antiochena, see under Tyre); Rakhlah (Arabic)
cities.site: Rakhlah, Qatana District, Rif Dimashq Governorate (eastern slope of Mount Hermon)
cities.greek_from_text: First attested as a city in 518, when its bishop Elias signed the synodal letter of the council of Tyre as 'bishop of Zenopolis'. The name implies that the village was raised to city rank under the emperor Zeno (474-491).
cities.until_text: Administration: the Hermon district fell to the Arab armies with Damascus in 634-636.
