Speech: the town has no evidence of its own after its bishop Anastasius at Constantinople in 553, so its end follows the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800), not a dated event.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek sanctuary inscriptions to 379; bishop Elias of Zenopolis, 518; bishop Anastasius at the council of Constantinople, 553
cities.ended_by: No named act: the area was taken with Damascus by the Arab armies in 634-636; no later evidence from the town.
cities.founder: Zeno (city rank and the name Zenopolis, inferred from the name)
cities.pre_greek_note: The modern name continues Rachlea of the Notitia Antiochena, probably a Semitic name, but it is not attested in a non-Greek source.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the village sanctuary of Leucothea, written by and for its officials and treasurers, from AD 60 to 379 (a building of 253, a new door of 379); a native mountain cult of the Hermon villages
cities.status_evidence: Bishop Elias 'of Zenopolis' at the council of Tyre, 518; bishop Anastasius at Constantinople, 553; see Rachlea under Tyre in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570); identification: Aliquot, IGLS XI, pp. 18-19
cities.note: The identification of Rachlea/Zenopolis with Rakhlah rests on the name and is accepted by Aliquot and, with a query, by the Barrington Atlas; Marakya has also been proposed. The temple inscriptions show a Greek-writing village community centuries before it became a city.

cities.other_names: Theodoroupolis/Theodorias (6th c., after the empress Theodora); Khunasira (Arabic)
cities.site: Khanasir, al-Safira District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: a see of Syria Prima with Greek building and dedicatory inscriptions of residents, 5th c.
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of northern Syria, 637. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of northern Syria by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah and Khalid ibn al-Walid, 637.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek dedications and building inscriptions of residents (5th-6th c.); the Greek-Syriac-Arabic inscription of nearby Zebed (512) shows the mixed milieu
cities.status_evidence: see of Syria Prima; Hierocles; Greek inscriptions (IGLS II)

cities.other_names: Emar (Akkadian, the Bronze Age city on the same site); Balis (Arabic); Barbalissos (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription)
cities.site: Maskanah (Meskene), Old Meskene (Balis), on the shore of Lake Assad, Maskanah District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Aquilinus of Barbalissos, exiled c. 431 as a supporter of Nestorius (Greek sources); an Antonius of Barbalissus appears only in the Arabic version of the Nicaea list (325).
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended when the town surrendered on terms to Habib ibn Maslama, c. 637. Speech: the people could stay and pay tax or leave, and most left for Mesopotamia or Hierapolis (al-Baladhuri); Arabs of Qays were settled on the abandoned estates, and the place became Balis. Any Greek speakers who stayed are not attested.
cities.fade_evidence: Most inhabitants emigrated at the surrender, c. 637.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered on terms to Habib ibn Maslama, c. 637; most inhabitants chose to leave for Mesopotamia or Hierapolis, and Qays tribesmen were settled on their estates (al-Baladhuri). Earlier Shapur I defeated a Roman army here, c. 253 (Shapur I's inscription); Justinian refortified it (Procopius, Buildings 2.9).
cities.pre_greek_note: Bronze Age Emar lies under the same site; it was destroyed c. 1185 BC and the link to the later town is not continuous.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see of Euphratensis with Greek-signing bishops; otherwise Aramaic-speaking
cities.status_evidence: See of Augusta Euphratensis under Hierapolis (Notitia Antiochena): bishops Aquilinus (c. 431) and Marinianus (5th c., in Theodoret), later Jacobite bishops (Michael the Syrian); a city of Euphratensis in Hierocles; the town is in Ptolemy (2nd c.).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Greek is otherwise attested only through bishops and the garrison (Dalmatian cavalry).

cities.site: Aleppo city (old city and citadel), Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucus I refounded Halab as Beroea, named after Macedonian Beroea, c. 300 BC, with a new street grid
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah and Khalid ibn al-Walid in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek bishops and writers (Acacius of Beroea, bishop 378-437). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah and Khalid ibn al-Walid, 637 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier burned by Khosrow I, 540, while the citadel held out (Procopius, Wars 2.7); taken by Khosrow II's army, c. 611. No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.bilingual_evidence: the old name Halab stayed in use; Syriac-speaking Christians and bilingual clergy in the 4th-6th c.
cities.status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; city coins; see of Syria Prima; Hierocles

cities.other_names: Flavia Chalcis (Roman city coins); Qenneshrin (Syriac); Qinnasrin (Arabic)
cities.site: Tell Qinnasrin and al-Hadir, south of Aleppo, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: listed by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities Seleucus I named after Greek and Macedonian places; named after Chalcis in Euboea, c. 300 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with Khalid ibn al-Walid's capture of the city in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. Qinnasrin became the capital of an Arab jund and later declined. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Taken by Khalid ibn al-Walid after his victory at Hazir, 637 (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari). Earlier Khosrow I extracted a ransom from it, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.12).
cities.status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; Pliny NH 5.81; Ptolemy; see of Syria Prima; Hierocles
cities.note: The 'Flavia Chalcis' city coins of the 1st-2nd c. may belong to this Chalcis or to Chalcis under Lebanon. The philosopher Iamblichus came from a Chalcis in Syria, probably this one.

cities.other_names: Krksy' (Parthian, Shapur I's inscription); Qerqesin (Syriac); Qarqisiya (Arabic)
cities.site: al-Busayrah, at the Khabur-Euphrates confluence, Deir ez-Zor Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Abrahamius of Circesium at the Council of Chalcedon, 451.
cities.until_text: Administration: surrendered to Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri, sent by Iyad ibn Ghanm, c. 640. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered without a fight to Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri, sent by Iyad ibn Ghanm, c. 640 (some sources 637).
cities.pre_greek_note: The earlier posts Phaliga and Nabagath lay nearby; no pre-Greek name of the site is secure.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a fortress town with a see whose bishops signed in Greek (from 451); otherwise Syriac-speaking
cities.status_evidence: See of Osrhoene under Edessa: bishops Abrahamius (Chalcedon 451; letter of 458), Nonnus (expelled 518), Davithas (536) and Thomas (553), then Jacobite bishops to the 11th c. (Michael the Syrian); Ammianus 23.5.1; Procopius, Buildings 2.6.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A fortress town; Greek is otherwise attested only through the garrison and the clergy. The Romans may have retaken it after 640; it was firmly Umayyad from 'Abd al-Malik's time (c. 690).

cities.other_names: Hagioupolis (late antique, after Saints Cosmas and Damian); Qurus (Arabic); Corice (Crusader)
cities.site: Nebi Huri, Afrin District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucus I founded it c. 300 BC and named it after Cyrrhus in Macedonia
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The city declined to a small town. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Theodoret of Cyrrhus wrote in Greek in the 5th c.; Justinian restored the walls (Procopius, Buildings 2.11). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army, 637 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier taken by Shapur I, c. 253 (Shapur I's inscription). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Theodoret (bishop 423-c. 460) describes a Syriac-speaking countryside and monks; the city itself wrote Greek
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.8; Tacitus Ann. 2.57 (legionary base); city coins; see (Theodoret); Hierocles
cities.note: The ruins lie in Syria, a few km south of the Turkish border.

cities.other_names: Dawsar (Arabic); Qal'at Ja'bar (Arabic, later name of the castle)
cities.site: Qal'at Ja'bar, on Lake Assad, al-Thawrah District, Raqqa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Nonnus of Dausara at the Council of Constantinople, 553.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 639/640. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 639/640.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A fortified place on the Euphrates with a see of the Greek-speaking church in the 6th c.
cities.status_evidence: See of Osrhoene under Edessa in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570); bishop Nonnus at Constantinople 553 (Le Quien; Janin).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Mainly a fortress on the Euphrates; the see is the only sign of a town. The medieval castle of Qal'at Ja'bar stands on the site, now an island in Lake Assad.

cities.other_names: Dura (local name, Isidore of Charax 1); Europos (Macedonian name)
cities.site: Tell al-Salihiyah, Abu Kamal District, Deir ez-Zor Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: founded c. 300 BC by Nicanor for Seleucus I as a Macedonian colony (Isidore of Charax 1); archaeology gives the early 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: Shapur I besieged and took the city in 256/257; its people were deported or scattered and the city was never resettled. Ammianus (23.5.8) passed it deserted in 363.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek parchments and papyri down to 256; the last coins in the siege deposits date to 256.
cities.ended_by: Besieged and taken by Shapur I, 256/257 (siege works and mines excavated); then abandoned. Earlier Parthian conquest, c. 113 BC; Roman from 165.
cities.pre_greek_note: The local name Dura is Semitic ('fortress'); there is no clear earlier town on the site.
cities.other_language: Aramaic (local, Palmyrene, Jewish), also Safaitic Arabic, Middle Persian and Latin
cities.bilingual_evidence: in the Parthian and Roman periods Semitic names and Aramaic and Palmyrene inscriptions, the synagogue's Aramaic texts; Greek stayed the language of contracts, most inscriptions and papyri
cities.status_evidence: Isidore of Charax 1; Greek civic institutions (strategos, epistates) in the parchments and papyri; excavated Hippodamian city
cities.note: Greek city with a long bilingual Parthian and Roman phase; Greek remained dominant in its documents.

cities.site: al-Jabbul, by the salt lake Sabkhat al-Jabbul, al-Safira District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Bassones of Gabbula at the Council of Nicaea, 325.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of northern Syria under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of northern Syria under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637.
cities.pre_greek_note: Assyrian texts name a Gabbulu in north Syria; the identification with Jabbul is plausible, not certain.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see whose bishops signed in Greek (Nicaea 325; 458); otherwise an Aramaic-speaking district
cities.status_evidence: See of Syria I: bishop Bassones at Nicaea 325; a bishop in the letter of 458; Ptolemy 5.15.17.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The district around the salt lake of Jabbul spoke Aramaic.

cities.site: Jindires (the tell in the town), Afrin District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Peter of Gindarus at the Council of Nicaea, 325, and at the council of Antioch, 341.
cities.until_text: Administration: the see had lapsed by the 6th c.; taken in the conquest of northern Syria, 637. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Its see is last attested in 341; in the 6th c. it had only a periodeutes. Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of northern Syria under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of the Greek-speaking church in 325-341 in the Aramaic-speaking district of Cyrrhestice.
cities.status_evidence: A town in Strabo (16.2.8, 'acropolis of Cyrrhestice'), Ptolemy and Stephanus ('a small town near Antioch'); a see with bishop Peter at Nicaea 325 and Antioch 341; under Theodosius I a small village that he fortified, with only a periodeutes under Justinian; absent from Hierocles and the Notitia Antiochena (Catholic Encyclopedia: Gindarus).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see was short-lived: by the 6th c. Gindarus was a large village. Before the province of Euphratensis was created its bishop signed among those of Coele Syria.
sources: Wikipedia: List of attendees of the First Council of Nicaea

cities.other_names: Bambyce (Βαμβύκη); Mabbog (Aramaic; Syriac Mabbug); Nappigu (Assyrian); Manbij (Arabic); Manbuk (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription)
cities.site: Manbij, Manbij District, Aleppo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: the Aramaic temple town became the polis Hierapolis under the Seleucids; Seleucid bronzes struck there from Antiochus IV (175-164 BC), later Greek city coins
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the city's surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: By the 5th-6th c. the city's church leaders (Philoxenus) wrote in Syriac. Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army, 637 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier Khosrow I extracted a ransom of 2,000 pounds of silver, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.6); taken by Shapur I, c. 253 (Shapur I's inscription). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Assyrian Nappigu is usually identified with Manbij.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Aramaic coin legends of the priest-kings (4th c. BC), the native cult of Atargatis (Lucian, De Dea Syria); Greek city coins and inscriptions; Syriac writers (Philoxenus of Mabbug, bishop 485-519)
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 16.1.27; Lucian, De Dea Syria; city coins; metropolis of Augusta Euphratensis; Hierocles
cities.note: The date of the first Greek coinage is not certain; a Seleucid date is generally accepted.

cities.site: on the Balikh, Raqqa Governorate (perhaps at or near Tell Hammam et-Turkman)
cities.greek_from_text: 'Ichnai, a Greek city, founded by Macedonians' (Isidore of Charax 1); early Seleucid
cities.until_text: Last recorded by Plutarch (Crassus 25, for 53 BC) and Isidore of Charax (c. AD 1); its end is unknown.
cities.fade_evidence: No record after the early Roman period.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the city disappears from the record after c. AD 1.
cities.status_evidence: Isidore of Charax 1; Plutarch, Crassus 25
cities.note: The site is not securely identified.

cities.site: Dibsi Faraj, on the right bank of the Euphrates east of Maskanah, Aleppo Governorate; the site is now under the waters of Lake Assad (Tabqa Dam)
cities.greek_from_text: Its bishop Paul attended the Council of Nicaea in 325, with both hands crippled in the persecution under Licinius (Theodoret, HE 1.7, who calls Neocaesarea "a fortress on the banks of the Euphrates"); later a see of Augusta Euphratensis in Hierocles
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637/638. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637/638.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see with Greek-signing bishops; Greek inscriptions in the excavated late Roman town at Dibsi Faraj
cities.status_evidence: Bishop Paul at Nicaea 325 (Theodoret HE 1.7); see of Augusta Euphratensis; Hierocles; excavations at Dibsi Faraj (Harper)
cities.note: Dibsi Faraj is usually identified with Athis in the early Roman period and with Neocaesarea later; the identification is probable, not certain. Occupied from the 1st to the 10th century, it was excavated before the dam flooded it. Theodoret calls the place a fortress; it counts as a city by its see.

cities.other_names: Callinicum (after Seleucus II); Leontopolis (Leo I, 466); Qalliniqos (Syriac); al-Raqqa and al-Rafiqa (Arabic)
cities.site: Raqqa city, Raqqa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: 'a Greek city founded by Alexander' (Isidore of Charax 1; Pliny NH 6.119); probably founded under Seleucus I; refounded as Callinicum by Seleucus II (Chronicon Paschale)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639/640; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Syriac dominated in late antiquity; Khosrow I razed the city and enslaved its people in 542. Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Iyad ibn Ghanm, 639/640 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier taken and razed by Khosrow I, who enslaved its people, 542 (Procopius, Wars 2.21). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.founder: Alexander (Isidore, Pliny) or Seleucus I; refounded by Seleucus II
cities.refounded_by: Seleucus II (Callinicum, c. 242 BC); Leo I (Leontopolis, 466); Justinian (walls)
cities.bilingual_evidence: in late antiquity a largely Syriac-speaking town with Syriac monasteries and a Jewish community (synagogue burned in 388)
cities.status_evidence: Isidore of Charax 1; Strabo 16.1.23; see of Osrhoene; Hierocles
cities.note: Cohen doubts Alexander as founder and prefers Seleucus I.

cities.site: al-Taybeh, north-east of Palmyra, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a see under Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Palmyrene, 634-637. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Palmyrene, 634-637.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A town of the Palmyrene in Ptolemy and a fort of the Strata Diocletiana, with a see in the 6th c.
cities.status_evidence: See under the metropolis of Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena ('Orizon'); a town in Ptolemy (Palmyrene); base of a legion (legio IV Scythica) in the Notitia Dignitatum.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Mainly a legionary fortress of the desert frontier; no bishop is known by name. A close call between a fort and a town.

cities.other_names: Resh Aina (Syriac 'head of the spring'); Colonia Rhesaena (Septimius Severus); Theodosiopolis (Theodosius I); Ras al-Ayn (Arabic); Serê Kaniyê (Kurdish)
cities.site: Ras al-Ayn, Hasakah Governorate, on the Turkish border opposite Ceylanpınar
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Antiochus of Resaina at the Council of Nicaea, 325. Theodosius I enlarged the town as Theodosiopolis, c. 380; the 3rd-c. colony coins of Septimius Severus are Latin.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 640 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: Taken, by some accounts by storm, in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 640 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.founder: Theodosius I (Theodosiopolis); earlier a colonia of Septimius Severus
cities.pre_greek_note: Adjacent Tell Fakhariya is Iron Age Sikani (Assyrian-Aramaic bilingual statue); it is a separate mound, so its name is not given as Resaina's.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a Roman colony and then a see with Greek-signing bishops in a Syriac-speaking region; Sergius of Reshaina (d. 536) translated Greek medicine and philosophy into Syriac
cities.status_evidence: See of Osrhoene under Edessa: bishop Antiochus at Nicaea 325 and later bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena; Roman colony (Septimius Severus).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Its people spoke Syriac; its native Sergius of Reshaina (d. 536) wrote in Syriac and translated from Greek. The ruins lie on the Syrian side of the border.

cities.other_names: Rhesapha; Raṣappa (Akkadian); Reṣeph (Hebrew Bible); Anastasiopolis (under Anastasius); Rusafa, Rusafat Hisham (Arabic)
cities.site: Resafa, south of the Euphrates, Raqqa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: the pilgrim town at the shrine of St Sergius got its first bishop shortly after 431 (from John of Antioch); city rank and metropolis under Anastasius (491-518)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest after the Yarmuk, c. 637-639; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town stayed Christian and became the residence of the caliph Hisham (724-743). The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions into the later 6th c. Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest after the Yarmuk, c. 637-639. Earlier Khosrow I extorted its church treasures from bishop Candidus, 542 (Procopius, Wars 2.20).
cities.pre_greek_note: An Assyrian provincial centre; the Roman fort and pilgrim town grew on or near it.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek building and dedicatory inscriptions of the 5th-6th c.; Syriac-speaking clergy and Arab (Ghassanid) patrons of the shrine of St Sergius
cities.status_evidence: see from c. 431; metropolis of Augusta Euphratensis under Anastasius; Procopius, Buildings 2.9
cities.note: Bilingual rather than Greek: a pilgrim town of an Aramaic- and Arabic-speaking region with Greek as the written language.

cities.site: Al-Suriyya, al-Suriyya, near al-Mansura, al-Thawrah District, Raqqa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Uranius of Sura, for whom the metropolitan Stephen signed at Chalcedon, 451; the town was the base of legio XVI Flavia Firma.
cities.until_text: Administration: finally taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637/638. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: Taken and burned by Khosrow I, who enslaved its people, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.5); bishop Candidus of Sergiopolis tried to ransom 12,000 captives. Rebuilt by Justinian (Buildings 2.9). Finally taken in the Arab conquest, 637/638 (no commander recorded for the town).
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see and a city in Procopius' narrative; Aramaic-speaking population
cities.status_evidence: See of Augusta Euphratensis under Hierapolis (Notitia Antiochena): bishops Uranius (451) and Marius (deposed 518); an unnamed bishop in Procopius' account of 540; a city in Hierocles and Procopius (Wars 2.5).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Greek is otherwise attested only through its garrison, officials and bishops.

cities.other_names: Tourmeda (Syrian name, Stephanus of Byzantium); Tiphsah? (Hebrew Bible)
cities.site: an Euphrates crossing in north Syria; not securely located (sites proposed between Jerablus and Raqqa)
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucus I refounded Thapsacus as Amphipolis (Pliny NH 5.87; Stephanus of Byzantium s.v. Amphipolis)
cities.until_text: No record of the city after Pliny; the end of Greek speech there is unknown.
cities.fade_evidence: Last mentioned as Amphipolis by Pliny (1st c. AD).
cities.ended_by: No named act: the city disappears from the record after the 1st c. AD.
cities.pre_greek_note: Tiphsah is commonly equated with Thapsacus, but the identification is not certain; Xenophon (Anab. 1.4.11) knew Thapsacus as a large city.
cities.status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57 (Amphipolis among Seleucus I's cities); Pliny NH 5.87; Stephanus of Byzantium; Cohen 2006
cities.note: The site is unlocated; the coordinates are Pleiades' rough placement.

cities.site: Halabiye, on the right bank of the Euphrates, Deir ez-Zor Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a see under Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637-640. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637-640.
cities.founder: Palmyra (under Zenobia, 3rd c.); rebuilt by Justinian
cities.bilingual_evidence: A walled town of the Euphrates with a see of the Greek-speaking church in the 6th c.
cities.status_evidence: See under the metropolis of Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena; Procopius (Buildings 2.8) calls it a small city, walled anew by Justinian.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A fortified town founded under Palmyra and named after its queen; Greek building inscriptions of Justinian's works belong to the builders. No bishop is known by name.

cities.other_names: Abila of Lysanias; Abilene (the tetrarchy, Luke 3:1)
cities.site: Suq Wadi Barada, Wadi Barada, Rif Dimashq Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek dedication by Nymphaios, freedman of the tetrarch Lysanias, under Tiberius (OGIS 606); the town was the seat of the tetrarchy of Abilene
cities.until_text: Administration passed to the Arabs with the Damascus region in 634-636. There is no later evidence for Greek speakers here; Aramaic survived in the nearby Qalamun villages. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Latin inscriptions of the road cut through the Barada gorge under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus at the expense of the Abilenes (CIL III 199-201); Greek inscriptions of residents; a see of Phoenice Libanensis in the 5th-6th centuries. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town came under the Arabs with the Damascus region in Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign, 634-636; the evidence for Greek speakers ends then.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Capital of an Ituraean tetrarchy with Semitic names in its Greek inscriptions; Greek dedications by residents from the reign of Tiberius; the Abilenes paid for the Roman road as a civic body (163-165)
cities.status_evidence: Capital of the tetrarchy of Abilene (Josephus; Luke 3:1); Ptolemy 5.15; bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis (Notitia Antiochena, Le Quien)
cities.note: The local shrine of Nabi Habil ('Abel') preserves the name. Civic status in the Roman period rests on its role as tetrarchic capital and later see.

cities.other_names: Pella (name of the Macedonian settlement, Strabo 16.2.10); Pharnake (earlier name, Strabo); Chersonesos (Strabo); Afamiya (Arabic)
cities.site: Qalaat al-Madiq, al-Suqaylabiyah District, Hama Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucus I founded it c. 300 BC on the site of Pharnake, also called Pella, as the military and elephant base of the kingdom (Strabo 16.2.10)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. Apamea had already been plundered by Khosrow I in 540 and burned, with its people deported, in 573. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek city inscriptions, mosaics and the Neoplatonist school (Numenius, Amelius) to the 3rd c.; Greek church inscriptions into the 6th c.; mass deportation by the Persians in 573 (Evagrius 5.10). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier blows: plundered by Khosrow I, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.11); taken and burned by Khosrow I's general Adarmahan, who deported its people, 573 (Evagrius 5.10; John of Ephesus 6.6).
cities.pre_greek_note: Pharnake is attested only in Greek (Strabo); the identification of the site with Bronze Age Niya (Akkadian, Egyptian) is disputed; the citadel tell has Bronze Age levels.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.10; city coins from the 2nd c. BC; metropolis of Syria Secunda; bishops from 325; Hierocles

cities.other_names: Arastan (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); al-Rastan (Arabic)
cities.site: Al-Rastan, al-Rastan District, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: listed by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities Seleucus I named after places in Macedonia; c. 300 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.refounded_by: held by the Emesene dynasts (Sampsigeramus) in the 1st c. BC (Strabo 16.2.10)
cities.status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; Strabo 16.2.10; Roman city coins with Greek legends; see of Syria Secunda (Mark of Arethusa, 4th c.); Hierocles
cities.note: Modern al-Rastan is generally held to continue the name Arethusa.

cities.site: Qara, Qalamoun, Rif Dimashq Governorate (proposed)
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Dadas of Chonochora, for whom the metropolitan Theodore of Damascus signed at Chalcedon (451); Dadas signed the letter of the bishops of Phoenice II to Leo I in 458.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Last bishop known: Alexander, expelled in 518. Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of the Greek-speaking church under Damascus in the Aramaic-speaking Qalamoun.
cities.status_evidence: See of Phoenice Libanensis under Damascus: bishop Dadas (451, 458); Alexander, a Miaphysite expelled in 518; Notitia Antiochena (c. 570). Identified with Qara (Wikipedia it, after Vailhe, Honigmann and Janin); 'Chonacara?' at Qara in the Barrington Atlas.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The identification with Qara is usual but tentative in the Barrington Atlas. Corada, a separate see under Damascus, is not this place. Le Quien wrongly gave it three bishops of Carrhae (Harran).

cities.other_names: Demetrias (civic coins, c. 87-84 BC); Colonia Damascus (under Philip the Arab); Dimashq, al-Sham (Arabic)
cities.site: Old City of Damascus, Damascus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Civic bronze coins naming the city Demetrias, c. 87-84 BC (after Demetrius III, who ruled from Damascus 96-87 BC); before that a Ptolemaic and, from 200 BC, Seleucid stronghold with a royal mint (from 128 BC)
cities.until_text: Administration: the city capitulated to the Arabs in 635 and was the Umayyad capital from 661; Greek stayed in the caliphal offices of Syria until the order to keep the registers in Arabic, c. 700-705 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the Greek-speaking Melkite elite (the family of Mansur ibn Sarjun, John of Damascus) lasted into the 8th century; by the 9th century the Melkites of Damascus wrote and spoke Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: John of Damascus (c. 675-c. 750) wrote in Greek and served in the caliph's administration before retiring to Mar Saba; Andrew of Crete was born at Damascus c. 660; Peter, metropolitan of Damascus, had his tongue cut out and was exiled to Arabia Felix (Yemen) by al-Walid II, 743 (Theophanes AM 6234; Chronicle of 1234); a fragment of Psalm 77 in Arabic written in Greek letters, found in the Umayyad mosque, was first dated to the late 8th c. but is now placed in the late 9th or early 10th c., and shows Greek script used by Arabic-speaking Christians; Melkite writing turns to Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Pauline Epistles of Sinai Ar. 151, translated from Syriac by Bishr ibn al-Sirri at Damascus, 867).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda after a siege, 635, and again after the battle of the Yarmuk, 636; Greek dropped from the registers by order of 'Abd al-Malik or al-Walid I, c. 700-705. No named act ended Greek speech, which faded with the Melkite shift to Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_name: Dimašqa (Akkadian, Amarna letters); Tmśq (Egyptian, list of Thutmose III); Dammeśeq (Hebrew Bible); Darmeśeq (Aramaic)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Aramaic was spoken in the city and its villages (Syriac and Christian Palestinian Aramaic texts); Arabic-speaking tribes in the hinterland; Greek was the civic and church language
cities.status_evidence: Civic coins as Demetrias (c. 87-84 BC) and Roman city coins; listed in the Decapolis by Pliny (NH 5.74); Roman colonia; metropolis of Phoenice Libanensis; bishops at Nicaea 325 and later councils; Hierocles
cities.note: Greek settlers were probably present earlier: the grid plan of the Old City is usually dated to the Hellenistic period, but the first civic evidence is the Demetrias coinage. Nicolaus of Damascus (b. c. 64 BC) and his father were leading Greek-speaking citizens. After c. 800 Greek lived on in Damascus only as the church language of Arabic-speaking clergy: a Greek scroll of the Liturgy of St James was copied for Damascus in the late 9th or early 10th c. (Vat. gr. 2282, with Arabic notes for the priest). From the mid-14th c. Damascus was the seat of the Orthodox patriarchs of Antioch, Arabic-speaking until 1724, with a few Greeks at their court in the 17th c. (Euthymios III of Chios, 1635-1647). From 1724 to 1898 Constantinople named Greek patriarchs, but they were often away (Sylvester for years at a time in the Danubian lands and Constantinople), and only single Greek clerics lived with them; the secretaries, the parish clergy and the people spoke Arabic. A small Greek community has existed since 1913 (about 150 members today), mostly Syrians of Greek descent. Neither is counted as a return of Greek speech.
sources: Jones, Cities of the Eastern Roman Provinces
Panchenko, Arab Orthodox Christians under the Ottomans 1516-1831 (2016)
Radle, 'The Liturgy of St James in Medieval Damascus', OCP 87 (2021) 341-352
Walbiner, 'The split of the Greek Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch (1724)', Chronos 7 (2003) 9-36

cities.site: probably al-Hafar, a village about 8 km south-east of Sadad, Homs Governorate (Sadad and Mahin have also been proposed); not at Hawwarin, which is Evaria
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Theodore of Danaba at the Council of Chalcedon, 451.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Last known bishop: Eulogius, 553. Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see with Greek-signing bishops (451, 458, 553)
cities.status_evidence: See of Phoenice Libanensis under Damascus: bishop Theodore at Chalcedon 451 and in the letter of 458 to Leo I; Eulogius at Constantinople 553; Notitia Antiochena; Danova on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The Barrington Atlas puts 'Danova' at Hawwarin, which is Evaria, a separate see counted on its own; Danaba is placed here near al-Hafar, its most likely separate site (Wikipedia: Danaba), and the point is only regional. Pleiades 668236 ('Danova') is plotted at Hawwarin and is not used.

cities.other_names: Hemesa; Ḥimṣ (Arabic); Colonia Emesa (from Caracalla/Elagabalus); Hims
cities.site: Homs city, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek epitaph of the Emesene prince C. Iulius Sampsigeramus on his tomb, AD 78/79; city coins with Greek legends from Antoninus Pius (138-161)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah early in 636 and again after the Yarmuk; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek writers from Emesa: Heliodorus (Aethiopica), bishop Nemesius (c. 400), Romanos the Melodist (born c. 490). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah (with Khalid ibn al-Walid), 636, and reoccupied after the Yarmuk, 636/637 (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari). Earlier taken by Khosrow II's army, 613. No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.refounded_by: Roman colonia under Caracalla or Elagabalus (early 3rd c.)
cities.pre_greek_note: The citadel tell has Bronze and Iron Age levels; no pre-Greek name of the town is securely attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Arab dynasty (Sampsigeramus) and the cult of Elagabal; Greek city coins, inscriptions and writers (Heliodorus, Nemesius, Romanos the Melodist)
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.10; city coins from 138-161; colonia; metropolis of Phoenice Libanensis (5th c.); Hierocles
cities.note: Homs continues Emesa/Hemesa, the Greek and Latin form of the local name. Bilingual rather than Greek because of the Arab dynasty and the native cult; the balance is a judgment.

cities.other_names: Hamath (Aramaic; Hebrew Bible); Amattu (Assyrian); Amathe (Greek); Hama (Arabic); Hamat (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription)
cities.site: Hama city, Hama Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Antiochus IV (175-164 BC) renamed Hamath Epiphania; Seleucid and later Roman city coins with Greek legends show a polis; the renaming alone would not prove one
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered on terms to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.pre_greek_name: Ḥamath (Aramaic; Hebrew Bible Ḥămāt; Assyrian Amattu)
cities.bilingual_evidence: the Aramaic name Hamath stayed in use beside Epiphania; Syriac-speaking Christians in late antiquity
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid and Roman city coins; see of Syria Secunda (bishops from 325); Hierocles
cities.note: No Greek settlers are attested; a renamed Aramaean royal city.

cities.site: Huwwarin, near Sadad, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: bishop Thomas of Euaria, 451; a suffragan of Damascus in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Yazid I died at Huwwarin in 683.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see in the Notitia Antiochena; Greek inscriptions of the district
cities.status_evidence: Bishop of Euaria, 451; native bishop John; made a city in 573; suffragan of Damascus (Georgius Cyprius); Greek and Syriac inscriptions in its churches
cities.note: Evaria is the modern Hawwarin, beside Mahin. The Barrington Atlas places 'Danova' (Danaba) at Hawwarin and Euareia 5 km to the north-east; the coordinates here follow the modern identification with Hawwarin.

cities.other_names: Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Heliopolitana (Roman); Baʿlabakk (Arabic)
cities.site: Baalbek, Baalbek-Hermel Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Augustus settled veterans here as part of the colony of Berytus, 15/14 BC; Septimius Severus made Heliopolis a colony of its own (c. 193-201). Greek is attested among residents from the 1st c. AD.
cities.until_text: Administration: Abu Ubayda took the city after the Roman defeat at Yarmuk (634, 636 or 637 in different accounts), by agreement according to most; it became a fortress (al-Qalʿa); Marwan II sacked it in 748. Speech: Greek-speaking residents left or shifted to Arabic; no evidence of a Greek-speaking community after the early 8th c. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 1st-6th c.; Constantine built a basilica and installed a bishop (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.58); pagan cult to the 6th c. (Malalas); Hierocles (Phoenice Libanensis); Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah after Yarmuk, 636/637 (al-Baladhuri); sacked by the Umayyad caliph Marwan II, 748.
cities.founder: Augustus (veteran colony with Berytus); Septimius Severus (separate colony)
cities.pre_greek_note: The Semitic name bʿlbk is first attested in the Mishnah (2nd c. AD, as a kind of garlic) and in 5th-c. Syriac; no securely identified pre-Greek name in earlier sources.
cities.other_language: Aramaic (and Latin, the official language of the colony in the 1st-3rd c.)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek dedications and epitaphs of residents beside the Latin of the colony; Aramaic-speaking population of the Bekaa and its pagan villagers in late antiquity (Theodoret; the Life of Rabbula).
cities.status_evidence: Roman colony; Greek and Latin inscriptions; bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: A Roman foundation with Latin public life, a Greek-speaking element and an Aramaic-speaking population; recorded as bilingual (Greek and Aramaic).

cities.site: Yabrud, Qalamun, Rif Dimashq Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis by late antiquity (Notitia Antiochena, under Damascus); a Roman temple of Jupiter (Zeus) of Iabruda, later the church of Constantine and Helena; Greek inscriptions of residents from the Roman period
cities.until_text: Passed to the Arabs with the Damascus region in 634-636. The see survived as an Arabic-speaking Melkite community; no evidence for Greek speech after the conquest. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the cult of Zeus Yabroudes; bishops of Iabruda in Melkite lists. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Damascus region, 634-636.
cities.pre_greek_note: Pleiades records an Akkadian form Jabrudu; the attestation should be checked.
cities.bilingual_evidence: An Aramaic-speaking district (Aramaic is still spoken in nearby Ma'loula); Greek dedications at the temple of Zeus Yabroudes and Greek epitaphs of residents
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.15 (Iabruda); bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis (Notitia Antiochena; Le Quien)
cities.note: Civic status rests on the see; Greek is the language of its public inscriptions, Aramaic the language of the district.

cities.other_names: Qadesh (Egyptian qdš; Hittite Kinza); Laodicea Scabiosa (Tabula Peutingeriana)
cities.site: Tell Nebi Mend, al-Qusayr District, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The Seleucid name Laodicea is attested from 221 BC, when Antiochus III set out from it into the Marsyas valley (Polybius 5.45.7-8), but no Hellenistic coins, inscriptions or settlers of the town are known. It is first named as a town of the region by Strabo (16.2.18, c. AD 20) and Pliny (NH 5.82, "Laodiceni ad Libanum"); its city coins with Greek legends (LAODIK. PROS LIBANO) begin under Septimius Severus.
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the conquest of the Homs region by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 636/637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The site later shrank to a village. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Homs region, 636/637; the town then declined.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.18; Pliny NH 5.82; Ptolemy 5.15; city coins with Greek legends under Septimius Severus, Julia Domna, Caracalla and Severus Alexander; see of Phoenice Libanensis; Hierocles
cities.note: A Seleucid foundation or renaming on the site of Qadesh; whether the kings settled Greeks or laid the city out anew is not known, so the Greek date follows the first sure evidence of a town (Strabo), as for Seleucia on the Belus. If only the city coins count, the date is c. 200.
sources: Wildwinds/RPC: Laodikeia ad Libanum (provincial coins, Severans only)

cities.other_names: Sizara (Ptolemy 5.15.16); Sezer; Sinzar (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); Shaizar (Arabic)
cities.site: Shaizar, Mahardah District, Hama Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation settled by colonists from Thessalian Larissa, who served in the first cavalry agema at Apamea (Diodorus 33.4a); c. 300 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The Roman garrison that held Shaizar from Basil II's conquest in 999 to the Banu Munqidh in 1081 does not count as a resident community. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
cities.pre_greek_note: Sinzar/Zinzar of the Amarna letters and the Egyptian lists is usually identified with Shaizar, but not certainly.
cities.status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; Diodorus 33.4a; Strabo 16.2.10; see of Syria Secunda; Hierocles
cities.note: Its Thessalian settlers are among the few attested Greek colonists in Seleucid Syria.

cities.site: Maryamin, northwest of Homs, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A see of Syria Secunda in the council lists and Hierocles, from about the 5th c.; the native town is attested from 333 BC (Arrian 2.13.8).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638.
cities.pre_greek_note: Hecataeus (in Stephanus) calls it a Phoenician city; Arrian (2.13.8) names Mariamme among the towns that surrendered to Parmenion in 333 BC; no non-Greek attestation of the name.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Phoenician town of the Aradian hinterland (Arrian 2.13.8); in Roman times a see whose bishops signed in Greek, in an Aramaic-speaking district.
cities.status_evidence: See of Syria II under Apamea (council lists; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The mosaic of women musicians (late 4th c.) is the town's best-known find. Located at Maryamin after the Barrington Atlas; some place it at Qal'at al-Hosn.

cities.other_names: Tadmor (Palmyrene Aramaic Tdmr; Akkadian Tadmar; Hebrew Bible); Hadriana Palmyra (Hadrian); Tadmur (Arabic)
cities.site: Palmyra ruins beside the town of Tadmur, Homs Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek-Palmyrene bilingual inscriptions of residents from the 1st c. AD, after the city came under Roman control (Tiberius); boule and demos attested in the later 1st c.
cities.until_text: Administration: the city surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid in 634. Speech: Palmyrene Aramaic disappears from inscriptions after 272-274; Greek inscriptions continue, fewer, until 562 (IGLS XVII). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.fade_evidence: Over 500 Greek inscriptions; the last dated Greek inscription is of 562; bishops from 325 (Marinus at Nicaea).
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid on his desert march, 634 (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari). Earlier sacked by Aurelian after its second revolt, 273; Marwan II razed its walls, 745.
cities.refounded_by: Hadrian (Hadriana Palmyra, 129); colonia in the early 3rd c.; Diocletian's camp; Justinian (walls)
cities.pre_greek_name: Tadmar (Akkadian, Mari and Assyrian texts); Tadmor (Hebrew Bible); Tdmr (Palmyrene Aramaic)
cities.bilingual_evidence: hundreds of Greek-Palmyrene bilingual inscriptions, the bilingual Tariff of 137; boule and demos in Greek; Palmyrene Aramaic the first language of most citizens
cities.status_evidence: boule and demos in bilingual inscriptions; Tariff of 137; Roman colonia; see (Marinus at Nicaea 325); Hierocles

cities.other_names: Raphanea; Rephania (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); Rafaniya (Arabic)
cities.site: Rafniyah, Masyaf District, Hama Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: 1st c. AD: the Raphanaei in Pliny (NH 5.82) and Raphanea in Josephus (BJ 7.97), beside the legionary fortress; city coins with Greek legends under Elagabalus
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; earlier taken by Shapur I, c. 253 (Shapur I's inscription).
cities.status_evidence: Josephus BJ 7.97; base of legio III Gallica; city coins under Elagabalus; see of Syria Secunda (bishops from 325, Bassianus at Nicaea, to 536); Hierocles; Georgius Cyprius
cities.note: The town grew beside a Roman legionary fortress; the Greek-speaking civilian community is inferred from its coins and see.

cities.site: Salamiyah, Salamiyah District, Hama Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: bishop Julian of Salamias at the consecration of Severus of Antioch, 512
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Homs region, 636.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a see by 512 and Greek inscriptions (temple of Zeus, later a church); an Aramaic-speaking district
cities.status_evidence: Bishop Julian at the consecration of Severus of Antioch, 512; church inscriptions of the 6th-7th c. (a church of the Theotokos dated 604)
cities.note: Its province is uncertain (Phoenice Libanensis or Syria Secunda). The Greek date is the first sure one; Greek may be older.

cities.other_names: Seleucobelus (late Roman); Seleucenses ad Belum (Pliny NH 5.82)
cities.site: probably near Jisr al-Shughur, Idlib Governorate (Pleiades); al-Suqaylabiyah, Hama Governorate, has also been proposed
cities.greek_from_text: First named as a town of Syria by Pliny (NH 5.82, AD 77) and Ptolemy; later the see of Seleucobelus in Syria Secunda. The dynastic name shows a Seleucid settlement, but no Hellenistic polis is attested.
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of northern Syria, 637/638.
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.82; Ptolemy; see of Syria Secunda (Seleucobelus); Hierocles
cities.note: The dynastic name shows a Seleucid settlement, but a city is attested only from Pliny and the later see. The site is not securely located: Pleiades and Cohen point to the Jisr al-Shughur area; others place it at al-Suqaylabiyah in the Ghab (Hama Governorate), whose name is usually derived from Seleucobelus.

cities.site: Tell Blakhiyah (Anthedon Harbour), north-west of Gaza City, Gaza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic town with a Greek name; taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC (Josephus AJ 13.357) and rebuilt by Gabinius (BJ 1.166); Herod renamed it Agrippias
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Gaza coast, 634-637. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested; the site was later abandoned. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Late Roman harbour town; bishops of Anthedon to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with Gaza by the army of Amr ibn al-As, 634-637
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 13.357, BJ 1.166, AJ 15.217; see of Palaestina I (Hierocles)
cities.note: Coordinates are for the excavated harbour town at Blakhiyah; the Pleiades point lies about 3 km inland. The Greek name may point to Greek settlers, but this is not attested.

cities.other_names: Pegai (Hellenistic); Ras al-'Ayn (Arabic); Migdal Afek / Mirabel (later fort)
cities.site: Tel Afek (Ras el-Ein) in the Yarkon National Park (Mekorot HaYarkon), between Rosh HaAyin and Petah Tikva, Central District
cities.greek_from_text: Herod founded Antipatris for his father Antipater, c. 9 BC (Josephus AJ 16.142-143), on the site of Hellenistic Pegai
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: the town had declined after the earthquake of 363; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: City coins under Elagabalus with Greek legends; bishops of Antipatris to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636
cities.pre_greek_name: ʾĂp̄ēq (Hebrew Bible); Apqu (Akkadian, Esarhaddon); ʾIpq (Egyptian, Thutmose III)
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 16.142-143; city coins (Elagabalus); see of Palaestina I

cities.site: Tel Arsuf (Apollonia National Park), Herzliya, Tel Aviv District
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic town with the Greek name Apollonia; held by Alexander Jannaeus and rebuilt by Gabinius (Josephus AJ 13.395; BJ 1.166)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with the other coastal towns in the Arab conquest, c. 640. Speech: Arsuf became a Muslim coastal stronghold; no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Late Roman town with churches and Greek inscriptions (Sozusa); Samaritan presence; Umayyad and Abbasid fortified town. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya's forces with the other coastal towns, c. 640 (Baladhuri)
cities.pre_greek_note: The Arabic Arsuf is often derived from the Phoenician god Reshef, but no non-Greek name of the town is attested.
cities.status_evidence: Josephus BJ 1.166; Pliny 5.69; Ptolemy 5.16.2; Hierocles (Sozusa); see of Palaestina I, with bishops in 449, 518 and 553
cities.note: The Greek date rests on the name and on Josephus; the excavations show a Hellenistic town over a Persian-period Phoenician settlement. The ruins lie in the Apollonia National Park at the northern edge of Herzliya; the site is also known by its medieval name, Arsuf.
sources: Roll and Ayalon, Apollonia and Southern Sharon

cities.site: Khirbat al-Beiyudat, Jordan valley north of Jericho, Jericho Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by the ethnarch Archelaus c. AD 6 for the workers of his date groves (Josephus AJ 17.340); first attested as a see with bishop Timotheus at the synods of Constantinople, 448 and 449, and Antiochus at Chalcedon, 451
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested; the site was later abandoned. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Church mosaic with Greek inscriptions of the 560s. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 17.340; Pliny 13.44 (its dates); bishops 448, 449 and 451; Madaba map; dated church mosaic inscriptions of the 560s at Khirbet el-Beiyudat
cities.note: A village-town that became a see; the Greek of its church is attested, but the speech of its early, probably Jewish, plantation workers is not, so it is dated only from the see.

cities.site: Tel Ashkelon National Park, Ashkelon, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic Greek city: Ascalonites in Greek inscriptions at Delos and Athens in the 2nd c. BC; its own era of freedom from 104 BC; the philosophers Antiochus and Aristus of Ascalon
cities.until_text: Administration: Mu'awiya took the city c. 640-644. Speech: Baladhuri says Roman forces later raided it and removed its people, and 'Abd al-Malik rebuilt and garrisoned it; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; Baladhuri on the Roman raid and the Umayyad resettlement
cities.ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, c. 640-644; later emptied in a Roman raid and resettled by 'Abd al-Malik (Baladhuri)
cities.pre_greek_name: ʾAšqəlōn (Hebrew Bible); Ashkelon (Egyptian, Merneptah stele); Asqaluna (Akkadian)
cities.status_evidence: Free city with its own era (104 BC) and Greek civic coins; Greek writers; see of Palaestina I (Longinus at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: Greek pottery in the city sacked by Nebuchadnezzar in 604 BC is evidence of trade, not of a Greek city. Its harbour, Maiumas of Ascalon, is noted as a close call.
sources: Fuks, Ascalon in the Hellenistic and Roman periods

cities.other_names: Azotus Mesogaios, Azotus Hippenos (late Roman); Ashdod (Hebrew Bible); Isdud (Arabic)
cities.site: Tel Ashdod by the former village of Isdud, Ashdod, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic town: Jonathan burned Azotus and its temple of Dagon in 147 BC (1 Macc 10:84); Pompey restored it to its citizens and Gabinius rebuilt it (Josephus AJ 14.75, 14.88)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: Isdud became a village; no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Azotus to the 6th c.; the Madaba map shows Azotus and Azotus Paralios. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of Palaestina, 634-640; Jonathan the Hasmonaean had burned the town, 147 BC (1 Macc 10:84)
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 14.75, 14.88; Pliny 5.68; Hierocles (Azotus Mesogaios); see of Palaestina I (Silvanus at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: The gap 147-57 BC follows Jonathan's destruction and Hasmonaean rule. Acts 8:40 places Philip the evangelist here. Tel Ashdod is a ruin a few kilometres south-east of the modern city of Ashdod (founded 1956), which takes the ancient name; the Arab village of Isdud on the site, which continued the name, was depopulated in 1948.

cities.site: Ashdod-Yam (Minat el-Qal'a), Ashdod, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: The harbour town of Azotus became a city of its own in late antiquity: Azotus Paralios in Hierocles (c. 527) and on the Madaba map
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: the site later became a Muslim coastal fort (Minat al-Qal'a); no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Late Roman town with Greek inscriptions; Islamic-period fort on the shore. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the coast, 630s-640s
cities.pre_greek_note: Asdūdimmu is usually taken as Ashdod's harbour; its identification with this site is probable, not certain.
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles (Azotus Paralios); Madaba map; see of Palaestina I
cities.note: Earlier part of the polis of Azotus; counted from when it is listed as a city in its own right.

cities.site: el-Araj (Beit HaBek) on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, or et-Tell c. 2 km inland to the north-north-east; both east of the Jordan mouth, Golan Heights
cities.admin1: Golan Heights (Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967)
cities.greek_from_text: Philip the Tetrarch raised the village of Bethsaida to a polis and named it Julias (Josephus AJ 18.28); dated before 2 BC (after Augustus' daughter) or c. AD 30 (after Livia-Julia)
cities.until_text: The town suffered in the Jewish War; at et-Tell the Roman settlement shrank after 67/68 and the site was abandoned by the 3rd-4th century. Evidence for Greek speech is thin throughout.
cities.fade_evidence: Josephus, Vita 398-406 (fighting near Julias, AD 67); excavations at et-Tell (Arav) and el-Araj (Notley, Aviam)
cities.ended_by: No named act: fighting near Julias in the Jewish War (Josephus, Vita 398-406, AD 67); the town then declined.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Jewish fishing town raised to a polis by Philip; the apostles Philip and Andrew from Bethsaida bore Greek names, and 'Greeks' approached Philip there (John 12:20-21)
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 18.28 and BJ 2.168 (polis named Julias); Pliny NH 5.71
cities.note: The location is disputed between et-Tell (excavated since 1987) and el-Araj on the shore, where recent excavations found a Roman-period settlement; the point is at el-Araj. Greek speech by residents is inferred, not directly attested.

cities.other_names: Straton's Tower (Στράτωνος Πύργος, Hellenistic); Caesarea Sebaste; Kaisareia Paralios; Colonia Prima Flavia Augusta Caesarensis (Vespasian); Qaysariyya (Arabic)
cities.site: Caesarea National Park and the town of Caesarea, Haifa District
cities.greek_from_text: Straton's Tower, a Hellenistic port town (Zenon papyri, 259 BC), was taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC and restored to its citizens as a free city by Pompey in 63 BC (Josephus AJ 14.76); Herod refounded it as Caesarea, 22-10/9 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended when Mu'awiya took the city in 640/641 after a long siege. Speech: the Greek-speaking élite left by sea or was taken captive; the shrunken Arab town of Qaysariyya is not known to have kept a Greek-speaking community.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and writers to the 6th c. (Procopius of Caesarea); the conquest of 640/641 with captives sent to the caliph (Baladhuri)
cities.ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan after a long siege, 640/641; Baladhuri reports thousands of captives sent to the caliph Umar
cities.refounded_by: Herod (as Caesarea, with a new city and harbour, 22-10/9 BC); Vespasian (Roman colonia, after 70)
cities.pre_greek_note: Straton's Tower is a Greek name, probably after a Sidonian king Straton (Abdashtart); no non-Greek name of the town is attested.
cities.status_evidence: Herodian foundation (Josephus AJ 15.331-341); Roman colonia; capital of Judaea and metropolis of Palaestina I; bishops from the 2nd c. (Eusebius); writers Eusebius and Procopius
cities.note: Jewish and Samaritan communities lived beside the Greek-speaking majority; the clash between Jews and Greeks here in AD 66 began the Jewish revolt. Counted as a Hellenized native town: Straton's Tower was already a free Greek city in 63 BC, and Herod rebuilt it as Caesarea on the same site.
sources: Holum et al., King Herod's Dream (1988)

cities.site: Beit Ras, Irbid Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Founded in 97/98, the start of the city's era, under Nerva or Trajan
cities.until_text: Taken by the Arabs in 635-636. Christian Greek speakers remained under the Umayyads: Peter of Capitolias, a local priest, was executed in 715. The town declined after the earthquake of 749. Peter of Capitolias (executed 715) shows a Greek-speaking Christian community after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750, with the range starting at 715.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek passion of Peter of Capitolias (executed 715 under al-Walid I); Greek inscriptions of churches. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 635-636; Peter of Capitolias was executed by order of al-Walid I in 715.
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Marcus Aurelius to Macrinus) with the era of 97/98; bishops from Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
cities.note: The Arabic name Beit Ras may continue a local Aramaic name; this is not attested before the Greek city.

cities.site: Unidentified site in the territory of Ascalon (Khirbat al-Sharaf? Sapharea?), Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Eliseus of Diocletianopolis at the synod of Seleucia, 359; the name points to a city created under Diocletian (284-305), but the name alone is not evidence.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the coastal plain, 634-640s (Ascalon was taken by Mu'awiya c. 640). Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the coastal plain, 634-640s; Ascalon, whose territory it shared, fell to Mu'awiya c. 640 (al-Baladhuri).
