cities.bilingual_evidence: A see carved out of the territory of Greek-speaking Ascalon; the language of its own people is not documented.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina I: bishop Eliseus at Seleucia 359; Hierocles (Palaestina I); Georgius Cyprius. Probably the see of 'Sariphaea' whose bishop Stephen was at the synod of Jerusalem, 536.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The site is unknown; it lay in the territory of Ascalon, and the point is the Barrington Atlas 'Sapharea?', only regional.

cities.other_names: Dor (Hebrew Bible); Dʾr (Phoenician); Du'ru (Akkadian); Tantura (Arabic village nearby)
cities.site: Tel Dor, by Kibbutz Nahsholim, Haifa District
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic Greek town: besieged by Antiochus III in 219 BC (Polybius 5.66); Greek civic coins later dated by the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the late Roman town had shrunk and was abandoned around the time of the Persian war and the Arab conquest of the coast (614-640). No later Greek community is attested.
cities.fade_evidence: Late Roman church with Greek inscriptions; the excavations show decline in the 6th-7th c. and abandonment
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town declined and was abandoned around the Arab conquest of the coast, 630s-640s
cities.pre_greek_name: Dor (Hebrew Bible); Dʾr (Phoenician, Eshmunazar II inscription); Du'ru (Akkadian); Dor (Egyptian, Wenamun)
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.66; freed by Pompey and rebuilt by Gabinius; Greek civic coins; see of Palaestina I (Hierocles)
cities.note: Pseudo-Skylax calls Dor a city of the Sidonians in the 4th c. BC; Attic pottery of the Persian period is trade, not a Greek city.
sources: Stern, Dor, Ruler of the Seas

cities.other_names: Baitogabra (Ptolemy); Beth Guvrin (Hebrew, rabbinic); Lucia Septimia Severa Eleutheropolis; Bayt Jibrin (Arabic); Bethgibelin (Crusader)
cities.site: Beit Guvrin-Maresha National Park and kibbutz Beit Guvrin, former village of Bayt Jibrin, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Septimius Severus made Baitogabra the city of Eleutheropolis, AD 199/200 (city era and coins)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken after the battle of Ajnadayn (634), nearby, in the following years. Speech: Bayt Jibrin became a small town; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and mosaics to the 6th-7th c.; Eusebius measured distances from it in his Onomasticon
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest after the battle of Ajnadayn, 634
cities.pre_greek_name: Bēt Guvrin (Hebrew and Aramaic, rabbinic texts)
cities.pre_greek_note: Josephus has Betaris/Begabris (BJ 4.447); the Semitic name appears in rabbinic texts.
cities.status_evidence: City coins and era; Eusebius, Onomasticon; see of Palaestina I (Maximus at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: Jewish and Aramaic-speaking Christian minorities lived here; Epiphanius of Salamis came from a nearby village.

cities.site: Emmaus-Nicopolis ruins by the former village of 'Imwas, Latrun area (Canada Park)
cities.greek_from_text: Elagabalus made Emmaus the city of Nicopolis, AD 221, after an embassy led by Julius Africanus (Eusebius, Chronicle; Jerome)
cities.until_text: Administration: the Arab army camped here in the conquest, and the plague of 'Amwas (639) struck it. Speech: the town shrank to a village; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Basilica with Greek inscriptions (5th-6th c.); bishops of Nicopolis to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: occupied in the Arab conquest of the 630s; the plague of 'Amwas, 639, hit the army camp there
cities.pre_greek_note: Emmaus is known from 1 Maccabees and Josephus (in Greek) and from rabbinic texts; no older non-Greek name is attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Julius Africanus, a Christian who wrote in Greek, lived here and won it city status; a Greek-Samaritan bilingual inscription; Greek church inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: City status 221; see of Palaestina I (Peter at Nicaea 325; Hierocles: Nicopolis)
cities.note: The site lies in the Latrun salient, held by Jordan from 1948 to 1967 and by Israel since 1967; the Arab village of 'Imwas was demolished in 1967. Jewish town in the Hasmonaean period; burned by Varus in 4 BC. The name Emmaus survived in the Arabic village name 'Imwas until 1967.

cities.site: Iksal, near Nazareth, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Parthenius of Exalus at the synod of Jerusalem, 536.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with Galilee after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with Galilee after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635 (Shurahbil ibn Hasana's command).
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Jewish village of Galilee in Josephus' time; a see of the Greek-speaking church by 536.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina II: bishop Parthenius at the synod of Jerusalem, 536; identified with Iksal (Josephus' Xaloth).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Known as a see from a single bishop; the identification with Iksal is the usual one.

cities.other_names: Gaba Hippeon, 'Gaba of the horsemen' (Greek); Gabae (Hierocles?)
cities.site: Tel Shush (Tell Abu Shusha), near Kibbutz Mishmar HaEmek, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: The city counted its years from 61/60 BC, when L. Marcius Philippus governed Syria, on its Greek coins (1st-3rd c. AD), and it was known as Gaba Philippi in Roman times; a Greek lead weight is dated by the years "of its establishment". Herod later settled his discharged cavalrymen there, c. 20 BC (Josephus AJ 15.294; BJ 3.36).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: City coins to the 3rd c.; a church and late Roman remains on the site; bishops of Gabae to 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636
cities.founder: L. Marcius Philippus, governor of Syria (city era of 61/60 BC)
cities.refounded_by: Herod (settled his discharged cavalrymen there, c. 20 BC)
cities.status_evidence: Greek city coins with an era of 61/60 BC; Josephus AJ 15.294; BJ 3.36; Pliny 5.75; see of Palaestina II (Gabae at Jerusalem 536)
cities.note: The site is disputed: Tel Shush (Abu Shusha) is the usual choice, with Sha'ar HaAmakim as an alternative.
sources: Jezreel Valley Regional Project: Tell Abu Shusha

cities.other_names: Seleucia (Seleucid name on coins, 2nd c. BC); ʿAzzah (Hebrew Bible); Ghazza (Arabic)
cities.site: Tell Harube and the old city of Gaza, Gaza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic Greek city: Polybius praises its loyalty when Antiochus III besieged it, 201 BC (16.22a); city coins as Seleucia in the 2nd c. BC. Alexander had taken it in 332 BC and resettled it with people from the neighbourhood (Arrian 2.27)
cities.until_text: Administration: the Roman army was defeated at Dathin in 634 and Gaza was taken by Amr ibn al-As c. 637. Speech: the Greek-speaking Christian community survived the conquest but, like the rest of the Palestinian Melkites, shifted to Arabic in the 8th-9th c.
cities.fade_evidence: The rhetorical school of Gaza (Aeneas, Procopius, Choricius) to the mid-6th c.; Greek church inscriptions into the 7th c.; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: Taken by Amr ibn al-As, c. 637, after the battle of Dathin (634); the Roman garrison was put to death in 638/639 (Passion of the Sixty Martyrs of Gaza). No named act ended Greek speech. Earlier, Alexander Jannaeus destroyed the city c. 96 BC (Josephus AJ 13.358-364)
cities.pre_greek_name: ʿAzzāh (Hebrew Bible); Ḫazzatu (Akkadian); Gḏt (Egyptian, Thutmose III)
cities.status_evidence: Greek civic coins (Hellenistic and Roman, era of 61 BC); rebuilt by Gabinius; Greek writers of the school of Gaza; see of Palaestina I (Asclepas at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: The gap 96-57 BC follows Jannaeus' massacre and destruction. The countryside spoke Aramaic and the city had Arab traders; the 'Minoa' legend is a legend. Its port, Maiumas-Constantia, is a separate entry.

cities.site: Daburiyya?, Daburiyya or Kafr Kama (proposed), Lower Galilee, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a city of Palaestina II by Hierocles (c. 527). The name honours the empress Helena (d. c. 329), so the city may go back to Constantine, but the name alone is not evidence of Greek-speaking residents.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with Galilee after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with Galilee after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635 (Shurahbil ibn Hasana's command).
cities.bilingual_evidence: A city and see of Palaestina II; the language of its people is not documented directly.
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina II); a see under Scythopolis in the lists of Palaestina II (Catholic Encyclopedia; Wikipedia it: Arcidiocesi di Scitopoli); no ancient bishop known by name.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The site is unknown: Daburiyya at the foot of Mount Tabor and Kafr Kama are proposed (Abel; TIR Iudaea-Palaestina 142), so the point is only regional.
sources: Tsafrir, Di Segni & Green, TIR Iudaea-Palaestina (1994) 142

cities.other_names: Antiochia by Hippos (Seleucid, on coins); Susita (Aramaic and Hebrew, rabbinic); Qal'at al-Husn (Arabic)
cities.site: Sussita (Hippos National Park), above Kibbutz Ein Gev, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucid town 'Antiochia by Hippos' (city coins); the excavations show a new Hellenistic town of the 3rd-2nd c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: a Christian town with Greek inscriptions until the earthquake of 749 destroyed it; it was then abandoned.
cities.fade_evidence: Churches with Greek inscriptions in use into the 8th c.; destruction layer of the earthquake of 749
cities.ended_by: No named act: the earthquake of 18 January 749 destroyed the city and it was abandoned
cities.status_evidence: Decapolis (Pliny 5.74); Greek city coins; see of Palaestina II
cities.note: Hippos lies on the east shore of the Sea of Galilee inside Israel's 1949 lines, not in the Golan Heights.
sources: Segal et al., Hippos-Sussita excavation reports

cities.site: Tel Yavne, Yavne, Central District
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic gentile town: Judas Maccabaeus attacked it and burned its harbour, c. 163 BC (2 Macc 12:8-9); a Greek letter of Antiochus V to the Sidonians at the harbour dates from 163 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Iamnia to the 6th c.; Samaritan and Christian communities in late antiquity. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of Palaestina, 634-640
cities.other_language: Hebrew and Aramaic (Jewish); Samaritan Aramaic in late antiquity
cities.bilingual_evidence: Philo (Legatio 200) calls Iamnia a mixed city, most of its people Jews and the rest foreigners; the rabbinic academy met here after AD 70; Greek bishops and inscriptions from the 4th c.
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 14.75, 14.88; Philo, Legatio 200-203; see of Palaestina I (Macrinus at Nicaea 325; Hierocles)
cities.note: Hellenistic Iamnia was a gentile town; after its conquest by the Hasmonaeans most of its people were Jews, hence bilingual. The harbour town (Iamnia Paralios) is listed separately as a close call.

cities.site: Herodian Jericho (Tulul Abu el-Alayiq) and the late Roman town under modern Jericho, Jericho Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A see by 325, when bishop Januarius attended the Council of Nicaea; residents already wrote Greek on the ossuaries of the Goliath family tomb in the early 1st c. AD, when Jericho was a toparchy capital, not a polis
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c.; the Umayyad palace of Khirbat al-Mafjar nearby marks the new order. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek church and monastery inscriptions to the 6th-7th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek and Aramaic inscriptions on the ossuaries of the 'Goliath' family tomb, 1st c. AD; Greek church inscriptions and bishop Januarius at Nicaea (325); a 6th-7th c. synagogue with a Hebrew and Aramaic mosaic
cities.status_evidence: Toparchy capital (Josephus BJ 3.55); see of Palaestina I (Januarius at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: City status before the 4th c. rests on its role as a toparchy capital; the coordinates are for the Roman town, not Tell es-Sultan.
sources: Hachlili, The Goliath Family in Jericho (BASOR 235, 1979)

cities.other_names: Antiochia in Jerusalem (Seleucid polis, 175-164 BC); Colonia Aelia Capitolina (Hadrian); Yerushalayim (Hebrew); al-Quds, Bayt al-Maqdis, Iliya' (Arabic)
cities.site: The Old City of Jerusalem
cities.greek_from_text: The high priest Jason made Jerusalem the polis of 'Antiochenes in Jerusalem', with a gymnasium and ephebes, under Antiochus IV, 175 BC (2 Macc 4:9-12)
cities.until_text: No end: Greek speakers have lived in Jerusalem without a long break from 175 BC to today. From the 9th c., when the Orthodox laity turned to Arabic, Greek was kept by the clergy and monks of the Holy Sepulchre and the patriarchate: the survey of c. 808 found Greek dominant among them; the service book of the Holy Sepulchre was copied in Greek in 1122; pilgrims saw Greek monks holding the choir and singing the office in Greek (Adorno, 1470-71); and the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, Greek by rule, has led the patriarchate since the 1530s. Lay Greeks settled again from the mid-19th c.
cities.until_basis: continuous: clergy and monks; lay Greeks again from the 19th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Continuity: a Greek loan contract written in Jerusalem, 115 (P.Mur. 114), and Hadrian's Greek letter from Jerusalem, 130; Egeria 47 (c. 384: the bishop preaches in Greek); the Commemoratorium (c. 808: 150 clergy and staff at the Holy Sepulchre under a synkellos; 11 hermits on the Mount of Olives singing the psalms in Greek, one in Arabic); Michael Synkellos and the Graptoi brothers writing Greek in the city (811-813); the synkellos Elias at Constantinople (869); Nasir-i Khusraw (1047); the Anastasis Typikon (Hagios Stavros gr. 43, copied 1122 by a lector of the Holy Sepulchre, with the homily translated into Arabic for those who could not read Greek); Daniel the Abbot (1106/07: the Orthodox priests over the Holy Sepulchre); the Greek homilies of Patriarch Athanasios II (1230s); the Greek decree of the synod of 1443; Adorno (1470-71) and Casola (1494) on the Greek monks and altars of the Holy Sepulchre; Fernberger (1592); Horn (c. 1740); the census of 1922 (c. 700-760 Greek speakers in Jerusalem); today the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre (c. 100-120 monks, almost all Greeks and Cypriots), the Patriarchal School of Sion and the Greek Consulate General (since 1862).
cities.ended_by: No end. Short interruptions: the Persian sack of 614 (clergy killed or deported; Modestus restored the churches within a few years); al-Hakim's destruction of the Holy Sepulchre, 1009 (the patriarch in hiding to 1013; rebuilt by 1048); the Latin takeover of the Holy Sepulchre, 1099 (the Greek priests back at the tomb by 1106/07; the patriarchs in exile to c. 1204); the Khwarazmian sack of 1244.
cities.pre_greek_name: Urusalim (Akkadian, Amarna letters); Rušalimum (Egyptian execration texts); Yərūšālayim (Hebrew Bible)
cities.other_language: Hebrew and Aramaic (Jewish), to 70; Christian Palestinian Aramaic in late antiquity; Arabic, the language of the Orthodox laity from the 9th c.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Gymnasium, ephebes and the polis of 'Antiochenes in Jerusalem', 175 BC (2 Macc 4:9-12); Greek-speaking Jews of the Second Temple (the Theodotos synagogue inscription; about a third of ossuary inscriptions in Greek; the 'Hellenists' of Acts 6:1); in Aelia, Egeria (c. 384) heard the bishop preach in Greek with translation into Aramaic and Latin
cities.status_evidence: 2 Macc 4:9-12; Roman colonia; Hierocles (Aelia); bishopric, patriarchate from 451
cities.note: 70-135: the city was the base of the Tenth Legion; Greek is attested there (P.Mur. 114, 115; Hadrian's letter, 130), though no civic or church community is. From the 9th c. the Greek speakers were the clergy and monks and, from the mid-19th c., a lay community again. The Greek clergy and monks count as a resident Greek-speaking community, with no long break; Greek used only in the liturgy by Arabic speakers would not. The Seleucid citadel (Akra) kept a Greek garrison until 141 BC. Before 175 BC: from Alexander (332 BC) Jerusalem was a Jewish temple city under its high priest, and its only Greek speakers were officials and the Ptolemaic garrison in the citadel, which Antiochus III drove out c. 200 BC (Josephus, AJ 12.133-138); garrisons do not count, so the record starts with Jason's polis of 175 BC.
sources: McCormick, Charlemagne's Survey of the Holy Land (2011)
Galadza, 'Greek liturgy in crusader Jerusalem', JMH 43 (2017) 421-437
Pahlitzsch, Graeci und Suriani im Palastina der Kreuzfahrerzeit (2001)
Saletti, 'Ululant more luporum', Annali online Ferrara (Adorno, 1470-71)
Bertram and Luke, Report... on the Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem (1921)

cities.site: Tel Yafo and Old Jaffa, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Tel Aviv District
cities.greek_from_text: Ptolemaic Greek town: Ptolemaic mint and Zenon papyri (259 BC); its gentile citizens drowned their Jewish neighbours c. 163 BC (2 Macc 12:3-7)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, c. 636. Speech: no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c.; the Christians of Yafa later spoke Arabic. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek Jewish and Christian epitaphs to the 4th-6th c.; bishops of Joppa to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken by the Arab army under Amr ibn al-As, c. 636; Simon the Hasmonaean had earlier expelled its gentile people, c. 142 BC (1 Macc 13:11)
cities.pre_greek_name: Yapu (Egyptian; Amarna letters); Yāfô (Hebrew Bible); Yappû (Akkadian, Sennacherib)
cities.other_language: Hebrew and Aramaic (Jewish), 142 BC to AD 67/68, and a Jewish community later
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Jewish town under the Hasmonaeans and Herod (1 Macc 13:11; 14:5); the Jewish cemetery of the 2nd-4th c. has mostly Greek epitaphs, some in Hebrew or Aramaic
cities.status_evidence: 2 Macc 12:3-7; freed by Pompey (Josephus AJ 14.76); Roman city coins (Flavia Ioppe); see of Palaestina I
cities.note: The gap 142-63 BC reflects the Hasmonaean expulsion of the gentile citizens. The Andromeda legend at Joppa is a legend, not evidence of a Greek town.

cities.other_names: Kefar 'Othnay (Hebrew and Aramaic, Mishnah); Caporcotani (Tabula Peutingeriana); Legio (camp of legio VI Ferrata); al-Lajjun (Arabic)
cities.site: Al-Lajjun, by Kibbutz Megiddo and Megiddo junction, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: The camp town became the city of Maximianopolis under Diocletian and Maximian, c. 300; the Greek mosaic of the Christian prayer hall at Kefar 'Othnay (c. 230) shows a Greek-speaking community before that
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: the place survived as the village of al-Lajjun; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Kefar 'Othnay church mosaic (Greek, c. 230); bishops of Maximianopolis to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636
cities.status_evidence: Bishop Paul of Maximianopolis at Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Palaestina II); see of Palaestina II; Eusebius, Onomasticon (Legio)
cities.note: Jerome placed Maximianopolis at Hadad-Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo; most scholars put it at Legio or at Rummana nearby. The legionary camp (from c. 120) itself does not count. The name Legio survived in the Arabic village name al-Lajjun, depopulated in 1948.
sources: Tepper and Di Segni, A Christian Prayer Hall of the Third Century CE at Kefar 'Othnay (2006)

cities.site: Tall ar-Rama, Jordan Valley, Balqa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Letoius of Livias at the Council of Ephesus, 431. Herod Antipas had walled the town of Betharamphtha and named it Julias, later Livias (Josephus AJ 18.27), c. AD 20, but that dynastic name is not by itself evidence of Greek-speaking residents.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Balqa, 634-636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Last bishop known: Zacharias, 536; pilgrims (Egeria; Theodosius) describe the town. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
cities.founder: Herod Antipas (walls and the name Julias/Livias, c. AD 20; no Greek settlers known)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Jewish town of Peraea refounded by Herod Antipas; a see of the Greek-speaking church from the 4th c.; the Greek and Aramaic documents of the Babatha archive show both languages in the region.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina I: bishops Letoius at Ephesus 431, Pancratius at Chalcedon 451 and Zacharias at the synod of Jerusalem 536 (Le Quien); Hierocles (Palaestina I); Josephus AJ 18.27 and BJ 2.168 for Herod Antipas' town; Ptolemy 5.16.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see alone now carries it; the Herodian dynastic name is not counted as evidence, so the date is that of the first bishop.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia: Livias (after Le Quien III 655)

cities.other_names: Lod (Hebrew); Diospolis (Septimius Severus, 199/200); Georgioupolis (late, after St George); al-Ludd (Arabic)
cities.site: Lod, Central District
cities.greek_from_text: Septimius Severus made Lydda the city of Diospolis, AD 199/200 (city era and coins)
cities.until_text: Administration: surrendered to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636, and was the first seat of the Arab district of Filastin. Speech: the caliph Sulayman moved the capital and much of the population to his new town of Ramla, c. 715; the Christians of Ludd later spoke Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; the synod of Diospolis (415); Ramla founded c. 715 (Baladhuri)
cities.ended_by: No named act: surrendered to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636; Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik moved its people to Ramla, c. 715 (Baladhuri)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek city coins of Diospolis (Septimius Severus); Greek inscriptions and bishops; a rabbinic centre in the 2nd-4th c.; Samaritans in late antiquity
cities.status_evidence: Greek city coins; see of Palaestina I (Aetius at Nicaea 325); synod of 415
cities.note: Before 200 Lydda was a Jewish toparchy capital, burned by Cestius Gallus in 66; the Greek city dates from Septimius Severus.

cities.other_names: Gazaion Limen, 'harbour of the Gazaeans' (Greek); Constantia (Constantine, c. 331); Neapolis (late Roman)
cities.site: The shore of Gaza City (al-Shati and al-Rimal area), Gaza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Constantine made the port of Gaza a separate city named Constantia after its people turned Christian, c. 331 (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 4.38; Sozomen 5.3)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with Gaza in the Arab conquest, c. 637. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Maiumas to the 6th c.; the synagogue of Gaza-Maiumas (508/509) with Greek dedications. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with Gaza by Amr ibn al-As, c. 637
cities.refounded_by: Julian put it back under Gaza (362); its separate see survived (Sozomen 5.3)
cities.status_evidence: Eusebius VC 4.38; Sozomen 5.3; see of Palaestina I; Hierocles
cities.note: Earlier the harbour of the Greek city of Gaza. The Jewish synagogue here (508/509) had Greek inscriptions.

cities.site: Tel Maresha, Beit Guvrin-Maresha National Park, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Sidonian community writing Greek in the painted tombs, 3rd c. BC; Marisa appears in the Zenon papyri, 259 BC
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the Parthians destroyed the city in 40 BC and it was not rebuilt; Beth Guvrin nearby took its place.
cities.fade_evidence: Destruction layer of 40 BC; no later occupation of the city
cities.ended_by: Destroyed by the Parthians in 40 BC, during their invasion in support of Antigonus (Josephus AJ 14.364; BJ 1.269). Earlier conquered by John Hyrcanus, c. 112 BC (AJ 13.257)
cities.other_language: Aramaic (Idumaean); Phoenician names among the Sidonian settlers
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek painted inscriptions in the tombs of the Sidonian community (Apollophanes, 'chief of the Sidonians in Marisa', 3rd-2nd c. BC); Greek graffiti, curse tablets and ostraca beside Aramaic ostraca of Idumaean residents
cities.status_evidence: Polis freed by Pompey and rebuilt by Gabinius; Sidonian community (tomb inscriptions); Zenon papyri
cities.note: Idumaean town; 'Aramaean town' is used for its Aramaic-speaking Idumaean base.
sources: Peters and Thiersch, Painted Tombs of Marissa (1905)

cities.other_names: Castrum Moenoenum (Notitia Dignitatum, fort); Ma'on (Hebrew); Khirbat al-Ma'in (Arabic)
cities.site: Horvat Ma'on (Khirbat al-Ma'in), near Nirim, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: 'A little town near Gaza' (Eusebius, Onomasticon); first attested as a see with bishop Zosimus at Ephesus (449) and Chalcedon (451).
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with the Gaza district in 'Amr ibn al-'As's conquest, 634-637. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Last bishop known: at the synod of Jerusalem, 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with the Gaza district in the Arab conquest, 634-637
cities.other_language: Aramaic (also Jewish Aramaic: the synagogue mosaic)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see whose bishops sat at the councils of 449, 451, 518 and 536; a Jewish community with an Aramaic synagogue inscription; Greek church mosaics in the neighbouring village of Kissufim (576).
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina I: bishop Zosimus at Ephesus 449 and Chalcedon 451; bishops at the synods of Jerusalem 518 and 536 (Le Quien). Later the fort Castrum Moenoenum (Notitia Dignitatum).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The one inscription from the site itself is the Aramaic dedication of its synagogue mosaic; the Greek church mosaics of the area are at Kissufim.

cities.other_names: Flavia Neapolis (Vespasian); Colonia Iulia Sergia Neapolis (Philip, 244); Nablus (Arabic); Shekhem (modern Hebrew usage)
cities.site: Nablus, Nablus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Vespasian founded Flavia Neapolis beside the Samaritan village of Mabartha, AD 72/73 (Josephus BJ 4.449; city era of 72/73)
cities.until_text: Administration: surrendered on terms to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians remained for a time; Samaritans and Christians later spoke Arabic. No Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; the Samaritan revolts of 484 and 529, crushed by Zeno and Justinian, cut the Samaritan population
cities.ended_by: No named act: surrendered on terms to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636
cities.pre_greek_note: Mabartha/Mamortha is known only from Josephus and Pliny. Biblical Shechem lies at Tell Balata, about 1.5 km east, and is a separate site.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek civic coinage from AD 72/73; Justin Martyr, a native who wrote in Greek (2nd c.); Greek inscriptions; the city was the centre of the Samaritans, who spoke Aramaic
cities.status_evidence: Josephus BJ 4.449; Greek city coins; Roman colonia; see of Palaestina I (Germanus at Nicaea 325)

cities.site: Tabaqat Fahl, North Jordan Valley, Irbid Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC (Polybius 5.70); the Macedonian name was given to the native town of Pihil, probably in the 3rd century BC
cities.until_text: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus c. 83 BC because the townspeople would not adopt Jewish customs (Josephus AJ 13.397); restored by Pompey. The Arabs defeated the Roman army at Fahl in 635; the Umayyad town was destroyed by the earthquake of 749. A smaller town went on after the earthquake. Pella has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest, so the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the West and East churches; Umayyad houses destroyed in the earthquake of 18 January 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 83 BC; restored by Pompey, 63 BC. Battle of Fahl, January 635 (Abu Ubayda, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Shurahbil ibn Hasana); the earthquake of 749 ruined the town.
cities.pre_greek_name: Pḥl (Egyptian execration texts and lists); Piḫilu (Akkadian, Amarna letters)
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.70; Josephus AJ 13.397; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
cities.note: The Greek name was later linked to Alexander's Pella; no Macedonian settlers are attested.
sources: Smith and McNicoll, Pella in Jordan

cities.site: Tel Bet Yerah (Khirbat al-Karak), south-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Ptolemaic foundation named for Philotera, sister of Ptolemy II; Antiochus III took it in 218 BC (Polybius 5.70.3-4)
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the Hasmonaeans took the town, and the Hellenistic settlement on the tell was abandoned in the early 1st c. BC.
cities.fade_evidence: Hellenistic houses and coins to the late 2nd c. BC; no later Greek town
cities.ended_by: Taken by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 100-80 BC (Syncellus lists Philoteria among his conquests)
cities.pre_greek_note: The tell holds a large Bronze Age town whose ancient name is not attested; Beth Yerah is a later rabbinic name.
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.70.3-4; Cohen 2006 (Philoteria)
cities.note: The identification with Tel Bet Yerah is generally accepted but not proven.

cities.site: Tell Rafah, Rafah, Rafah Governorate (on the line between the Gaza Strip and Egypt)
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic town, 'the first city of Coele Syria towards Egypt' (Polybius 5.80), by which Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III in 217 BC; taken by Alexander Jannaeus and rebuilt by Gabinius (Josephus AJ 13.357; BJ 1.166)
cities.until_text: Administration: on the route of the Arab invasion of 633/634, taken with the rest of the Gaza district. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Roman city coins with Greek legends (2nd-3rd c.); bishops of Raphia to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken by the army of Amr ibn al-As in the invasion of 633/634
cities.pre_greek_name: Rapiḫu (Akkadian, Sargon II); Rph (Egyptian, Seti I)
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.80-86; Josephus BJ 1.166; Roman city coins dated by an era of 57 BC (Gabinius); see of Palaestina I (5th-6th c.)
cities.note: Tell Rafah lies on or very near the line between the Gaza Strip and Egypt; the main ruins are counted to the Gaza Strip here, as the set's area rules say.

cities.other_names: Nysa (Hellenistic dynastic name); Bet She'an (Hebrew); Baysan (Arabic)
cities.site: Tel Beit She'an and Beit She'an National Park, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: A Greek city by 218 BC, when Antiochus III took it (Polybius 5.70.4); probably a Ptolemaic foundation of the 3rd c. BC, also called Nysa
cities.until_text: Administration: surrendered to the Arab armies after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians remained; the Umayyad market inscription of Hisham's reign (c. 737/738) is in Arabic, and the earthquake of 749 ruined the city centre, after which Baysan was a small Arabic-speaking town.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek building inscriptions into the 7th c.; Cyril of Scythopolis (6th c.); Arabic market inscription of Hisham (c. 737/738); earthquake of 18 January 749
cities.ended_by: No named act: surrendered after the battle of Fahl, 635; the earthquake of 749 destroyed the city. Earlier the sons of John Hyrcanus took it, c. 107 BC, and its people went into exile (Josephus AJ 13.280; Megillat Ta'anit)
cities.pre_greek_name: Bēt Šəʾān (Hebrew Bible); Bt-šꜣr (Egyptian, New Kingdom)
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.70.4; Decapolis (Pliny 5.74); Greek city coins; metropolis of Palaestina II; bishop Patrophilus at Nicaea 325
cities.note: The gap 107-63 BC follows the Hasmonaean conquest and the exile of its people. Jewish and Samaritan minorities lived in the late Roman city. Counted as a Hellenized native town: a Ptolemaic (re)foundation is likely, but neither settlers nor a new layout are attested.

cities.other_names: Samaria (Greek); Sebaste (Herod, 27 BC); Colonia Lucia Septimia Sebaste (Septimius Severus); Sebastiya (Arabic)
cities.site: Sebastia, Nablus Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Macedonian colony settled after the Samaritans killed Alexander's governor Andromachus, 331 BC (Curtius 4.8.9-11); Eusebius credits the settlement to Perdiccas
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: Sebaste had shrunk to a small town around the shrine of John the Baptist; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; pilgrims' accounts of the shrine. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Earlier John Hyrcanus besieged, took and razed Samaria, c. 108/107 BC (Josephus AJ 13.275-281)
cities.founder: Alexander or Perdiccas (Macedonian settlers); Herod refounded it as Sebaste
cities.refounded_by: Pompey/Gabinius 63-55 BC; Herod 27 BC (Sebaste, 6,000 settlers); Septimius Severus (colonia, c. 201)
cities.status_evidence: Macedonian colony (Curtius; Eusebius); Herodian foundation (Josephus AJ 15.292-298); Roman colonia; see of Palaestina I (Marinus at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: The gap 108-57 BC follows Hyrcanus' destruction. The Samaritan centre was at Shechem and Mount Gerizim, not in the Macedonian city.

cities.other_names: Autocratoris (Antipas); Eirenopolis Neronias (coins, AD 68); Diocaesarea (2nd c.); Tzippori (Hebrew); Saffuriyya (Arabic)
cities.site: Tzippori National Park, by the former village of Saffuriyya and moshav Tzippori, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: First city coins with Greek legends, AD 67/68 (Eirenopolis Neronias Sepphoris); Antipas had rebuilt the town as his capital, c. 4 BC (Josephus AJ 18.27)
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of Galilee, 634/635. Speech: the town shrank to the village of Saffuriyya; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; bishops of Diocaesarea to the 6th c.; damage in the Jewish revolt against Gallus (351/352) and the earthquake of 363
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of Galilee, 634/635
cities.pre_greek_name: Ṣippōrī (Hebrew and Aramaic, Mishnah and Talmud)
cities.pre_greek_note: The name is attested in Hebrew only in rabbinic texts, later than Josephus' Greek Sepphoris; it is the native name of the town.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek city coins (AD 68; Diocaesarea from Hadrian to Caracalla); Greek civic institutions; Greek and Aramaic inscriptions in the 5th-c. synagogue mosaic; Greek inscriptions of the Christian town
cities.status_evidence: Greek civic coins; Josephus; see of Palaestina II (Diocaesarea)

cities.site: Khirbat Suq Mazin, near Deir al-Balah, Deir al-Balah Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a city of Palaestina I by Hierocles (c. 527) and as a see of the province.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken with the Gaza district in 'Amr ibn al-'As's conquest, 634-637. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken with the Gaza district in the Arab conquest, 634-637
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of the Greek-speaking church of Palaestina I in the Gaza district, where the countryside also spoke Aramaic.
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina I); counted as a see of Palaestina I under Caesarea in the church lists; no bishop is known to us by name.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see itself is thinly attested: no bishop of Sycomazon has been found. The site at Khirbat Suq Mazin near Deir al-Balah is a proposal.
sources: Tsafrir, Di Segni & Green, TIR Iudaea-Palaestina (1994)

cities.site: Ancient Tiberias and Hammat, south of the modern city, Northern District
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Herod Antipas c. AD 18-20 and named for Tiberius (Josephus AJ 18.36-38)
cities.until_text: Administration: surrendered on terms to Shurahbil ibn Hasana, 634/635, and became the capital of the Arab district of al-Urdunn. Speech: no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek synagogue and church inscriptions to the 6th-7th c.; bishops of Tiberias to the 6th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: surrendered to Shurahbil ibn Hasana on terms, 634/635 (Baladhuri)
cities.pre_greek_note: The rabbis identified Tiberias with biblical Rakkath; this is a tradition, not a firm attestation. Josephus says Antipas built it over graves.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek civic institutions (a boule of 600, archon, dekaprotoi: Josephus, BJ 2.641; Life 64-69, 296); Greek city coins; Greek dedications in the Hammat Tiberias synagogue (4th c.); seat of the Jewish Patriarchate and of the Aramaic Jerusalem Talmud
cities.status_evidence: Josephus AJ 18.36-38 and Life; Greek civic coins; see of Palaestina II

cities.other_names: Seleukeia (on coins); Abila of the Decapolis
cities.site: Quwaylibah (Tell Abil), Irbid Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins as Seleukeia Abila, dated by the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC, and a city of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74). Antiochus III took Abila in 218 BC (Polybius 5.71), but that passage says nothing of Greek speakers, and the name Seleukeia alone does not prove a Seleucid polis.
cities.until_text: Taken by the Arabs in 635-636; the town continued under the Umayyads and was damaged by the earthquake of 749. No later evidence for Greek speech. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the basilicas (6th-7th centuries); Umayyad occupation; earthquake of 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 635-636.
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.71; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins (Seleukeia Abila, Pompeian era); bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
cities.note: The name Seleukeia is known from the Roman-period coins; no Hellenistic Greek text of the city is known.

cities.site: Daraa, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends from the later 2nd century (Marcus Aurelius) to Gallienus, dated by the era of the province of Arabia; a polis by the 3rd century
cities.until_text: Taken in the Arab conquest of the Hauran, 634. The see continued, but there is no evidence of Greek speech beyond the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of residents into the 6th century; the last bishop known from the councils signed at Constantinople in 553
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: City coins showing the aniconic cult stone of Dushara (Dusares Theos); Nabataean and Arab names in the Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: City coins; Ptolemy 5.17; bishops at Seleucia 359, Constantinople 381, Chalcedon 451 and Constantinople 553
cities.note: Coin dates for the start of civic issues vary; the polis is secure by the Severan period.
sources: Spijkerman, The Coins of the Decapolis and Provincia Arabia (1978)

cities.site: As-Sanamayn, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Sopater 'of Errhe' among the bishops of Arabia at the Council of Nicaea, 325; the see is probably Aere, whose residents' Greek inscriptions go back to the 2nd c. (temple of Tyche, 191), when it was a village.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the temple of Tyche (191) and of the village. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek dedications of residents with Arab names at the temple of Tyche (AD 191) and other Greek inscriptions of the village.
cities.status_evidence: A see of Arabia named Erra/Errhe: bishop Sopater at Nicaea 325 (list of signatories); titular see 'Erra'. Aere was a large village and road station on the Damascus-Bostra road with Greek inscriptions of its residents.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts) as a see of the Greek-speaking church, and here Greek inscriptions of the residents are known. But the identification of the see of Erra with Aere (as-Sanamayn) is only a proposal; if it is wrong, Aere was a village. Vailhe reads the see's name in the Notitia Antiochena as Erra or Hierapolis.

cities.other_names: Metrocomia ('mother-village') of the Bacatheni (church lists); Safut? (Arabic)
cities.site: Safut, north-west of Amman, Balqa Governorate (tentative)
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Alypius of Bacatha at the second Council of Ephesus, 449.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Balqa, 634-636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Anthony, 649, after the conquest. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Balqa, 634-636; its bishop Anthony still corresponded with Rome in 649.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A 'mother-village' of the Philadelphene (Epiphanius) with bishops of the Greek-speaking church from 449 to 649.
cities.status_evidence: See with bishops Alypius (Ephesus 449), Gregory (451 or 518; the lists differ), Barachus (532/536) and Anthony (letters with Pope Martin I, 649) (Le Quien; Fedalto); listed as 'Metrocomia' under Petra and as Bacatha in the lists of Arabia; Epiphanius (Panarion) calls Bacatha a metrokomia of the Philadelphene.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A large village (metrokomia) that became a see, like Neila. The site is unknown; Safut near as-Salt is a tentative identification, so the point is only regional. The church lists put it under Petra or under Bostra; the two entries are probably one see.

cities.site: Busan, Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A Greek inscription names its bishop Menas, 573
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635; there is no later Greek evidence. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Inscription of bishop Menas (573). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Village of the Jabal al-Arab with Arab names in its Greek inscriptions; Safaitic texts in the steppe nearby
cities.status_evidence: Bishop attested in an inscription (573); titular see 'Bosana'
cities.note: A village with a bishop late in the 6th century; whether this was a full see or a rural bishop is unclear.

cities.other_names: Nea Traiane Bostra (from 106); Colonia Bostra (under Severus Alexander); Busra (Nabataean bṣrʾ); Busra al-Sham (Arabic)
cities.site: Busra al-Sham, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Made capital of the new province of Arabia as Nea Traiane Bostra when Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom, 106
cities.until_text: Administration: Bostra was the first Syrian city to surrender to the Arabs, 634. Speech: Greek inscriptions of residents continue through the 6th century; the Melkite see lasted, but the town became Arabic-speaking in the 8th-9th centuries.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek building inscriptions of the 6th century (cathedral 512/513); a Greek-writing bishop Stephen early 8th century (Le Quien); Arabic inscriptions from the Umayyad period
cities.ended_by: Surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid, with Shurahbil ibn Hasana, 634 (al-Baladhuri); no named act ended Greek speech.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Amarna Busruna is usually identified with Bostra.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean royal city under Rabbel II with Nabataean inscriptions into the 2nd century; the cult of Dushara-A'ra and the games Actia Dusaria; Arabic speakers in town and countryside; Greek civic inscriptions, coins and clergy
cities.status_evidence: Provincial capital of Arabia from 106; city coins; Roman colonia; metropolitan see of Arabia; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Greek became the language of public life only after 106; the Nabataean and Arab population stayed.

cities.other_names: Septimia Canatha (colonia under Septimius Severus); Gabinia (?); Qanawat (Arabic)
cities.site: Qanawat, Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Coins dated by the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC; one of the cities of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74)
cities.until_text: Passed to the Arabs in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Greek inscriptions of residents run into the 6th century; there is no evidence of Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the temple of Zeus Megistos and of the churches built into the 'Seraya'; bishops of Canatha at the councils
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635.
cities.refounded_by: Pompey (era of 64/63 BC); Septimius Severus (colonia Septimia Canatha)
cities.pre_greek_note: The identification of biblical Kenath with Qanawat is traditional but not proven.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean inscriptions at Canatha and at the nearby sanctuary of Si'; Safaitic and Arab names in the district
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Claudius to Domitian) with the Pompeian era; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15; Josephus BJ 1.366 (battle of Canatha, 32 BC); bishop's see of Arabia
cities.note: Some scholars distinguish Kanatha at Qanawat from a second Kanata at al-Kerak in the Hauran and give the Decapolis coins to one or the other; Qanawat is the usual identification.

cities.site: Buraq, northern edge of the Lajat, Rif Dimashq Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Chilon of Constantia at the Council of Constantinople, 381 (Le Quien put him at Nicaea, wrongly). The name honours the house of Constantine, but the dynastic name alone is not evidence.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.founder: an emperor of the house of Constantine (the name only)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of the province of Arabia, where the villagers of the Hauran set up Greek inscriptions with Arab names.
cities.status_evidence: See of Arabia under Bostra: bishops Chilon at Constantinople 381 and Solemus at Chalcedon 451 (Mansi); Notitia Antiochena. Waddington identified it 'with much likelihood' with Buraq, which had its own era and inscriptions of building works under Constantine.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts) as a see of the Greek-speaking church. If Waddington's identification with Buraq on the northern edge of the Lajat is right, the town's own inscriptions are known; it is not proven.

cities.site: Tell al-Ash'ari, Daraa Governorate (proposed)
cities.greek_from_text: Stephanus of Byzantium calls Dion a foundation of Alexander; the Macedonian name points to early Hellenistic settlers. First secure mention: taken by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 83 BC (Josephus AJ 13.393)
cities.until_text: Freed by Pompey in 63 BC; coins under the Severans. Its later history is little known; no evidence for Greek speech after the Arab conquest. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: City coins of the Severan period dated by the Pompeian era; a see 'Dia' in some lists. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 83 BC and freed by Pompey in 63 BC; it passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15; Josephus AJ 13.393, 14.75; city coins (Septimius Severus to Caracalla)
cities.note: The site is disputed: Tell al-Ash'ari in Syria, on the slopes of the Yarmuk valley, is generally assumed (two coins of Dion found in a tomb there); Kropp has suggested that the town centre lay at nearby Tafas, and Husn and Tell al-Husn in Jordan have also been proposed. The Alexander foundation may be a later claim. The coins (Septimius Severus to Caracalla, AD 204-208) use the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC.

cities.site: Al-Suwayda, Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Soada received civic status as Dionysias under Commodus, c. 180-185; Greek was already used beside Nabataean in the 1st century BC
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. No evidence of Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the basilica and of residents into the 6th century; bishops of Dionysias in the 5th-6th centuries
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Greek-Nabataean bilingual tomb inscription (Hamrat, 1st c. BC); Arab names in the Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.15; city inscriptions (a "lord builder Dionysos" honoured as founder); bishops Severus at Nicaea 325, Elpidius at Constantinople 381 and Maras at Chalcedon 451, and Peter in an inscription (Waddington 2327); Hierocles 723; Georgius Cyprius 1072; Notitia Antiochena (under Bostra)
cities.note: The grant of civic status under Commodus rests on inscriptions as read by Sartre and others; the exact year is not fixed.

cities.site: Tell Hisban, Amman Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins of Elagabalus (218-222) with Greek legends; Herod had fortified the place earlier (Josephus AJ 15.294)
cities.until_text: Passed to the Arabs in the conquest of the Balqa' (634-636); the see continued, but there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek mosaic inscriptions of churches (6th century); bishops of Esbus from 431; the mosaicist Staurachios 'of Esbus' signed the Greek floor of St Stephen at Umm ar-Rasas (756/785)
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Balqa', 634-636.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Arab and Nabataean names in the Greek inscriptions of the district; Herod settled soldiers in the Esebonitis
cities.status_evidence: City coins of Elagabalus; Ptolemy 5.16; bishop Zosys at Ephesus 431; Hierocles (Arabia)

cities.other_names: Antiocheia and Seleukeia (Seleucid names); Pompeia; Umm Qais (Arabic)
cities.site: Umm Qais, Irbid Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC as the strongest place in the district (Polybius 5.71); Menippus the Cynic was born there in the 3rd century BC
cities.until_text: Destroyed after a ten-month siege by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC and rebuilt by Pompey in 63 BC. Taken by the Arabs in 635-636; Umayyad occupation; damaged by the earthquake of 749, after which the town declined. The baths of Gadara at Hammat Gader were restored in 662 with a Greek inscription naming Mu'awiya and John of Gadara as the local supervisor, so the town's Greek is attested after the conquest. The date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750; the range starts at 662.
cities.fade_evidence: The Greek writers Menippus, Meleager, Philodemus, Theodorus and Oenomaus; Greek inscriptions of churches into the 6th-7th centuries; earthquake of 749. Greek building inscription of 5 December 662 (year 726 of the city, 42 of the Arabs) at Hammat Gader, the baths of Gadara: restored under Mu'awiya by the governor 'Abd Allah son of Abu Hashim, with John of Gadara supervising the work (Green and Tsafrir 1982; Hasson 1982). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 100 BC; rebuilt by Pompey, 63 BC. Passed to the Arabs in 635-636 (no named act for the city).
cities.refounded_by: Pompey 63 BC (for his freedman Demetrius of Gadara)
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 5.71; Josephus AJ 13.356, BJ 1.155; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; bishops at Nicaea 325 and later; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
cities.note: Meleager calls Gadara 'Attic among the Syrians'. The founder of the Hellenistic city is not known.

cities.site: Jerash, Jerash Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City era from Pompey's settlement of 63 BC and a city of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74). The name Antiocheia on the Chrysorhoas points to a renaming under Antiochus IV (175-164 BC), but the name alone does not prove a Greek polis, and the Hellenistic remains are not Greek texts; local traditions of Alexander or Perdiccas as founder are legends.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs in 634/635; an Umayyad provincial town with a mosque beside the churches. Speech: Greek inscriptions of residents run to 611 (church of Bishop Genesius). The earthquake of 18 January 749 wrecked the town, but it lived on as a smaller Abbasid settlement. With no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest, the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek church inscriptions to 611 (church of Bishop Genesius); Umayyad mosque and houses; earthquake of 18 January 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: Taken in the Arab conquest of 634/635, probably by troops under Shurahbil ibn Hasana; the earthquake of 749 ruined the town.
cities.pre_greek_note: Bronze and Iron Age remains lie under the city; no pre-Greek name is attested in non-Greek sources.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean and Arab names and a few Nabataean inscriptions in the Roman period; the countryside spoke Aramaic and Arabic
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; boule and demos in many Greek inscriptions; bishops at Seleucia 359 and Chalcedon 451; Hierocles (Arabia)
cities.note: Counted as a Hellenized native town: the Seleucid renaming is not matched by attested settlers, and the claims of Macedonian origin (Alexander, Perdiccas) are later civic traditions. Greek institutions are secure from the 1st century BC.
sources: Kraeling (ed.), Gerasa: City of the Decapolis (1938)

cities.site: Shaqqa, Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The village of Saccaea became the city of Maximianopolis under the Tetrarchs, c. 286-305; Greek inscriptions of residents from the 2nd century
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 'Kaisariye' and of churches; bishops of Maximianopolis in Arabia
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Arab names in the Greek inscriptions; a village of the Trachonitis-Hauran raised to a city
cities.status_evidence: Renamed city under the Tetrarchs; bishop's see of Arabia (councils; Notitia Antiochena)

cities.site: Madaba, Madaba Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends under the Severans (early 3rd century)
cities.until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs in 634-636. Speech: the Christian community still laid floors with Greek inscriptions under the Umayyads and early Abbasids (Church of the Virgin, 767); the town declined in the 9th century.
cities.fade_evidence: Madaba mosaic map (6th century); Greek mosaic inscriptions to 767 (Church of the Virgin) and at nearby Umm ar-Rasas (718, 756)
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the community dwindled in the 9th century.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean inscriptions of the 1st century AD; Arab names in the Greek mosaic inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Severan period); bishops of Medaba (councils); Hierocles (Arabia)
cities.note: The latest Greek mosaic inscriptions may have been written by Arabic-speaking Christians; the end date is an estimate.

cities.site: Khirbet en-Nila (proposed), As-Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed as a see of Arabia under Bostra in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570), as 'Neila or Nilakome'.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of the province of Arabia in the Hauran, where villagers set up Greek inscriptions with Arab names.
cities.status_evidence: A see of Arabia under Bostra in the Notitia Antiochena ('Neila or Nilakome', Vailhe); titular see Neila; 'Nelkomia/Neela?' in the Barrington Atlas (69 E4).
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A village (kome) that became a see; the site follows the Barrington Atlas, which marks it with a question mark.

cities.site: Nawa, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Its bishop Petronius attended the Council of Ephesus in 431 (Jobius at Chalcedon, 451); Greek inscriptions of residents are known from the town
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek funerary and building inscriptions (Roman and late Roman); bishops of Neve at the councils
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.other_language: Aramaic (including a Jewish community) and Arabic
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Jewish community with a synagogue (remains and Aramaic inscriptions); Arab and Aramaic names in the Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: Bishops Petronius at Ephesus 431 and Jobius at Chalcedon 451; Notitia Antiochena (under Bostra); Georgius Cyprius; Greek inscriptions (Revue biblique 3, 625)
cities.note: A large Hauran town that became a see; its first known bishop is from 431.

cities.site: Al-Mismiyah, northern Lajat, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: The metrokomia ("chief village") of the Trachonitis in a Greek edict of the governor Julius Saturninus, 185-187 (OGIS 609); a bishop's see whose bishops attended Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451)
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek edict of Julius Saturninus; the 'praetorium' temple of 160-169 with Greek inscriptions; bishops of Phaena
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: The 'metrokomia of the Trachon' with Arab names in its Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: Metrokomia of the Trachon (OGIS 609, on the temple); many Greek inscriptions of residents; bishops at Ephesus 431 and Chalcedon 451
cities.note: A chief village rather than a polis in the Roman period; counted from its first known bishop, 431.

cities.site: Amman Citadel and downtown, Amman Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Zeno Cotylas, a ruler with a Greek name, held Philadelphia as its tyrant c. 135 BC (Josephus AJ 13.235; BJ 1.60). Ptolemy II (285-246 BC) had renamed Rabbath-Ammon after himself (Stephanus; Jerome), but the Zenon papyri (259 BC) still call the district the Ammanitis and Polybius (5.71) calls the town Rabbatamana in 218 BC.
cities.until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs c. 635-636; an Umayyad governor's seat with a palace on the citadel. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians lived there into the Umayyad period; the earthquake of 749 damaged the town, and Arabic replaced Greek by the 9th century. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of churches in the 6th-7th centuries; Umayyad citadel; earthquake of 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act recorded for the city: it passed to the Arabs in the conquest of 635-636.
cities.pre_greek_name: Rabbat Bnê ʿAmmôn (Hebrew Bible); Bīt-Ammān (Akkadian, the kingdom)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean and Arab names in Greek inscriptions; Arabic-speaking countryside; Christian Palestinian Aramaic in the region
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins with Greek legends; Greek civic inscriptions; bishop's see of Arabia; Hierocles
cities.note: Ptolemaic soldiers settled in the district (Zenon papyri), but settlers in the city itself are not directly attested, so it is counted as a Hellenized native town. The renaming is known only from later writers; the Zenon papyri and Polybius still use the native name.

cities.site: Shahba, Suwayda Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Philip the Arab founded the city at his birthplace, 244-249 (Aurelius Victor 28.1), laid out with walls, theatre and baths
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. The town shrank; no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and mosaics of the 3rd-4th centuries; bishops of Philippopolis in Arabia
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Founded at the native village of the emperor Philip 'the Arab'; Arab names in the Greek inscriptions of residents
cities.status_evidence: Aurelius Victor 28.1; city coins of Philip; colonia; bishop's see of Arabia
cities.note: A new imperial foundation on a village site; It could also be counted a Greek city, as a Roman foundation.

cities.site: unlocated; Pleiades places it at the Raphon of 1 Maccabees in the Hauran, Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Listed among the cities of the Decapolis by Pliny (NH 5.74); the Raphon of 1 Maccabees 5:37 was then a settlement, not a known polis
cities.until_text: Known only from Pliny and Ptolemy; no later civic evidence. It may have merged into the territory of another city.
cities.fade_evidence: No inscriptions or coins securely assigned; not in the late Roman lists
cities.ended_by: No named act: the city drops out of the record after the 2nd century.
cities.status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15
cities.note: The location is uncertain: proposals include the Raphon of 1 Maccabees in the Hauran and a site south of Damascus; the Decapolis listing is the only evidence of civic status.

cities.site: Izra', Daraa Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A bishop's see of Arabia by the 6th century; Greek dedication of the church of St George by John son of Diomedes, 515
cities.until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscription of the church of St George (515) and of the church of St Elias (542)
cities.ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek building inscriptions of residents with Arab and Aramaic names; the Christian community still worships in the 6th-century church
cities.status_evidence: Greek dedication of the church of St George, 515, by John son of Diomedes, a proteuon (leading councillor) of the town (IGLS XV 244); bishop's see of Arabia (Le Quien; titular see Zorava)
cities.note: Counted as a village that became a see; its Christian community, now Arabic-speaking, is continuous.

cities.other_names: Aelana; Ailana; Berenike (Josephus); Ayla (Arabic); Elath (Hebrew Bible)
cities.site: Aqaba, Aqaba Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A city and bishopric by 325, when its bishop attended Nicaea; garrison of Legio X Fretensis from c. 300; earliest purpose-built church (late 3rd century)
cities.until_text: Its lord John son of Ru'ba made a treaty with Muhammad at Tabuk in 630; an Islamic walled town (Ayla) was built beside the old one c. 650. No later evidence for Greek speech. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Church of c. 300; bishops of Aila to the 6th century; the new Islamic town of Ayla (c. 650). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: John son of Ru'ba, lord of Ayla, submitted to Muhammad by treaty at Tabuk, 630 (Ibn Ishaq); the caliphate built a new town beside it c. 650.
cities.pre_greek_note: Biblical Elath is often placed at Tell el-Kheleifeh nearby rather than under Aila itself.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean port; its Christian lord in 630, John son of Ru'ba, bore a Greek name and an Arab patronym
cities.status_evidence: Bishop at Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Palaestina III); Notitia Antiochena
cities.note: Greek-speaking residents are inferred mainly from the church and garrison; the population was largely Nabataean and Arab.

cities.site: Tel Arad, west of the modern town of Arad, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop Stephen of Arad at the synod of Jerusalem, 518 (Le Quien).
cities.until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs with the Negev in the 630s. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Last bishop known: Stephen, 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs with the Negev in the 630s.
cities.pre_greek_name: 'Arad (Hebrew Bible; Egyptian 'rd in Shoshenq I's list)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A village of the Negev that became a see of Palaestina III.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra: bishop Stephen at the synods of Jerusalem, 518 and 536 (Le Quien); Eusebius (Onomasticon) calls Arad a village.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A village that became a see; the late Roman settlement is placed at or near Tel Arad, whose Hellenistic Greek ostraca belong to a garrison.

cities.site: Al-Rabba, Karak Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends (Rabbathmoba-Areopolis) under the Severans; a Greek census return of 127 in the Babatha archive was filed there
cities.until_text: Passed to the Arabs in 634-636. The see continued for a time; there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 4th-6th centuries; bishops of Areopolis; the city on the Madaba map. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
cities.pre_greek_note: Greek 'Areopolis' was linked to biblical Ar of Moab; the identification is uncertain.
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Nabataean town of Moab; Babatha's documents (Greek and Aramaic, 2nd century) were registered at Rabbathmoba; Arab names in its Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Severans); Babatha papyri (P.Yadin 16); bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
sources: Yadin and others, The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period (P.Yadin 16)

cities.site: Gharandal, Tafilah Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Its bishops are listed from 431 (Gams, after Le Quien).
cities.until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the neighbouring towns of Adhruh and Jarba had made treaties with Muhammad in 630. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Last bishop known: 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the neighbouring towns of Adhruh and Jarba had made treaties with Muhammad in 630 (Ibn Ishaq).
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of Palaestina III in an Arab and Nabataean district.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra, with bishops from 431 to 536 (Le Quien; Gams); Hierocles.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known.

cities.site: Udhruh, Ma'an Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Bishop John of Augustopolis at the Council of Ephesus, 431.
cities.until_text: Administration: the people of Adhruh made a treaty with Muhammad during the Tabuk expedition, 630; the region passed to the Arabs in 634-636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop John, 536; the Petra papyri (6th c.). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: The people of Adhruh submitted to Muhammad by treaty during the Tabuk expedition, 630 (Ibn Ishaq; al-Waqidi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: A see of Palaestina III beside a legionary fortress; the Greek Petra papyri (6th c.) name the place.
cities.status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra: bishop John at Ephesus 431; a second John at the synod of Jerusalem, 536; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena.
cities.note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Augustopolis is usually placed at Udhruh, a legionary fortress with a small town and a church outside its walls; the identification is common but not certain.

cities.site: Al-Karak, Karak Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends under the Severans
cities.until_text: Passed to the Arabs in 634-636. A Christian community survived into the Crusader and Ottoman periods, Arabic-speaking; there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: City shown on the Madaba map; bishops of Charachmoba; the later Christians of Karak used Arabic.
