Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
cities.pre_greek_name: Qîr-Ḥareśet / Qîr Môʾāb (Hebrew Bible, 2 Kings 3:25; Isaiah 15:1)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Nabataean and then Arab town of Moab; the Greek name keeps the Aramaic karka, 'fortified town'
cities.status_evidence: City coins (Severans); Ptolemy 5.16; bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina III)

cities.site: Halutza (Khalasa) ruins, Ramat HaNegev, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: Greek city by the 4th c.: Zenobius and other rhetors from Elusa; listed by Ptolemy (5.16.10) as a town of Idumaea; a Nabataean town since the 2nd c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration: the Negev came under the caliphs in the 630s. Speech: Greek papyri at nearby Nessana run to c. 690, when Arabic took over the tax documents; Elusa was abandoned by the 8th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Nessana papyri (Greek to c. 690; Greek-Arabic bilingual documents from the 670s); abandonment of the town in the 7th-8th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the Negev came under the caliphs in the 630s; Greek gave way to Arabic in the documents by c. 690 and the town was abandoned
cities.pre_greek_note: A Nabataean inscription of the 2nd c. BC found at Elusa names a king Aretas; no non-Greek form of the town's name older than the rabbinic Halutza is attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: The sophist Zenobius of Elusa taught Greek rhetoric at Antioch (d. 354) and Libanius writes of rhetors from Elusa; Greek inscriptions and papyri; in Jerome's Life of Hilarion (25) the townspeople greet Hilarion in 'Syriac', a Semitic tongue, and worship Venus
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.16.10; Hierocles (Palaestina III); see of Palaestina III with bishops from the 5th c.; Madaba map; Nessana papyri
cities.note: Some scholars think Elusa was the capital of Palaestina III for a time.

cities.site: Mamshit National Park, near Dimona, Southern District
cities.greek_from_text: First attested as a city in late antiquity: Hierocles lists Mampsis in Palaestina III; Greek church inscriptions of the late 4th-5th c.
cities.until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the town was abandoned in the 7th c., around the Arab conquest of the Negev.
cities.fade_evidence: Late Roman churches and houses; abandonment in the 7th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town was abandoned around the Arab conquest of the 630s
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek mosaic inscriptions in its two churches (late 4th-5th c.) and Greek epitaphs; a Nabataean town in origin with Arab names among its people
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles (Palaestina III); Eusebius, Onomasticon; see of Palaestina III
cities.note: A small walled town; its civic rank rests on Hierocles and the church lists.

cities.other_names: Reqem (Nabataean rqmw); Hadriane Petra Metropolis; Colonia Antoniniana Petra
cities.site: Petra, beside the town of Wadi Musa, Ma'an Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Annexed by Trajan in 106 and made a metropolis (Hadriane Petra Metropolis from 114 or 130); Greek was already used in Nabataean Petra for some inscriptions in the 1st century
cities.until_text: Capital of Palaestina III. The city declined after the earthquakes of 363 and 551; the Greek Petra papyri end in the 590s; there is no record of its conquest, and the town was largely abandoned by the 7th-8th century.
cities.fade_evidence: Petra papyri (537-593), burnt in the church c. 600; Greek inscriptions of the churches; earthquakes of 363 and 551
cities.ended_by: No named act: the city declined after the earthquakes of 363 and 551; the Arab conquest of the 630s is not recorded for Petra.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Nabataean royal capital with Nabataean inscriptions to the 4th century; the Petra papyri (6th century) are Greek documents of landowners with Arabic names and Arabic field names
cities.status_evidence: Nabataean capital; metropolis of Arabia; city coins; Roman colonia; metropolitan see of Palaestina III; Hierocles; Petra papyri
cities.note: Greek became a main language only under Roman rule; Nabataean Aramaic and Arabic stayed in use.
sources: Frosen and others, The Petra Papyri I-V

cities.site: Khirbet Faynan, Wadi Araba, Tafilah Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: A see of Palaestina III by the 5th century; earlier a mining settlement where Christian convicts worked in the 300s
cities.until_text: Mining and the town declined in the 7th century; passed to the Arabs in the 630s. No later evidence for Greek speech.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek Christian tombstones from the cemetery; bishops of Phaeno (5th-6th centuries)
cities.ended_by: No named act: the mining town declined and passed to the Arabs in the 630s.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Copper mines worked by convicts, including Christians from Egypt and Palestine (Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 7, 13); Greek Christian tombstones; a local Arab population
cities.status_evidence: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine; bishops of Phaeno; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
cities.note: A mining settlement that became a see; whether it was a city in more than the church's sense is doubtful.

cities.other_names: Zoora; Segor; Zoar (Hebrew Bible); Ghor es-Safi (Arabic)
cities.site: Ghor es-Safi, southeast of the Dead Sea, Karak Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek legal documents of residents of the district of Zoara in the Babatha archive, from 110
cities.until_text: A see of Palaestina III. Greek Christian tombstones dated by the era of Arabia run from the 4th to at least the 6th century. Passed to the Arabs in the 630s; the later Islamic town of Zughar was Arabic-speaking. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek tombstones of the an-Naq cemetery (mid-4th to 6th century and later); Jewish Aramaic tombstones (4th-6th centuries); the city on the Madaba map. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in the 630s.
cities.bilingual_evidence: The Babatha archive (Mahoza in the district of Zoara, 110-132) in Greek, Nabataean and Jewish Aramaic; Jewish Aramaic tombstones and some 400 Greek Christian tombstones from the town
cities.status_evidence: Babatha papyri; Ptolemy 5.16 (Zoara); bishops of Zoara; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
cities.note: Whether Zoara was a polis in the 2nd century is unclear; it is secure as a see by the 4th-5th century.
sources: Meimaris and Kritikakou-Nikolaropoulou, Inscriptions from Palaestina Tertia Ia (2005)
Yadin and others, The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period

cities.site: unlocated; on the Pallacopas canal west of the Euphrates, towards the Arabian side, perhaps near Najaf or Kufa, Najaf Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: In spring 323 BC Alexander sailed down the Pallacopas canal, founded and walled a city there and settled in it Greek mercenaries who volunteered and men unfit for service by age or wounds (Arrian, Anab. 7.21.7)
cities.until_text: Never mentioned again after Arrian's account of its foundation; it probably did not survive long after Alexander's death. Some identify it with the Alexandria near Babylon of the Alexander Romance.
cities.fade_evidence: Only Arrian 7.21.7 (from Aristobulus); no later trace
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town is not heard of after its foundation
cities.status_evidence: Alexander foundation with Greek settlers (Arrian, Anab. 7.21.7); Cohen 2013
cities.note: A real foundation with Greek settlers, but unlocated and without any later history; the phase is given as the foundation year only, with the possible end in the range.
sources: Wikipedia: List of cities founded by Alexander the Great

cities.other_names: Weh-Andiyok-Khosrow, 'Khosrow's better Antioch' (Middle Persian); Rumagan (Persian); al-Rumiyya (Arabic); perhaps Mahoze Hadatta, 'the New City' (Syriac)
cities.site: near Salman Pak (al-Mada'in), Baghdad Governorate; exact site not identified
cities.greek_from_text: Khosrow I founded it near Ctesiphon for the people of Antioch whom he had taken captive in 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.14.1-4; al-Tabari)
cities.until_text: The captives of Antioch were Greek speakers; the town still had about 30,000 people in the late 6th c., and John of Ephesus (writing to the 580s) knows it. No Greek text from the town survives, and its people lived among Syriac- and Persian-speaking neighbours, so Greek speech probably faded within a few generations. The Arabs took it by treaty with the other towns of al-Mada'in in 637; as al-Rumiyya it was briefly the residence of the caliph al-Mansur in 754-755, when Abu Muslim was killed there, and it was deserted by the 10th c.
cities.fade_evidence: Procopius, Wars 2.14 (540s); John of Ephesus, HE III.6.19 (late 6th c.) still names the city; the Arabic name al-Rumiyya, 'the Roman (town)', recalls its origin
cities.ended_by: No named act for Greek speech, which is not attested after the late 6th c. In the Arab conquest of al-Mada'in the vanguard of Khalid ibn Urfuta, in the army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, made a treaty with the people of al-Rumiyya, who could leave or stay and pay tribute; Sa'd entered al-Mada'in in March 637 (al-Tabari; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Madaen)
cities.other_language: Syriac (deportees from Sura, Callinicum and Batnae and the local population)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Procopius (Wars 2.14.1-4): Khosrow I settled the captives of Antioch here, built them a bath and a hippodrome and brought their charioteers and musicians; Jacob of Edessa names captives from Antioch, Sura, Beroea, Apamea, Callinicum and Batnae
cities.status_evidence: Royal Sasanian foundation laid out on the plan of Antioch, with bath and hippodrome (Procopius, Wars 2.14; al-Tabari); about 30,000 inhabitants in the late 6th c.
cities.note: A town built for captives. Classed as bilingual because the deportees came from both Greek- and Syriac-speaking towns.
sources: Canepa 2009, The Two Eyes of the Earth

cities.other_names: Chalasar (its name in Isidore's day, Parthian Stations 2)
cities.site: Karastel, near Baqubah, Diyala Governorate; identification probable
cities.greek_from_text: First attested through the Greek historian Apollodorus of Artemita, author of the Parthika, c. 100 BC (Strabo 2.5.12, 11.7.3, 11.11.1); probably a Seleucid foundation of the 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 2, c. AD 1) calls it 'a Greek city' on the Silla river. By AD 36 Tacitus (Ann. 6.41) lists Halus and Artemita as 'Parthian towns', in contrast with the 'Macedonian' foundations, which may mean that Greek no longer marked it. Later the Sasanian palace town of Dastagird lay nearby.
cities.fade_evidence: Apollodorus of Artemita, c. 100 BC; Isidore 2 (c. AD 1): 'a Greek city'; Tacitus Ann. 6.41 (AD 36): a Parthian town
cities.ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested c. AD 1
cities.pre_greek_note: Isidore says the city was by then called Chalasar, a name known only from his Greek text; whether it was the older native name is unknown.
cities.status_evidence: Isidore, Parthian Stations 2 ('a Greek city'); Strabo 16.1.17 (city of Apolloniatis); Apollodorus of Artemita; Cohen 2013
cities.note: The site is not excavated and the identification with Karastel is not certain. Whether it was a Seleucid colony or a Hellenized native town (Chalasar) is unknown.

cities.site: Babil, north of Hillah, Babil Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Antiochus IV settled a community of Greek citizens (politai) in Babylon c. 173/172 BC: the politai first appear in the Politai Chronicle (BCHP 13) in 172 BC, the Greek Community Chronicle (BCHP 14) says they 'entered Babylon at the command of Antiochus' and anointed themselves like the politai of Seleucia, and OGIS 253 (166 BC) calls Antiochus IV 'founder of the city'. Greeks had lived in Babylon since Alexander (331 BC), whose time the first theatre is dated to.
cities.until_text: The politai appear in cuneiform texts until 77 BC; the Greek ephebic list of 111/110 BC (under Mithridates II) shows the gymnasium still active. A Greek inscription recording a repair of the theatre and its stage building by one Dioskourides is dated by its letter forms to the 2nd c. AD, the last evidence of the Greek community. Strabo (16.1.5) already calls Babylon largely deserted, and Trajan in 116 is said to have seen only mounds and ruins (Cassius Dio 68.30.1). The Greek community faded with the town itself.
cities.fade_evidence: Politai in the astronomical diaries 169-77 BC; Greek ephebic victor list, 111/110 BC (Louvre); Graeco-Babyloniaca (cuneiform texts transcribed in Greek letters), 1st c. BC; last cuneiform tablet AD 79/80; Greek inscription for the repair of the theatre and its stage building, naming one Dioskouri[des], dated to the 2nd c. AD by its letter forms only (Livius: 'The Babylon theater inscription'); Trajan saw only mounds and ruins, 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.1); Severus found Babylon deserted, 198 (Cassius Dio 76.9.3)
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town declined after Seleucia drew away its people (Pliny 6.122; Strabo 16.1.5); the Greek community is last attested in the 2nd c. AD
cities.other_language: Babylonian Akkadian (temple and scribal circles of the Esagila, written until AD 79/80) and Aramaic (common speech)
cities.bilingual_evidence: A community of Greek citizens (politai) with its own gymnasium and theatre lived beside the Babylonian temple community; Greek ephebic victor list of 111/110 BC; Greek theatre-repair inscription of the 2nd c. AD
cities.status_evidence: Greek politai, gymnasium and theatre (BCHP 13-14; OGIS 253; ephebic list of 111/110 BC); Alexander's capital
cities.note: The Greek polis was a community of citizens inside a Babylonian city that kept its temple assembly, so it is classed as bilingual. Alexander died here in 323 BC.
sources: van der Spek 2005, 'Ethnic segregation in Hellenistic Babylon'
Livius: BCHP 14 (Greek Community Chronicle); Babylon theater inscription

cities.other_names: Alexandria (Alexander); Antiochia (Antiochus IV); Karka d-Maishan (Syriac); Astarabad-Ardashir (Sasanian refoundation); Spasinou Charax
cities.site: Jebel Khayabir (Naysan), north of Basra, Basra Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Alexander founded it as Alexandria in 324 BC on an artificial mound, settling invalid Macedonian soldiers and people from the royal town of Durine (Pliny 6.138); Antiochus IV refounded it as Antiochia after a flood, completed 166/165 BC; later Hyspaosines rebuilt its dykes and gave it his name (Pliny 6.139)
cities.until_text: Greek administration ended when Hyspaosines, the Seleucid governor of Mesene, made himself king after 141 BC; the Greek language lived on under his dynasty, whose coins carry Greek legends: Hyspaosines (125-121 BC), Artabazos (48/47 BC) and Mithradates (AD 142/143). The geographer Isidore of Charax wrote in Greek c. AD 1. From the second half of the 2nd c. AD the coins are uninscribed or carry Aramaic legends in the local dialect. Ardashir I ended the kingdom in 221/222. No Greek-speaking community is attested in the Sasanian town.
cities.fade_evidence: Isidore of Charax, Greek writer from the city, c. AD 1; Greek-legend coins of the kings of Characene to Mithradates (AD 142/143), then Aramaic legends from the later 2nd c. AD; Greek and Palmyrene inscriptions at Palmyra honouring the caravans and merchants of Spasinou Charax, 1st-2nd c. AD
cities.ended_by: No named act for Greek speech: Ardashir I conquered Mesene in 221/222, killed its last king Bandu and refounded Charax as Astarabad-Ardashir (al-Tabari)
cities.refounded_by: Antiochus IV (as Antiochia, 166/165 BC); Hyspaosines of Characene, governor from 166/165 BC and independent from c. 141-139 BC (as Spasinou Charax)
cities.other_language: Aramaic, and Arabic in the Characene kingdom (Palmyrene and local Aramaic inscriptions; Aramaic legends replace Greek on the royal coins in the 2nd c. AD)
cities.bilingual_evidence: Royal coins of Characene with Greek legends, later with Aramaic legends; a mixed population of Greeks, Aramaeans, Arabs and Palmyrene traders
cities.status_evidence: Alexander foundation (Pliny 6.138-139); capital of Characene; royal coinage with Greek legends; Isidore of Charax
cities.note: Greek city by foundation; how far Greek remained the main language under the Characene kings (2nd c. BC to 3rd c. AD) is uncertain. The site at Jebel Khayabir (Naysan), north of Basra, is now confirmed by the aerial, drone and geophysical surveys of Stefan Hauser's team (University of Konstanz), which mapped its walls, streets, canals and very large housing blocks.
sources: Hauser, Konstanz survey (reported in Archaeology, Feb. 2026)

cities.other_names: Demetrias on the Tigris (coin legend 'of the Demetrians on the Tigris')
cities.site: unlocated; Strabo puts it near Arbela (Erbil), the coins 'on the Tigris'; Erbil or Nineveh Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: No source records the foundation: the name points to Demetrius I Soter (162-150 BC), perhaps after his victory over the rebel Timarchus c. 160 BC, or to Demetrius II (145-139 BC); the civic bronze coins of the 'Demetrians on the Tigris', with Tyche and tripod, belong to the same period if they are this city's
cities.until_text: The civic coins belong to the Seleucid period; Assyria passed to Parthia and the kings of Adiabene from the 120s BC. Strabo (16.1.4, c. AD 20) still names Demetrias as a city near Arbela. Nothing later is known.
cities.fade_evidence: Civic bronze coinage, 2nd c. BC; Strabo 16.1.4 (c. AD 20); Stephanus s.v. Demetrias
cities.ended_by: No named act: no evidence after Strabo
cities.status_evidence: Civic bronze coinage with Greek legend (DEMETRIEON TON PROS TOI TIGREI); Strabo 16.1.4 ('the city of Demetrias'); Stephanus
cities.note: Site unknown; it may have been a refoundation of an Assyrian town. The 'on the Tigris' coins are usually given to this Demetrias, but they might belong to another city under a temporary dynastic name (Seleucia on the Tigris has been suggested); without them the city rests on Strabo and Stephanus alone.

cities.site: Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus, east Mosul, Nineveh Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Resettled in the Seleucid period; Greek inscriptions, Greek cults and civic officials (strategos and epistates of the city) of the late Hellenistic and Parthian period
cities.until_text: The Greek inscriptions belong to the 1st c. BC and the 1st c. AD; Damis, a Greek-writing companion of Apollonius of Tyana, came from Ninos in the 1st c. AD. Tacitus (Ann. 12.13) mentions the city in AD 49. No Greek evidence is known after the 2nd c. AD; the town lived on as an Aramaic-speaking Christian centre opposite Mosul.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek civic inscriptions, 1st c. BC-1st c. AD (Reade 1998); Damis of Nineveh, 1st c. AD; marble Herakles Epitrapezios, 2nd c. AD; by 554 Nineveh was a see of the Church of the East, with Syriac as its language
cities.ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested in the 1st-2nd c. AD
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek inscriptions, one on a shrine of the Sebitti and one naming a strategos and epistates of the city; Greek sculpture (Hermes; Herakles Epitrapezios, 2nd c. AD); Damis of Nineveh, whose memoirs Philostratus says were written in Greek (Life of Apollonius 1.3, 1.19)
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid refoundation as a polis with 'at least the superficial forms of Hellenistic city organization' (Oates 1968, 61); Greek inscriptions of the Parthian period naming a strategos and epistates of the city, and Greek dedications (Reade 1998); Greek sculpture (Herakles Epitrapezios); Damis of Ninos (Philostratus); Tacitus Ann. 12.13 (AD 49)
cities.note: Nineveh was a small town after 612 BC; the Greek inscriptions show a Greek-style civic government in Parthian Adiabene, but the size of the Greek-speaking community is unknown. Philostratus' Damis may be a literary invention.
sources: Oates 1968, Studies in the Ancient History of Northern Iraq, 61
Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage: Nineveh

cities.other_names: Seleucia ad Tigrim (Latin); Seliq/Sliq, later Sliq Kharawta, 'ruined Seleucia' (Syriac), part of Mahoze; Coche was the quarter on the opposite bend where the Sasanian Veh-Ardashir rose c. 230
cities.site: Tell Umar, near al-Mada'in (Salman Pak), Baghdad Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucus I founded it on the Tigris near Opis as his eastern capital, c. 307-305 BC (Strabo 16.1.5; Pliny 6.122; Appian Syr. 58); Antiochus I moved settlers from Babylon there in 275/274 BC (Babylonian astronomical diary)
cities.until_text: Greek administration ended when Mithridates I of Parthia took the city in 141 BC, but the polis lived on as a self-governing Greek city under Parthian rule: Tacitus (Ann. 6.42) praises its council of 300 and says it had 'not sunk into barbarism' but kept the ways of its founder. Its Greeks fought the Syrians and then, reconciled with them, massacred the city's Jews c. AD 35-40 (Josephus AJ 18.372-379) and held out against the Parthian kings in a seven-year revolt, AD 35-42 (Tacitus Ann. 11.8-9). Trajan's generals Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander burned it in 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.2). In 165 the army of Avidius Cassius, under Lucius Verus, sacked and burned it after it had received the Romans as friends (Cassius Dio 71.2.3; HA Verus 8.3-4); Eutropius (8.10) and Orosius (7.15.3) speak of 400,000 people taken. When Septimius Severus came in 198 he found it deserted (Cassius Dio 76.9.3). The Sasanian city of Veh-Ardashir later rose beside the site, with no attested Greek-speaking community.
cities.fade_evidence: Civic bronze coins with Greek legends (Tyche types), struck into the 1st c. AD; Greek and Parthian bilingual inscription on the bronze Herakles that Vologases IV set up in the temple of Apollo at Seleucia after conquering Mesene, AD 150/151; Greek ostraca and seal impressions from the excavations; deserted by 198 (Cassius Dio 76.9.3)
cities.ended_by: Sacked and burned by the Roman army of Avidius Cassius under Lucius Verus, 165 (Cassius Dio 71.2.3; HA Verus 8.3-4), after Trajan's generals Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander had burned it in 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.2)
cities.pre_greek_note: Built near the old town of Opis (Akkadian Upi), which it replaced; the exact relation of the two sites is uncertain.
cities.other_language: Aramaic, spoken by the 'Syrians' of the city and by its Jewish community, beside Greek by the 1st c. AD
cities.bilingual_evidence: Josephus (AJ 18.372-379) describes the Greeks and the Syrians as the two parties of the city c. AD 35-40, with the Jews siding with the Syrians
cities.status_evidence: Seleucid royal foundation; council of 300 (Tacitus Ann. 6.42); civic coinage; 600,000 inhabitants in Pliny 6.122; Strabo 16.1.16
cities.note: The largest Greek city of the East after Antioch and Alexandria. Treated as a Greek city with a bilingual period because Aramaic-speaking Syrians and Jews formed a large part of the population by the 1st c. AD.

cities.other_names: Uruk (Akkadian; Sumerian Unug); Erech (Hebrew Bible); Orchoe (Ptolemy 5.20.7); Orcheni, its astronomers (Strabo 16.1.6; Pliny 6.123); Warka (Arabic)
cities.site: Tell al-Warka, Al-Muthanna Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek seal legends of the record office and Greek double names of residents from the late 3rd c. BC; no Greek civic institutions are attested
cities.until_text: The last Greek text is an honorary decree found in the Gareus temple, which dates the temple to 422 of the Seleucid era, AD 110/111 (Meier 1960); a decree in Greek implies that the town's assembly still used Greek. The cuneiform temple culture ended in the 1st c. BC, and the Parthian town declined in the 2nd-3rd c. AD.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek seal impressions of the record office, 3rd-2nd c. BC; Greek name of Anu-uballit Kephalon, 202/201 BC; Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, AD 110/111
cities.ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested at Uruk in AD 110/111; the town shrank and was largely deserted by early Sasanian times
cities.other_language: Babylonian Akkadian (temple scribes and astronomers) and Aramaic
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek names in the leading Babylonian families (Anu-uballit Nikarchos, governor under Antiochus II; Anu-uballit Kephalon, builder of the Bit Resh, 202/201 BC); thousands of clay sealings with Greek seal legends of the city's record office (chreophylakes of Orchoi); a Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, AD 110/111
cities.status_evidence: Ancient city with temple assembly; Greek record office (chreophylax) seal impressions; Greek honorary decree of AD 110/111; Ptolemy 5.20.7; Strabo 16.1.6
cities.note: Whether more than a Hellenized elite spoke Greek at Uruk is debated; Greek double names may be honorific. Kept on the strength of the Greek record office and the Greek honorary decree of AD 110/111.
sources: Meier 1960, Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, Baghdader Mitteilungen 1

cities.site: Bushehr (proposed), Bushehr peninsula, Bushehr province (proposed; Rishahr and Tawwaj are other candidates)
cities.greek_from_text: Founded or refounded by Antiochus I, probably while co-ruler with Seleucus I (c. 294-281 BC), with colonists sent at his request by Magnesia on the Maeander (OGIS 233).
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid into the reign of Antiochus IV (royal coins struck there, 175-164 BC); Persis then passed to its own frataraka dynasts and under Parthian overlordship (c. 140 BC). Speech: the last evidence of the Greek city is the decree of 205 BC and the coins of Antiochus IV.
cities.fade_evidence: Decree of the Antiochenes accepting the Leukophryena of Magnesia, 205 BC (OGIS 233; I.Magnesia 61); Seleucid royal coins of the mint of Antioch in Persis under Antiochus IV.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Seleucid rule in Persis ended under the frataraka dynasts and Mithridates I of Parthia (c. 140 BC); nothing is known of the city later.
cities.founder: Antiochus I (with colonists from Magnesia on the Maeander)
cities.status_evidence: OGIS 233 (I.Magnesia 61): decree of the boule and demos, with executive magistrates and treasurers, 205 BC; Antiochus III's letter to Magnesia after receiving its envoys at Antioch in Persis (OGIS 231).
cities.note: A full Greek polis whose site is unknown; Bushehr follows Pleiades and recent work. Rew-Ardashir (Rishahr), a Sasanian deportee town on the same peninsula, is a separate entry.

cities.site: near Aradan (Khuvar/Choara), Garmsar area, Semnan province (proposed)
cities.greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation named after Apama, wife of Seleucus I (c. 300-280 BC); one of the Macedonian foundations of Media in Strabo 11.13.6.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian advance into Choarene and Media in the 2nd c. BC (Mithridates I, c. 148/147 BC). Speech: no evidence of the Greek community after the Seleucid period; Isidore (late 1st c. BC) still names Apameia as a city.
cities.fade_evidence: No inscriptions; known from Strabo, Pliny and Isidore only.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the region passed to the Parthians, decisively under Mithridates I c. 148/147 BC.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (Macedonian foundation); Pliny NH 6.43 (Apamea Rhagiane); Isidore of Charax 8 (city of Choarene).
cities.note: Location unknown; the Barrington Atlas places it tentatively near Aradan with Choara, though Pliny keeps Apamea and Choara apart.

cities.site: Bishapur ruins near Kazerun, Fars province
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Shapur I c. 266 and peopled in part with Roman captives (Chronicle of Seert).
cities.until_text: Administration: Sasanian city and East-Syrian see; taken by the Arabs in the conquest of Fars (640s). Speech: no attestation of Greek speakers after the founding generation.
cities.fade_evidence: Roman-style floor mosaics and Greek letters on Shapur I's monument (3rd c.); nothing later.
cities.ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; the city fell in the Arab conquest of Fars in the 640s.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Named by the Chronicle of Seert among the cities peopled with Shapur I's captives; Roman-style mosaics and Greek letters on Shapur I's monument point to Roman workmen.
cities.status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert; Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam; royal city of Shapur I.
cities.note: Roman captives certainly worked there; a lasting Greek-speaking community is not directly attested.

cities.site: unlocated, in western Parthia between the Caspian Gates and Hecatompylos (Semnan province)
cities.greek_from_text: Named by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities Seleucus I founded in Parthia, with Soteira, Charis, Hecatompylos and Achaia; Pliny names it among the cities of Parthia (6.44) and places it with Issatis on the west side, short of the desert (6.113). No foundation date is recorded: the reign of Seleucus I (312-281 BC).
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Arsaces I's Parni took Parthia c. 238 BC; Antiochus III campaigned there in 209 BC (Polybius 10.28-31) but left the land to Arsaces II; then Parthian. Speech: nothing is known of the town after its foundation. The end is an estimate, as for Hecatompylos.
cities.fade_evidence: No inscriptions or coins; known only from Appian and Pliny.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Parthia was taken from the Seleucids by Arsaces I c. 238 BC; nothing is recorded of the town.
cities.status_evidence: Appian, Syr. 57 (foundation of Seleucus I); Pliny 6.44, 6.113.
cities.note: Unlocated: the point marks western Parthia, west of Hecatompylos, following Pliny. Earlier left out because Parthia spans north-eastern Iran and southern Turkmenistan; Pliny's placing puts it in Iran. The Muse's name is one of Seleucus' Greek names for new cities, not a dynastic name.

cities.site: Sarpol-e Zahab, Kermanshah Province (Iran), near the Iraqi border
cities.greek_from_text: Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 3, late 1st c. BC) calls Chala 'a Greek city' in Chalonitis
cities.until_text: Known as Greek only from Isidore. Later Hulwan was a Sasanian and early Islamic town on the Khorasan road, with no attested Greek speakers.
cities.fade_evidence: Isidore 3 (late 1st c. BC/early 1st c. AD) is the only evidence
cities.ended_by: No named act: no evidence after Isidore
cities.status_evidence: Isidore, Parthian Stations 3 ('a Greek city'); Cohen 2013
cities.note: Lies in Iran, just across the border from Iraq; included here because it sits on the road from Seleucia through Apolloniatis. The identification of Chala with Hulwan is usual but not certain.

cities.site: unlocated, in the Seleucid satrapy of Parthia (Semnan or Razavi Khorasan province)
cities.greek_from_text: Named only by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities Seleucus I founded in Parthia. No date is recorded: the reign of Seleucus I (312-281 BC).
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Arsaces I's Parni took Parthia c. 238 BC; Antiochus III campaigned there in 209 BC (Polybius 10.28-31) but left the land to Arsaces II; then Parthian. Speech: nothing is known of the town after its foundation. The end is an estimate, as for Hecatompylos.
cities.fade_evidence: Known only from Appian's list.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Parthia was taken from the Seleucids by Arsaces I c. 238 BC; nothing is recorded of the town.
cities.status_evidence: Appian, Syr. 57 (foundation of Seleucus I).
cities.note: Unlocated: the point marks the satrapy of Parthia, whose centre was Hecatompylos, in present-day Iran. Appian names it with Calliope and Hecatompylos; nothing places it in Turkmenistan. Known only from one list, the weakest case among the Parthian foundations.

cities.other_names: Weh-Andiyok-Shabuhr, 'Shapur's better Antioch' (Middle Persian); Bet Lapat (Syriac); Bendosaboron (late Greek form); Jundaysabur (Arabic)
cities.site: Shahabad (Eslamabad) village near Dezful, Khuzestan province
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Shapur I for captives from Antioch (taken 253 and/or 260) and named 'Shapur's better Antioch'; the archaeology shows no earlier settlement.
cities.until_text: Administration: Sasanian city, later capital of Khuzistan and East-Syrian metropolitan see of Bet Huzaye; surrendered to the Arabs c. 638. Speech: the deportees' Greek is not recorded after the founding generations; their descendants merged into the Syriac- and Persian-speaking Church of the East, and teaching in the city's school was in Syriac.
cities.fade_evidence: Chronicle of Seert on the Antiochene clergy and bishop Demetrianus (3rd c.); the synod of 410 already lists Bet Lapat as a Syriac see; no later attestation of Greek speakers.
cities.ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; the city surrendered to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari's army c. 638.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Founded for captives from Antioch; the Antiochene clergy elected a successor to their bishop Demetrianus there (Chronicle of Seert); deportee churches in Persis and Khuzistan used both Greek and Syriac.
cities.status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert; Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam on the settlement of Roman captives; East-Syrian metropolitan see from 410.
cities.note: The Greek-speaking community is inferred from the Antiochene origin of the settlers and the Chronicle of Seert; how long it kept Greek is unknown.

cities.site: Shahr-e Qumis, between Semnan and Damghan, Semnan province
cities.greek_from_text: Named by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities founded by Seleucus I in Parthyene; Curtius (6.2.15) calls it 'founded by Greeks' when Alexander arrived there in 330 BC.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Arsaces I's Parni took Parthyene c. 238 BC; Antiochus III recaptured Hecatompylos in 209 BC (Polybius 10.28) but left Parthia to Arsaces II; then a Parthian royal city. Speech: no evidence of a Greek-speaking community under Parthian rule.
cities.fade_evidence: No Greek inscriptions; the excavated remains at Shahr-e Qumis are Parthian.
cities.ended_by: Taken by Arsaces I of Parthia c. 238 BC; retaken by Antiochus III in 209 BC and left to the Parthians; no later trace of Greeks.
cities.status_evidence: Appian, Syr. 57 (foundation of Seleucus I); Curtius 6.2.15; Polybius 10.28; Strabo 11.9.1.
cities.note: The identification with Shahr-e Qumis is widely accepted but not proven; Curtius' 'founded by Greeks' for 330 BC is likely anachronistic.

cities.site: unlocated, in the Rey/Tehran plain, Tehran province (region only)
cities.greek_from_text: Macedonian foundation near Rhagai (Strabo 11.13.6), early Seleucid period.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian conquest of Media under Mithridates I (c. 148/147 BC). Speech: nothing is known of the city after its mention by Strabo.
cities.fade_evidence: None; known only from Strabo.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Media conquered by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (one of the Greek cities founded by the Macedonians in Media).
cities.note: Some link it with the Heraclea founded by Alexander and refounded by Antiochus as Achais (Pliny 6.48), which other sources put in Areia; the location is unknown and the point is a placeholder near Rhagai.

cities.other_names: Niphaunda (Ptolemy); Nihavand (Middle Persian/Arabic); Mah al-Basra (early Islamic)
cities.site: Nahavand, Hamadan province
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by a King Antiochus (probably Antiochus I, 281-261 BC) and named after a queen Laodice; listed by Strabo (11.13.6) among the Macedonian foundations of Media.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Mithridates I of Parthia conquered Media c. 148/147 BC. Speech: the last evidence of the Greek city is the stele of 193 BC; nothing is known of it under Parthian rule.
cities.fade_evidence: Stele of 193 BC (Menedemos to the magistrates and city of Laodicea, with Antiochus III's edict for the cult of Queen Laodice); a short honorary inscription for Menedemos, governor of the Upper Satrapies; an Ionic capital.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Media conquered by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC; no later trace of the Greek community.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6; Pliny NH 6; Nehavend stele of 193 BC: Menedemos' covering letter to Apollodotos and to the city of Laodicea (its archons and the city), with Antiochus III's ordinance on the cult of Queen Laodice (Robert 1949; Axon 1.2, 2017)
cities.note: The stele, a chance find at Nahavand, fixes the location; the Kermanshah copy of the same edict comes from a different place.

cities.site: Qal'a-ye Sam, south of Zahak, Sistan, Sistan and Baluchestan province
cities.greek_from_text: The walled site belongs to the post-Achaemenid and possibly Parthian period (Italian mission under Scerrato, 1959-61); the Greek ostraca date from its occupation, probably the 3rd-2nd c. BC (unchecked). The date is an estimate.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid, then probably Graeco-Bactrian, then Parthian; from the late 2nd c. BC Drangiana was settled by the Sakas (Sakastane). Speech: no Greek writing is known after the ostraca. The end is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: The published ostraca (Pugliese Carratelli 1966, pp. 34-35); unpublished ones noted by Sherwin-White and Kuhrt.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Drangiana passed to the Parthians and the Sakas; nothing is recorded of the site.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek ostraca written on the spot: five published, one of 12-13 lines (Pugliese Carratelli 1966), others unpublished.
cities.status_evidence: Greek ostraca (Pugliese Carratelli 1966; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Epigraphy ii, under Drangiana/Sistan).
cities.note: Called a fortified site; whether it was a town, a fortress or a residence is debated (Iranian Journal of Archaeological Studies). Admitted as uncertain because everyday Greek writing was found there, by the same rule as Ora and Emshi Tepe in the Central and South Asia set. If it was only a fort, it is a place where Greek speakers lived rather than a city.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Epigraphy ii (Greek inscriptions from ancient Iran): https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/epigraphy-ii/
Pugliese Carratelli, East and West 16 (1966), pp. 34-35
Plan, form and function of a 'fortified' site in the Iranian Sistan (Iranian Journal of Archaeological Studies): https://ijas.usb.ac.ir/article_6734.html

cities.site: Rishahr, south of Bushehr city, Bushehr province
cities.greek_from_text: Roman captives settled by Shapur I after his campaigns of 253-260 in a town founded by Ardashir I (Chronicle of Seert).
cities.until_text: Administration: Sasanian; metropolitan see of Fars from 424; taken by the Arabs in the early 640s. Speech: the 'Roman' church with Greek liturgy is recorded for the deportee generations only; later bishops of Rew-Ardashir worked in Syriac and Persian.
cities.fade_evidence: Chronicle of Seert on the Roman and Carmanian churches (3rd c.); metropolitan see of Fars at the synod of 424 (Syriac); no later attestation of Greek speakers.
cities.ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; Uthman ibn Abi al-As defeated the governor Shahrak at Rishahr and took the town in the early 640s (al-Baladhuri).
cities.pre_greek_note: The town predates the arrival of the deportees by a few decades; earlier occupation on the Bushehr peninsula goes back to the Elamite period (Liyan).
cities.bilingual_evidence: The Chronicle of Seert says the deportees built two churches there, one for the Romans and one for the Carmanians, with liturgy in Greek and Syriac.
cities.status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert: a church of the Roman captives beside a church of the Carmanians, with the liturgy in Greek and in Syriac (the Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage, 'Fars', calls the report of a Greek and Syriac liturgy in 3rd-c. Fars plausible); East-Syrian metropolitan see of Fars (424)
cities.note: The Hellenistic Antioch in Persis may have stood on the same peninsula; the two are kept apart because both sites are uncertain and the communities are five centuries apart. A second Rew-Ardashir/Reishahr, near Arrajan on the Fars-Khuzestan border, is also known; the metropolitan see and the deportee town are usually placed on the Bushehr peninsula.
sources: Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage: Fars

cities.other_names: Ragā (Old Persian, Bisotun inscription); Rages (Book of Tobit); Europos (Seleucus I); Arsakia (Parthian); Ray/Rey (Persian, Arabic)
cities.site: Rey, south of Tehran, Tehran province
cities.greek_from_text: Refounded by Seleucus I Nicator as Europos, c. 300 BC (Strabo 11.13.6).
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian conquest of Media under Mithridates I (c. 148/147 BC); the Parthians renamed the city Arsakia. Speech: no evidence of Greek speakers after the conquest; Isidore of Charax calls Rhaga the largest city of Media.
cities.fade_evidence: No Greek inscriptions known; the Parthian renaming Arsakia (Strabo 11.13.6).
cities.ended_by: Taken by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC and renamed Arsakia; no later trace of Greeks.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Refounded by Seleucus I as Europos, named after his Macedonian home town, and counted by Strabo among the Greek cities founded by the Macedonians; the old Median town of Ragā remained a large native centre.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (founded by Nicator as Europos; Macedonian foundation); Isidore of Charax 7.
cities.note: Classed bilingual because Europos was a refoundation of a large Median town; Strabo is the only evidence for the Macedonian settlers.

cities.site: unlocated, in ancient Hyrcania (Golestan or Mazandaran province)
cities.greek_from_text: First and only evidence: Greeks living in the city at Antiochus III's siege, 209 BC (Polybius 10.31); the community probably dated from the early Seleucid period.
cities.until_text: Administration: Hyrcania was under the Parthians from c. 235 BC; Antiochus III took Sirynx in 209 BC and then left the region to Arsaces II. Speech: the Greek residents were massacred by the defenders before the city fell.
cities.fade_evidence: Polybius 10.31 (siege of 209 BC).
cities.ended_by: The Greek residents were killed by the city's native and Parthian defenders during Antiochus III's siege, 209 BC (Polybius 10.31).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Polybius (10.31) says that when Antiochus III's siege was about to succeed, the native defenders killed the Greeks living in the city, a resident Greek community.
cities.status_evidence: Polybius 10.31 (a strong city of Hyrcania with Greek residents).
cities.note: A Greek minority in a fortified Hyrcanian city; how large it was, and whether it ever formed a civic body, is unknown. Location unknown; the point marks the Hyrcanian plain.
sources: Walbank, Historical Commentary on Polybius II, on 10.31

cities.greek: Σοῦσα, Σελεύκεια ἡ πρὸς τῷ Εὐλαίῳ
cities.other_names: Šušan/Šušun (Elamite); Shushan (Hebrew Bible); Seleucia on the Eulaios (Seleucid); 'the city of the Phraateans in Susa', after Phraates IV refounded it c. 31/30 BC (Greek inscriptions); Shush (Persian), al-Sus (Arabic)
cities.site: Shush, Khuzestan province
cities.greek_from_text: Greco-Macedonian settlers under the early Seleucids; the city was refounded as Seleucia on the Eulaios by a Seleucid king (Seleucus I or Antiochus I?), the exact date uncertain; Greek inscriptions from the 3rd c. BC.
cities.until_text: Administration: Seleucid until c. 147-140 BC; Elymaean kings seized the city briefly and Mithridates I of Parthia took it from them c. 140 BC; Parthians held it to at least AD 45, then Elymaean kings from the later 1st c. AD; Sasanian from 224. Speech: the Greek polis kept its institutions under Parthian rule (Artabanus II confirmed the election of the city treasurer Hestiaios in AD 21), but Greek traditions weakened and disappeared under Elymaean rule from the later 1st c. AD (Encyclopaedia Iranica). No dated Greek inscription is later than the early 1st c. AD.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek dedications and manumissions of the 2nd-1st c. BC; two epigrams for the irrigation official Zamaspes (first decade of the 1st c. AD); letter of Artabanus II to the magistrates, December AD 21 (SEG 7.1); a Greek hymn to Apollo of the 1st c. AD; no later dated Greek text (Encyclopaedia Iranica: Epigraphy ii).
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Taken by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 140 BC; Greek civic life faded after the Elymaean kings took Susa in the later 1st c. AD; taken by the Sasanian Ardashir I in 224; razed by Shapur II in the 4th c. (Syriac and Arabic tradition).
cities.founder: a Seleucid king (refoundation as Seleucia; Seleucus I or Antiochus I?)
cities.other_language: Aramaic and the local Elamite/Iranian speech of the native population
cities.bilingual_evidence: A Greek polis (Seleucia on the Eulaios) with council, assembly, archons, treasurers and gymnasium, living beside a large native population with Iranian, Semitic and Elamite names; about fifty Greek inscriptions (dedications, manumissions to Nanaia, epigrams).
cities.status_evidence: Greek civic institutions (boule, archons, treasurers, gymnasium) in Greek inscriptions (Rougemont, IGIAC 1-50); letter of Artabanus II to the city, AD 21; Seleucid mint.
cities.note: Greek polis inside a large native town; classed bilingual. The Greek community lasted at least into the early 1st c. AD.

left_out.name: Enkomi (Late Bronze Age town; Alashiya?)
left_out.reason: Late Bronze Age town abandoned c. 1075-1050 BC, when Salamis was founded nearby. Aegean pottery and 12th-c. rebuilding are often linked to Aegean settlers, but its texts are in Cypro-Minoan, not Greek; no positive evidence of Greek speech. Its successor Salamis is listed.

left_out.name: Maa-Palaeokastro
left_out.reason: Short-lived fortified settlement of c. 1200 BC on a headland north of Paphos, sometimes attributed to Aegean newcomers; a stronghold, not a city, and no Greek text.

left_out.name: Pyla-Kokkinokremos
left_out.reason: Short-lived fortified hilltop settlement of c. 1200 BC with Aegean-type pottery; a stronghold, not a city, and no Greek text.

left_out.name: Hala Sultan Tekke
left_out.reason: Large Late Bronze Age harbour town abandoned in the 12th c. BC; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Kalavasos-Ayios Dhimitrios
left_out.reason: Late Bronze Age town abandoned c. 1200 BC; Cypro-Minoan texts; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Vouni
left_out.reason: Palace of the 5th c. BC above the bay of Soloi, burnt c. 380 BC; a royal residence, not a city.

left_out.name: Palaea (between Kition and Amathus)
left_out.reason: Strabo 14.6.3 calls it 'a small town' (polichnion); site unknown; no civic evidence.

left_out.name: Arsinoe near Paphos
left_out.reason: Strabo 14.6.3 names it only as a place with a landing, between Zephyrion and Hierokepis; no civic evidence.

left_out.name: Hierokepis (Geroskipou)
left_out.reason: The sacred garden of Aphrodite near Paphos (Strabo 14.6.3); a sanctuary and village, not a city.

left_out.name: Leukolla
left_out.reason: A harbour between Arsinoe and Cape Pedalion (Strabo 14.6.3); no town.

left_out.name: Thronoi
left_out.reason: Cape (and perhaps a small place) on the south-east coast in the geographers; no civic evidence.

left_out.name: Kinyreia
left_out.reason: Named by Pliny (NH 5.130) among the lost towns of Cyprus; unlocated, no evidence beyond the name.

left_out.name: Epidaurum
left_out.reason: Named by Pliny (NH 5.130) among the towns of Cyprus; unlocated and otherwise unknown.

left_out.name: Lefkara
left_out.reason: Seat of the Greek bishop of Amathus/Limassol from 1260 to 1571 under the Latin settlement (Bulla Cypria); a large village, not a city or a see in its own right before 1260.

left_out.name: Solea (seat of the Greek bishop of Soloi/Nicosia)
left_out.reason: Valley of villages where the Greek bishop of Soloi resided from 1260; no town.

left_out.name: Morphou
left_out.reason: Medieval village with the monastery of Agios Mamas; a town only in modern times.

left_out.name: Kolossi
left_out.reason: Hospitaller commandery and castle of the 13th-15th c.; not a town.

left_out.name: Kantara, Buffavento and St Hilarion
left_out.reason: Medieval castles of the Kyrenia range; forts, not towns.

left_out.name: Makaria
left_out.reason: Coastal place on the north coast in the geographers; no civic evidence.

left_out.name: Lambousa
left_out.reason: Not a separate city: the late antique coastal town of Lapethos (listed under Lapethos).

left_out.name: Episkopi
left_out.reason: Not a separate city: the 7th-c. successor of Kourion, which kept its see (listed under Kourion).

left_out.name: Tell Sukas (Šuksu)
left_out.reason: A native coastal town (Ugaritic Šuksu) with a Greek community, Greek sanctuary and cremation burials c. 675-552 BC (Riis); no evidence that it was a self-governing Greek polis, and the Greek phase ended with a destruction c. 552 BC. A trading settlement inside a Phoenician/Aramaean town; reject as a city, but a serious candidate.

left_out.name: Chalcis sub Libano (Anjar / Majdal Anjar)
left_out.reason: Capital of the Ituraean principality (Ptolemy son of Mennaeus, Lysanias) and of Herod of Chalcis (41-48). The Greek coins of the tetrarchs are royal issues. City coins of 'Flavia Chalcis' (era of AD 92, Trajan to Marcus Aurelius) were once given to this Chalcis (Wildwinds still does) but RPC III assigns them to Chalcis ad Belum; the site is uncertain (Anjar or Majdal Anjar) and no see is known. Not enough positive evidence of a Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Carne / Karnos
left_out.reason: The naval station (epineion) of Aradus (Strabo 16.2.12; Pliny 5.79); a harbour of the Aradian state, not a separate city; no civic coinage or see.

left_out.name: Enhydra
left_out.reason: A small place of the Aradian mainland (Strabo 16.2.12); no civic status known.

left_out.name: Simyra (Tell Kazel?)
left_out.reason: Bronze and Iron Age town (Ṣumur); Strabo and Pliny still name Simyra, and Tell Kazel has Hellenistic levels, but there is no civic coinage, see or Greek civic evidence. Reject; identification with Tell Kazel is also debated.

left_out.name: Baetocaece (Hosn Suleiman)
left_out.reason: A temple estate and village of Zeus of Baetocaece in the territory of Aradus; Greek royal and imperial letters and a Greek-speaking village community are attested, but it was a sanctuary-village, not a city.

left_out.name: Trieres
left_out.reason: A fortified place taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC (Polybius 5.68); a fort or village, not a city.

left_out.name: Gigarta
left_out.reason: A stronghold of the Ituraean brigands in Strabo 16.2.18 and a name in Pliny; no civic status.

left_out.name: Kalamos (Qalamoun)
left_out.reason: A village or fort taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC (Polybius 5.68); no civic status.

left_out.name: Theouprosopon (Ras Chekka)
left_out.reason: A promontory with a fort (Strabo 16.2.15-18); the 551 earthquake caused a landslide here; not a city.

left_out.name: Palaebyblos
left_out.reason: A place named by Strabo 16.2.19 between Byblos and Berytus; no civic status.

left_out.name: Ornithopolis ('Ornithon polis')
left_out.reason: Named as a small town between Tyre and Sidon by Pseudo-Scylax, Strabo 16.2.24 and Pliny 5.76; location uncertain; no coins, see or Greek civic evidence. A Phoenician town of the Sidonian territory.

left_out.name: Leontopolis (Leonton polis)
left_out.reason: Named by Strabo 16.2.22 between Berytus and Sidon; unlocated; no civic evidence.

left_out.name: Palaetyrus (Ras el-Ain / Ušû)
left_out.reason: The mainland settlement of Tyre; in Greek and Roman times part of the territory of Tyre, not a separate city.

left_out.name: Umm el-Amed
left_out.reason: A Phoenician town of the Persian and Hellenistic periods with Phoenician inscriptions; abandoned in the 1st c. BC; no Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Aphaca (Afqa)
left_out.reason: Sanctuary of Aphrodite Aphakitis, destroyed under Constantine; a sanctuary, not a city.

left_out.name: Niha (Hosn Niha)
left_out.reason: Temple village of the Bekaa with Greek and Latin inscriptions; a village sanctuary.

left_out.name: Qalaat Faqra
left_out.reason: Sanctuary with Greek inscriptions of the Ituraean and Roman periods (Agrippa II); not a city.

left_out.name: Gerrha (Anjar)
left_out.reason: An Ituraean fort named by Strabo 16.2.18; the Umayyad town of Anjar (c. 714) was founded after the conquest. Not a Greek city.

left_out.name: Antiochia sub Libano
left_out.reason: A name in Pliny 5.77 (Antiochia Libani); unlocated; a dynastic name with no other evidence.

left_out.name: Mons Casius sanctuary (Jebel Aqra)
left_out.reason: A mountain sanctuary of Zeus Kasios on the Turkish-Syrian border; not a city.

left_out.name: Leukos Limen (Minet el-Beida)
left_out.reason: The Bronze Age harbour of Ugarit; no Greek city.

left_out.name: Seleucia Pieria
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Antioch on the Orontes
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here (Antakya, Hatay).

left_out.name: Rhosus
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Al Mina
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Iamnia Paralios (Yavne-Yam), harbour of Iamnia
left_out.reason: Harbour town of Iamnia. A community of Sidonians there received a Greek letter of Antiochus V in 163 BC, and Pliny and Ptolemy speak of two Iamnias, but the harbour never appears as a city or see of its own in Hierocles or the church lists; counted with Iamnia.

left_out.name: Maiumas of Ascalon
left_out.reason: Harbour of Ascalon; in late antiquity one of the three municipal districts of Ascalon's territory (with Diocletianopolis), but no see or civic coinage of its own is securely attested, unlike Maiumas of Gaza (Constantia).

left_out.name: Shechem (Tell Balata)
left_out.reason: Samaritan town of the Hellenistic period, destroyed by John Hyrcanus c. 107 BC. The petition of the 'Sidonians in Shechem' to Antiochus IV (Josephus AJ 12.258-264) is of disputed authenticity, and there are no Greek civic institutions, coins or inscriptions of residents. Flavia Neapolis, founded nearby in 72, is listed as a city.

left_out.name: Mount Gerizim (Samaritan temple town)
left_out.reason: Samaritan sanctuary and town; its inscriptions are mainly Aramaic and Hebrew; destroyed by John Hyrcanus c. 111 BC. A sanctuary town without Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Phasaelis
left_out.reason: Founded by Herod for his brother Phasael (Josephus AJ 16.145), but it was a palm-grove estate town in the Jordan valley with no Greek civic institutions, coins or inscriptions of residents; a village on the Madaba map.

left_out.name: Nessana (Nitzana)
left_out.reason: A village with a fort and a military unit; its Greek papyri (6th c. to c. 690) are key evidence for the end of Greek in the Negev, but it was not a city.

left_out.name: Sobata (Shivta)
left_out.reason: A village (kome) in the Nessana papyri, with churches and Greek inscriptions; no civic status.

left_out.name: Oboda (Avdat)
left_out.reason: Nabataean cult centre and late Roman town with Greek inscriptions, but not a city or see in Hierocles or the church lists.

left_out.name: Rehovot-in-the-Negev (Ruhayba)
left_out.reason: Large Negev village with churches and Greek inscriptions; no civic status.

left_out.name: Beersheba (Berosaba)
left_out.reason: Garrison town and 'very large village' (Eusebius, Onomasticon), known for the Greek tax edict of the 6th c.; no city status or see is attested.

left_out.name: Arethusa (Josephus AJ 14.75)
left_out.reason: A town Pompey restored, unlocated and possibly a confusion with Arethusa in Syria.

left_out.name: Magdala-Taricheae
left_out.reason: Jewish toparchy town with a Greek name and a hippodrome (Josephus BJ 2.599); no Greek civic institutions or coins; taken by Vespasian in 67 and later a village.

left_out.name: Beth She'arim (Besara)
left_out.reason: Jewish town and necropolis with many Greek epitaphs (3rd-4th c.), largely of Jews brought from the diaspora for burial; a large village, not a city.

left_out.name: Kedesh (Kadasa)
left_out.reason: Tyrian village with a Persian and Hellenistic administrative building and Greek seal impressions of officials; officials do not make a Greek town and it had no civic status.

left_out.name: Ekdippa (Achzib)
left_out.reason: Phoenician town, later a Roman village and road station; no Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Sycaminum (Tel Shiqmona)
left_out.reason: Called a polis by Strabo (16.2.27) but later a village (Eusebius); no civic institutions, coins or see.

left_out.name: Crocodilon polis (Tel Tanninim)
left_out.reason: Listed by Strabo and Pliny; a small coastal settlement with no Greek civic evidence, already defunct by Pliny's time.

left_out.name: Tel Anafa
left_out.reason: Rich Hellenistic building with Greek finds in the Hula valley, an estate or administrative centre, not a city.

left_out.name: Beth Zur (Bethsoura)
left_out.reason: Hellenistic and Hasmonaean fortress.

left_out.name: Mesad Hashavyahu
left_out.reason: Coastal fort of the late 7th c. BC with East Greek pottery, probably of Greek mercenaries; a fort, not a city.

left_out.name: Tel Kabri
left_out.reason: East Greek pottery of the 7th c. BC at a Phoenician site; trade or mercenaries, not a Greek city.

left_out.name: Bitylion
left_out.reason: A see of Palaestina I, but the site (Sheikh Zuweid) lies in North Sinai, Egypt, outside the area.

left_out.name: Hebron
left_out.reason: Idumaean and Jewish town, a village in late antiquity (Eusebius); no Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Bethlehem
left_out.reason: Village with the basilica of the Nativity; not a see before the Crusades.

left_out.name: Nazareth
left_out.reason: Jewish village; no civic status.

left_out.name: Kapharnaoum (Capernaum)
left_out.reason: Jewish village with a synagogue; no civic status.

left_out.name: Gophna and the other Jewish toparchy capitals (Thamna, Acraba, Herodium, Engaddi, Narbata)
left_out.reason: District capitals of Judaea and Samaria, Jewish towns and forts speaking Aramaic and Hebrew; no Greek civic institutions; Gophna was a village later.

left_out.name: Atabyrion (Mount Tabor)
left_out.reason: Hilltop fortress taken by Antiochus III (Polybius 5.70.6); a fort.

left_out.name: Tel Dan (Laish-Dan)
left_out.reason: Sanctuary with a Greek and Aramaic dedication 'to the god who is in Dan' (2nd c. BC); a cult site, not a city.

left_out.name: Eitha (Hit)
left_out.reason: A large Hauran village with Greek inscriptions (a strategos in 232; church of St Sergius 354/355), but neither polis status nor a bishop is securely attested.

left_out.name: Gamala
left_out.reason: Jewish town of the Gaulanitis destroyed by Vespasian in 67; no Greek civic institutions.

left_out.name: Seleucia (Gaulanitis)
left_out.reason: A fortified village held by Josephus in 66-67 (BJ 4.2); the dynastic name alone is not evidence of a polis.

left_out.name: Sogane (Gaulanitis)
left_out.reason: Fortified village in Josephus (BJ 2.574, 4.4); not a city.

left_out.name: Hippos (Sussita)
left_out.reason: A Greek city of the Decapolis, but its site lies west of the 1967 line on the east shore of the Sea of Galilee and belongs to the Israel & Palestine group.

left_out.name: Admedera (Dumayr)
left_out.reason: Road station and Roman fort with a temple on the Damascus-Palmyra road; not a city.

left_out.name: Ma'loula and Saidnaya
left_out.reason: Aramaic-speaking villages and monasteries; no civic status.

left_out.name: Si' (Seeia)
left_out.reason: Nabataean and Roman sanctuary near Canatha with Greek and Nabataean inscriptions; a sanctuary, not a city.

left_out.name: Salkhad (Salcha)
left_out.reason: Nabataean town and later fortress of the Jabal al-Arab; no polis status or see attested.

left_out.name: Mothana (Imtan)
left_out.reason: Hauran village with Greek and Nabataean inscriptions and a cavalry post; a village.

left_out.name: Hauran villages with Greek inscriptions (e.g. Shaqra, Sha'ara, Hebran, Inkhil, Sheikh Miskin)
left_out.reason: Villages and metrokomiai with Greek inscriptions of their residents, but never poleis or sees.

left_out.name: Arbela (Irbid)
left_out.reason: A large village in the territory of the Decapolis cities (Eusebius); no polis status or see attested.

left_out.name: Amathus (Tell Ammata)
left_out.reason: A Hasmonean stronghold and one of Gabinius' five councils (57 BC); a Jewish town without evidence of Greek speakers, and a village in Eusebius.

left_out.name: Tyros (Iraq al-Amir)
left_out.reason: The palace and estate (Birta) of the Tobiad Hyrcanus, 2nd century BC; a residence, not a city.

left_out.name: Abila of Peraea (Tall al-Kafrayn)
left_out.reason: A village (Abel-shittim) in the Jordan Valley; no civic status.

left_out.name: Umm al-Jimal
left_out.reason: A large town of the late Roman Hauran with many churches and Greek inscriptions, but neither polis status nor a bishop is attested; its ancient name (Thantia?) is uncertain.

left_out.name: Kastron Mefaa (Umm ar-Rasas)
left_out.reason: A fort and Christian village with Greek mosaic inscriptions to 756; not a city or see.

left_out.name: Rihab, Ziza and Mount Nebo
left_out.reason: Christian villages, a fort and a monastic sanctuary with Greek inscriptions; not cities.

left_out.name: Machaerus and Callirrhoe
left_out.reason: Herodian fortress and spa; not cities.

left_out.name: Hauarra (Humayma)
left_out.reason: Nabataean foundation of Aretas III and a Roman fort; a village and garrison post, not a city.

left_out.name: Mahoza (Babatha's village)
left_out.reason: A village in the district of Zoara; its Greek documents are counted under Zoara.

left_out.name: Betthorus (Lejjun) and other legionary forts of the limes Arabicus
left_out.reason: Legionary and auxiliary forts; not cities.

left_out.name: Karnaim (Sheikh Saad) and Ashtaroth (Tell Ashtara)
left_out.reason: Biblical towns of Bashan that were villages in the Roman period (Eusebius); no civic status.

left_out.name: Aphek (Fiq) and Qasrin
left_out.reason: Villages of the Gaulanitis (a Jewish village with a synagogue at Qasrin); no civic status.

left_out.name: Qasr al-Hallabat, Azraq and Deir al-Kahf
left_out.reason: Roman forts of the desert frontier; not cities.

left_out.name: Dibon (Dhiban)
left_out.reason: Moabite town that was a large village in the Roman period (Eusebius); no civic status.

left_out.name: Europos (Carchemish, Jerablus/Karkamış)
left_out.reason: Straddles the border: the citadel and inner town of Carchemish, where the Hellenistic and Roman Europos stood, lie on the Turkish side (Karkamış); only the outer town reaches Jerablus in Syria. A Seleucid foundation and later see of Euphratensis, so it lies in present-day Turkey.

left_out.name: Nisibis (Nusaybin; modern Qamishli opposite)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here: the ruins are in Nusaybin, Turkey. Qamishli on the Syrian side is a 20th-c. town.

left_out.name: Dara / Anastasiopolis
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here (Oğuz, Mardin).

left_out.name: Constantina / Tella (Viranşehir)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Carrhae (Harran)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Batnae (Suruç)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Zeugma / Seleucia on the Euphrates
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Androna (al-Andarin)
left_out.reason: A large late antique kome with over 50 Greek inscriptions (baths, kastron of 558); never a city or see.

left_out.name: Occaraba
left_out.reason: Station and garrison post (Notitia Dignitatum) east of Hama; no secure evidence of a see or civic status found.

left_out.name: Theleda
left_out.reason: A village with monasteries in the limestone massif; no civic status.

left_out.name: Paradeisos / Triparadeisos (near Jusiyah)
left_out.reason: A Persian and Seleucid royal park (the partition of Triparadeisos, 321 BC) and a town of the Laodicene in Pliny (NH 5.82) and Ptolemy; no Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Heraclea (Cyrrhestice)
left_out.reason: Seleucid name known from Ptolemy and Stephanus; unlocated and with no further evidence of a city.

left_out.name: Thannuris (Tell Tuneinir)
left_out.reason: Fort on the Khabur (Procopius, Buildings 2.6); no civic status.

left_out.name: Tetrapyrgium (Qseir as-Saile)
left_out.reason: Fort on the road to Sergiopolis; no civic status.

left_out.name: Dead Cities of the limestone massif (al-Bara, Serjilla, Ruweiha, Telanissos/Deir Sim'an and others)
left_out.reason: Large villages and a pilgrimage centre with many Greek inscriptions; none was a city or see before the conquest.

left_out.name: Arra (Ma'arrat al-Nu'man)
left_out.reason: Road station and village in late antiquity; a town only in the Arab period.

left_out.name: Litarba (al-Atarib)
left_out.reason: Village and road station; no civic status.

left_out.name: Nazala (al-Qaryatayn)
left_out.reason: Road station and village on the Damascus-Palmyra road; no civic status.

left_out.name: Batnae (Cyrrhestice, near al-Bab)
left_out.reason: Julian (Ep. 98) stayed at this Batnae between Beroea and Hierapolis in 363 and called it a place with a barbarian name but Greek in character; a village or estate, not a city. Not the Batnae of Osrhoene (Suruç, in Turkey).

left_out.name: Megara, Apollonia, Kasiana and Lysias (Apamene)
left_out.reason: Greek-named settlements and forts that Strabo (16.2.10) lists as dependent on Apamea; unlocated or forts, with no civic status of their own.

left_out.name: Unlocated Seleucid names in Appian Syr. 57 (Maronea, Callipolis, Achaea, Oropus, Perinthus, Tegea, Heraea, Astacus)
left_out.reason: Appian lists them among Seleucus I's Greek-named cities in Syria and beyond; none is located, so none can be mapped.

left_out.name: Ctesiphon (Ktesiphon)
left_out.reason: Parthian royal winter residence, built up as a 'very large village' beside Seleucia so that the Parthian troops need not be quartered in the Greek city (Strabo 16.1.16); later the Sasanian capital. No Greek civic institutions or resident Greek-speaking community of its own is attested; the Greek community of the twin cities lived in Seleucia. In 614 Khosrow II brought some 35,000 captives from Jerusalem to Ctesiphon (Sebeos), a captive group in a Persian and Aramaic capital. A royal residence, not a Greek city; the deportee city of Antioch of Khosrow nearby is entered separately.

left_out.name: Veh-Ardashir (Coche)
left_out.reason: Sasanian city founded by Ardashir I c. 230 beside the deserted Seleucia; Persian, Aramaic and Jewish; seat of the catholicos of the Church of the East (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Buzurg-Shapur (Ukbara)
left_out.reason: Town of Shapur I north of Ctesiphon, listed among the places where he settled Roman captives (Encyclopaedia Iranica, Deportations). Unlike Gundeshapur and Rew-Ardashir, where the Chronicle of Seert reports separate Greek and Syriac churches, no Greek-speaking community is attested here.

left_out.name: Shadh-Shapur (Dayr Mikhraq, Mesene)
left_out.reason: Town of Shapur I in Mesene, listed among the places where he settled Roman captives (Encyclopaedia Iranica, Deportations); unlocated, and no Greek-speaking community is attested.

left_out.name: Vologesias
left_out.reason: Parthian royal foundation of Vologases I near Babylon; caravan town of Palmyrene traders (Aramaic); no Greek civic community.

left_out.name: Opis
left_out.reason: Babylonian town (Akkadian Upi) where Alexander's army mutinied in 324 BC; superseded by Seleucia; no Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Sittake
left_out.reason: Persian-period city (Xenophon, Anab. 2.4.13) that gave its name to Sittakene; no Greek evidence; the Greek city of the district was Artemita (or Apollonia).

left_out.name: Neapolis on the Euphrates
left_out.reason: Greek-named place on the Euphrates near the Royal Canal in Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 1); no other evidence of Greek settlers or civic institutions; unlocated. Possibly a Seleucid foundation, but the name is the only evidence.

left_out.name: Laodicea in Mesopotamia
left_out.reason: Pliny (6.117) lists a Laodicea with Seleucia and Artemita among the towns of Mesopotamia; unlocated and known only by its dynastic name, which is not enough by itself.

left_out.name: Apamea in Sittakene
left_out.reason: Pliny names a second Apamea, surrounded by the Tigris and divided by the Archous, in Sittakene; unlocated, known only by its dynastic name, and possibly a doublet of Apamea in Mesene, which is entered.

left_out.name: Borsippa
left_out.reason: Babylonian temple town of Nabu; Antiochus I rebuilt the Ezida and recorded it in Akkadian (Antiochus cylinder, 268 BC); no Greek community.

left_out.name: Nippur
left_out.reason: Babylonian temple town, a Parthian fortress and town; no Greek civic community or Greek-speaking residents attested.

left_out.name: Larisa (Nimrud, Kalhu)
left_out.reason: Deserted Assyrian capital that Xenophon calls Larisa (Anab. 3.4.7); later only a village; no Greek city.

left_out.name: Karka d-Beth Slokh (Kirkuk)
left_out.reason: Ancient Arrapha. The Syriac History of Karka d-Beth Slokh credits a king Seleucus with building its walls, and the name may contain his name, but no Greek inscription, coin or settler is known; a later legend is not evidence. Its Church of the East see was Syriac. It has been suggested as the site of Demetrias, which is entered separately.

left_out.name: Arbela (Erbil)
left_out.reason: Capital of Adiabene; Aramaic-speaking; its Church of the East see was Syriac. No Greek civic institutions or Greek-speaking community attested. The Greek city of Demetrias lay nearby.

left_out.name: Assur
left_out.reason: Parthian-period city with Aramaic inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Hatra
left_out.reason: Arab-ruled Aramaic-speaking city of the 1st-3rd c. AD with hundreds of Aramaic inscriptions; Greek and Latin appear only in a handful of texts, the Latin ones from the Roman garrison of the 230s. Left out by the rule for places where Greek was only the language of officials or a garrison; destroyed by Shapur I c. 240.

left_out.name: Singara
left_out.reason: Roman colonia (Aurelia Septimia Singara) and base of legio I Parthica from Septimius Severus; its coins under Gordian III have Latin legends; the townspeople spoke Aramaic. No resident Greek-speaking community attested. Taken by Shapur II in 360 and its people deported (Ammianus 20.6).

left_out.name: Anatha (Ana)
left_out.reason: Island fortress on the Euphrates (Isidore 1); Roman garrison in the 3rd c.; surrendered to Julian in 363 and its people resettled in Syria (Ammianus 24.1.6-9). A fort, not a Greek city.

left_out.name: Is (Hit, Aipolis)
left_out.reason: Bitumen town on the Euphrates (Herodotus 1.179; Isidore 1); Aramaic; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Peroz-Shapur (Pirisabora, Anbar)
left_out.reason: Sasanian fortified city, burned by Julian in 363 (Ammianus 24.2.9-22); Aramaic, Persian and Jewish population; no Greek community.

left_out.name: al-Hira
left_out.reason: Capital of the Lakhmid Arab kings; Christian Arabs with a Syriac church; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Teredon (Diridotis)
left_out.reason: Babylonian port at the head of the Gulf (Strabo 16.3.2); Arrian (Ind. 41) calls Diridotis a village; trading place without civic status or Greek community.

left_out.name: Forat (Perat d-Maishan)
left_out.reason: Trading town of Characene (Pliny 6.145); Church of the East see (Syriac); no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Nisibis
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkey; not counted here.

left_out.name: Ikaros (Failaka)
left_out.reason: Seleucid fortress with temples and a settlement on Failaka island. Greek inscriptions: a dedication of Soteles the Athenian and the soldiers to Zeus Soter, Poseidon and Artemis Soteira, and a stele with a letter of the Seleucid official Ikadion to Anaxarchos and Anaxarchos' covering letter to the inhabitants of Ikaros (3rd c. BC), on the island's sanctuary and its inhabitants' privileges. A garrison and a dependent settlement, without evidence of civic status; the Hellenistic occupation ended around the 1st c. BC.

left_out.name: Tylos (Bahrain)
left_out.reason: Island under Seleucid and then Characene rule; a Greek dedication by Kephisodoros, strategos of Tylos and the islands, for King Hyspaosines (c. 130 BC) and a few Greek epitaphs show officials and some Greek usage, but the people spoke Aramaic and Arabic and no city with Greek civic status is attested.

left_out.name: Gerrha (Thaj?)
left_out.reason: Arab trading city of the Gulf coast (Strabo 16.3.3; Polybius 13.9, visit of Antiochus III in 205 BC); coins with Aramaic and Hasaitic legends; no Greek community. Its site (Thaj or near Hofuf) is disputed.

left_out.name: Hegra (Mada'in Salih)
left_out.reason: Nabataean city; after 106 a Roman garrison town, with a Latin building inscription of 175-177 naming the civitas Hegrenorum. The people spoke Arabic and wrote Nabataean Aramaic; Greek is barely attested. No Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Leuke Kome
left_out.reason: Nabataean harbour on the Red Sea with a Roman customs post and a centurion (Periplus 19); a trading post; site uncertain (perhaps near al-Wajh or Aynunah).

left_out.name: Dedan (al-Ula)
left_out.reason: Dadanite and Lihyanite kingdom capital; North Arabian and Aramaic inscriptions; no Greek.

left_out.name: Najran
left_out.reason: Christian Arab city of South Arabia, known from the martyrs of 523 (Greek and Syriac hagiography); its people spoke Arabic and Sabaic; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Ampelone
left_out.reason: Pliny (6.159) lists 'Ampelome, a colony of the Milesians' among Arabian towns; unlocated and otherwise unknown, probably a garbled report. No evidence.

left_out.name: Eudaimon Arabia (Aden)
left_out.reason: Harbour town of the Periplus (26); in the 4th c. a church for Roman merchants (Philostorgius 3.4); a trading place with visiting Greek-speaking merchants, without a Greek civic community.

left_out.name: Kane (Qana, Bir Ali)
left_out.reason: Hadrami frankincense port (Periplus 27); Mediterranean traders visited; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Zafar
left_out.reason: Himyarite capital; a church built by Theophilus the Indian under Constantius II (Philostorgius 3.4); Sabaic and Arabic; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Dioskourides (Socotra)
left_out.reason: The Periplus (30) says the few inhabitants were a mixture of Arabs, Indians and Greeks who had come to trade; Greek graffiti of sailors in the Hoq cave (1st-3rd c. AD); Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550, Christian Topography 3.65) says the islanders spoke Greek, descended from settlers sent by the Ptolemies, with clergy ordained in Persia. A Greek-speaking community is thus attested, but the island had no city or civic status and was ruled from the Hadrami kingdom.

left_out.name: Sumhuram (Khor Rori, Moscha Limen)
left_out.reason: Hadrami fortified port of the frankincense trade (Periplus 32); South Arabian inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: ed-Dur (Omana?)
left_out.reason: Coastal town with Roman glass, coins and pottery and Aramaic inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Mleiha
left_out.reason: Inland town of the 3rd c. BC-3rd c. AD; local coins of Abiel imitate Alexander's tetradrachms with Aramaic legends; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Tayma
left_out.reason: North Arabian oasis town (residence of Nabonidus); Aramaic and Taymanitic inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Mouza (Muza)
left_out.reason: Red Sea port of the Periplus (21, 24) with Arab merchants and visiting ships; a trading place without Greek residents or civic status.

left_out.name: Ardericca (Eretrian deportees in Kissia)
left_out.reason: Darius I settled the Eretrians captured in 490 BC on a royal estate (stathmos) called Ardericca in Kissia, 210 stades from Susa; Herodotus (6.119) says they still kept their old language in his day, and Philostratus (VA 1.23-24) has Apollonius visit their descendants in the 1st c. AD. A Greek-speaking community, but a village on a royal estate, not a city; site unlocated (Barrington 93).

left_out.name: Ampe (Milesian deportees)
left_out.reason: Darius I settled the Milesians deported in 494 BC at Ampe on the Erythraean Sea near the mouth of the Tigris (Hdt. 6.20). A deportee settlement with no evidence of civic status or later Greek speech; unlocated (Barrington 93), possibly in Iraq.

left_out.name: Avroman (Kuh-e Salan parchments)
left_out.reason: Greek parchments of 88/87 and 22/21 BC record land sales between local people with Iranian names in a village of Hawraman; Greek as a documentary language in a village, not a city.

left_out.name: Persepolis (Parsa)
left_out.reason: Royal and ritual centre. Greek finds are graffiti of Greek quarrymen (6th-5th c. BC), a Greek tablet of c. 500 BC in the royal archive, and a few later dedications: Greek craftsmen and officials, no Greek city or civic community.

left_out.name: Istakhr
left_out.reason: Persian city (Sasanian dynastic centre); a single Greek document; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Pasargadae
left_out.reason: Achaemenid royal site; Greek only in isolated finds.

left_out.name: Kangavar (Concobar)
left_out.reason: Isidore of Charax 6: a temple of Artemis; sanctuary and station, not a Greek city.

left_out.name: Bisotun (Bagistana)
left_out.reason: Herakles relief dedicated by Hyakinthos son of Pantauchos in 148 BC for the viceroy Kleomenes, and Parthian royal reliefs of Mithridates II and Gotarzes II with Greek legends: Greek of officials at a sanctuary and road station.

left_out.name: Kermanshah (copy of Antiochus III's Laodice edict)
left_out.reason: Findspot (region) of a copy of Antiochus III's edict of 193 BC and of a lost Greek epitaph of Eumenes son of Demetrios; a Greek official text and one Greek burial, but no Greek city known there.

left_out.name: Khurha
left_out.reason: Hellenistic/Parthian temple with Ionic columns; a sanctuary, not a city.

left_out.name: Karafto cave
left_out.reason: Cave with a Greek inscription invoking Herakles; not a city.

left_out.name: Shami
left_out.reason: Elymaean sanctuary (bronze statue of a Parthian prince); Greek used by the Elymaean court only.

left_out.name: Masjed-e Soleyman
left_out.reason: Elymaean terrace sanctuary; no Greek civic community.

left_out.name: Bard-e Neshandeh
left_out.reason: Elymaean terrace sanctuary; no Greek civic community.

left_out.name: Izeh/Malamir and Tang-e Sarvak (Elymaean reliefs)
left_out.reason: Elymaean royal centre and rock reliefs with Elymaic Aramaic inscriptions; Greek only on royal coins.

left_out.name: Qal'a-ye Yazdegerd
left_out.reason: Parthian mountain stronghold and palace; not a city.

left_out.name: Tall-e Zahhak (Fasa)
left_out.reason: Settlement mound with an isolated Hellenistic Greek find; no Greek city attested.

left_out.name: Kharg (Arakia)
left_out.reason: Island with Parthian-period tombs and a Christian monastery; no Greek town.

left_out.name: Harmozeia (Hormuz)
left_out.reason: Coastal district where Nearchus met Alexander (Arrian, Ind. 33); no Greek settlement.

left_out.name: Mesambria (Persis coast)
