left_out.reason: Peninsula on the Persian coast named by Nearchus (Arrian, Ind. 39); a Greek rendering of a local name, no Greek settlement.

left_out.name: Tabai (Persis)
left_out.reason: Place where Antiochus IV died in 164 BC (Polybius 31.9); no evidence of a Greek community.

left_out.name: Aspadana/Gabai (Isfahan)
left_out.reason: Persian royal residence; no Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Gazaka/Ganzak (Atropatene)
left_out.reason: Capital of Atropatene and later Sasanian fire temple centre; no Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Zadracarta (Hyrcania)
left_out.reason: Hyrcanian capital where Alexander camped (Arrian 3.25); no Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Tambrax (Hyrcania)
left_out.reason: Unwalled Hyrcanian city with a palace, taken by Antiochus III in 209 BC (Polybius 10.31); no Greek residents mentioned.

left_out.name: Seleucia on the Erythraean Sea
left_out.reason: A Greek polis named in the Magnesian dossier of c. 205 BC, but unlocated: it may lie in Iraq (Mesene) or on the Iranian or Arabian shore of the Gulf. Not placed in Iran without a site.

left_out.name: Alexandria in Persis
left_out.reason: Listed in the Magnesian dossier (OGIS 233) according to Encyclopaedia Iranica; location and history unknown.

left_out.name: Achaia/Achais
left_out.reason: Seleucid foundation (Appian, Syr. 57; Strabo 11.10.1 places Achaia in Areia; Pliny 6.48 has Heraclea refounded as Achais), in present-day Afghanistan or Turkmenistan: counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Shushtar (Tostar)
left_out.reason: Shapur II settled Roman captives there (Encyclopaedia Iranica, Deportations ii), and tradition links the Band-e Kaisar dam to Valerian's army; the captives came mainly from Syriac-speaking Mesopotamian towns and no Greek-speaking community is attested.

left_out.name: Eranshahr-Shapur (Karkha de Ledan, Ivan-e Karkheh)
left_out.reason: Built by Shapur II near Susa for deportees from Bezabde, Singara and Amida (359-360); the deportees were mainly Syriac-speaking and no Greek-speaking community is attested.

left_out.name: Veh-az-Amid-Kavad (Ram-Kavad, Arrajan)
left_out.reason: Founded by Kavad I for the captives of Amida (502/503), more than 80,000 by Joshua the Stylite; Amida's people were mainly Syriac speakers, Procopius says Kavad later let them go home, and no Greek-speaking community is attested.

left_out.name: Charax Spasinou (Alexandria/Antioch in Susiana)
left_out.reason: In Iraq (Jebel Khayabir near Basra); covered by the Iraq research.

left_out.name: Alexandria in Arachosia (Kandahar)
left_out.reason: In present-day Afghanistan: counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Prophthasia (Farah)
left_out.reason: In present-day Afghanistan: counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Alexandria in Areia (Herat)
left_out.reason: In present-day Afghanistan: counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Antiochia in Margiana (Merv)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkmenistan: counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Nisa (Mithradatkert)
left_out.reason: In present-day Turkmenistan; the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia leaves it out too: an Arsacid royal fortress, whose Greek art belongs to the court and whose documents are Parthian.

left_out.name: Eruandashat (Yervandashat)
left_out.reason: Royal capital of the late Orontids (c. 200 BC), on the Araxes at the Turkish border; no Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Artaxata (Artashat, Khor Virap)
left_out.reason: Capital of the Artaxiad kings, founded by Artaxias I c. 176 BC (Strabo 11.14.6; the story that Hannibal planned it is a legend). It had a theatre, and Greek was used at court (Euripides' Bacchae performed before Artavasdes II and Orodes II in 53 BC, Plutarch, Crassus 33). Garsoian (Encyclopaedia Iranica) lists Greeks among its residents beside Armenians, Jews and Syrians, but gives no evidence, and no Greek civic institutions, coins or residents' inscriptions are known; Roman garrisons (Corbulo 58-59, Trajan 114-117) were soldiers. Taken by Corbulo 58, razed 59; destroyed by the Persians in the 360s.

left_out.name: Armavir (Armaouira, Argishtikhinili)
left_out.reason: Urartian city and Orontid capital. Seven Greek inscriptions of the 3rd-2nd c. BC (found 1911 and 1927, with literary quotations) belong to the royal court; Encyclopaedia Iranica: 'nothing has been found at Armavir which would suggest a Hellenistic city'. No Greek-speaking townspeople attested.

left_out.name: Garni (Gorneae)
left_out.reason: Royal fortress and summer residence with the temple and Tiridates I's Greek building inscription and a Greek mosaic inscription in the bath. Court and royal work only; not a city.

left_out.name: Kainepolis (Vagharshapat)
left_out.reason: Armenian town where the Romans under Statius Priscus set a garrison in 163 after destroying Artaxata; as the 'New City' (Kainepolis) it became the capital of Armenia, later the Armenian royal and church centre (Etchmiadzin). Roman soldiers left Latin inscriptions; no Greek-speaking civic community is attested.

left_out.name: Dvin (Doubios)
left_out.reason: Armenian royal and Persian administrative capital from the 4th c., seat of the Armenian catholicos; not Greek-speaking.

left_out.name: Tigranakert (Artsakh)
left_out.reason: Armenian royal foundation of the Hellenistic period (Tigranes I or II) with Hellenistic-style walls and finds; no Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Kabalaka (Chabala, Qabala)
left_out.reason: Capital of Caucasian Albania (Pliny 6.29, Ptolemy); no Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Partav (Barda)
left_out.reason: Capital of Caucasian Albania from the 5th c. (Perozabad); Albanian and Armenian, not Greek.

left_out.name: Naxuana (Nakhchivan)
left_out.reason: Town of Armenia in Ptolemy 5.12; no Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Urania (Ourania) (Possibly the ruins at Aphendrika, north-east of Rizokarpaso (Dipkarpaz), Famagusta district)
left_out.reason: Urania (Ourania) is known from a single passage: Demetrius Poliorcetes 'took by storm Urania and Carpasia' in 306 BC (Diodorus 20.47.2). Diodorus does not call it a city, nothing else is known of it, and its site is uncertain. A fortified place without evidence of civic status is left out, as is Arsinoe near Paphos.

left_out.name: Apamea in Mesene (unlocated in the Tigris delta; Pleiades places it east of the Tigris in Wasit Governorate)
left_out.reason: Known only from its dynastic name (after Apama, mother of Antiochus I) and a few lines in Pliny and Stephanus. Its site is unknown, and no coins, inscriptions or settlers attest a Greek-speaking city; a dynastic name alone is not enough.

left_out.name: Apollonia (Apolloniatis) (unlocated, Diyala plain east of the Tigris, Diyala Governorate)
left_out.reason: Known only from its name, from the district of Apolloniatis named after it (Polybius 5.43-54) and from Stephanus. Its site is unknown and it may be the same place as Artemita; no coins, inscriptions or settlers attest a Greek-speaking city.

left_out.name: Seleucia on the Hedyphon (Ja Nishin (Jan-e Shin) on the Jarahi river, Ramhormoz area, Khuzestan province (proposed))
left_out.reason: A large native town of Elymais renamed Seleucia by a Seleucid king. The dynastic renaming is the only Greek evidence; no coins, inscriptions or settlers attest a Greek-speaking city.

left_out.name: Ecbatana (Epiphania) (Hamadan)
left_out.reason: The Median capital, renamed Epiphaneia under Antiochus IV and seat of a Seleucid royal mint and treasury. Greek here is attested for the court and the mint, but no Greek civic inscription, city coin or resident Greek community is known from Hamadan; Polybius' 'Greek cities' of Media are other towns.

left_out.name: Alexandria in Carmania (unlocated in Carmania; perhaps Tepe Yahya (Soghun valley) or near Golashkerd, Kerman province)
left_out.reason: Listed by Pliny, Ptolemy and Ammianus, but scholars doubt that it existed as a foundation of Alexander; its site is unknown and there is no Greek evidence beyond the name.

left_out.name: Charax (Rhagiane) (unlocated, east of Rey towards the Caspian Gates, Tehran or Semnan province)
left_out.reason: Named by Isidore of Charax (7) as a town of Rhagiane where the Parthian king Phraates I settled the Mardi. The Greek name 'Charax' (stockade) is the only Greek evidence, and its site is unknown.

left_out.name: Klimata of Phoenice Libanensis in Hierocles (Magludon, Salton Bourkaiou)
left_out.reason: Hierocles lists rural districts (klimata) of Phoenice Libanensis beside its cities; districts are not cities. The klima of the Iabrudeni is counted under Iabruda.

left_out.name: Gabara (Galilee)
left_out.reason: With Sepphoris and Tiberias one of the three largest towns of Galilee in Josephus (Vita 123); a Jewish town (usually put at 'Arraba) with no Greek civic institutions, coins or Greek-speaking community; not a see.

left_out.name: Bathyra (Batanaea)
left_out.reason: A village colony of Babylonian Jewish horsemen settled by Herod under Zamaris (Josephus AJ 17.23-31); a military settlement, not a city, and unlocated (Pleiades 682531).

left_out.name: Caeciliana (Qal'at Najm)
left_out.reason: A Euphrates crossing and road station of the Roman itineraries (Pleiades 658418), later the Arab castle of Qal'at Najm; no civic status or see.

left_out.name: Arsinoe 'in the Aulon' (Coele Syria)
left_out.reason: A Ptolemaic foundation named by Stephanus (Ethnica) as a city of Syria 'in the Valley' (Cohen 2006 discusses it); unlocated, possibly a short-lived name of a city counted elsewhere, so it cannot be mapped.

left_out.name: Birtha (Osrhoene)
left_out.reason: A see and Justinianic fortress of Osrhoene, placed at Birecik (Pleiades 658412); in Turkey, outside the area.

left_out.name: Saana, Ina, Samulis and Abida (Ptolemy 5.15, Coele Syria/Decapolis)
left_out.reason: Names in Ptolemy's list of the towns of Coele Syria and the Decapolis; unlocated or villages (Samulis is tentatively placed in the Golan-Hauran borderland, Pleiades 678371), with no coins, inscriptions or see that would make them cities.

left_out.name: Ptolemy's towns of the Palmyrene (Cholle, Putea, Adada, Adacha, Goaria, Casama, Odmana, Atera)
left_out.reason: Road stations, forts and villages of the Palmyrene listed by Ptolemy; several are military posts of the Notitia Dignitatum (Casama, Pleiades 678085). None was a city or see; Rhesapha, Palmyra, Danaba and Aueria/Evaria are counted separately.

left_out.name: Ptolemy's minor towns of northern Syria (Chalybon, Thema, Derrhima, Athis, Asaphidama, Tolmidessa, Coara, Nazama, Thelmenissus, Ariseria, Rhegias, Niara)
left_out.reason: Names in Ptolemy's Chalybonitis, Chalcidice, Apamene and Cyrrhestice; villages and road stations (Ariseria/Ad Serta and Niara are itinerary stations), with no coins, see or civic evidence.

left_out.name: Isidore of Charax's other Euphrates stations (Giddan, Belesi Biblada, Merrha, Asich)
left_out.reason: Isidore (Parthian Stations 1) calls only Nicephorium and Ichnae 'Greek cities' (and Dura a Macedonian foundation) on this stretch; the other stops are villages and forts.

left_out.name: Kelonai (Celonae), the Boeotians of Xerxes' time
left_out.reason: Diodorus (17.110.4-5) says that on his march from Sittakene towards Bagistana Alexander came to Kelonai, where Boeotians settled by Xerxes had become bilingual: they spoke the local language but kept most of their Greek speech and some Greek customs. A Persian-period settlement of deportees, never called a city, and unlocated somewhere on the road from Babylonia into Media (Iraq or western Iran; perhaps the district later called Chalonitis). A note for Chala, not a city.

left_out.name: Laodicea in Persis
left_out.reason: A Laodicea founded by Antiochus on the borders of Persis is listed among the Seleucid foundations (Pliny 6.115; Cohen 2013); it may be the Laodicea in Mesopotamia, which is also rejected. Unlocated and known only by its dynastic name, which is not enough by itself.

left_out.name: Thilabous and Izan (Euphrates island towns in Isidore)
left_out.reason: Island forts and small towns on the Euphrates below Anatha in Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 1); no Greek settlers, institutions or inscriptions.

left_out.name: Girsu (Telloh), shrine of Adad-nadin-ahhe
left_out.reason: The Sumerian mound was reoccupied in the Hellenistic period: a palace of the local ruler Adad-nadin-ahhe built with his stamped bricks, a Greek-Aramaic bilingual inscription and a Hellenistic shrine on the ruins of the E-ninnu (a Seleucid cult place). A local dynast's seat and a sanctuary, not a Greek-speaking town.

left_out.name: Apologos (al-Ubulla)
left_out.reason: Market town of Characene at the head of the Gulf (Periplus 35); later a see of the Church of the East (Syriac). A trading place with no Greek civic community.

left_out.name: Okelis (Khor Ghurayrah)
left_out.reason: Anchorage and watering place at the Bab el-Mandeb (Periplus 25; Pliny 6.104); a harbour station, not a town with Greek residents.

left_out.name: Farasan islands
left_out.reason: A Latin inscription of AD 144 from Great Farasan (Portus Ferresanus) shows a Roman naval and military outpost (a detachment of legio II Traiana); not a Greek town.

left_out.name: Dumatha (Dumat al-Jandal)
left_out.reason: Arab oasis town at the end of the Roman desert frontier, garrisoned by Roman troops according to an inscription found elsewhere (Pleiades 29548); Nabataean and Arabic; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Ruwwafa
left_out.reason: Desert temple with Greek-Nabataean bilingual building inscriptions of AD 166-169, set up by the Thamudic confederation for Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus: a sanctuary of an Arab tribal group, not a town.

left_out.name: Asaak (Astauene) and Ragau (Apavarktikene)
left_out.reason: Parthian towns of north-east Iran in Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 11 and 13): Asaak, where Arsaces was proclaimed king and an everlasting fire was kept, and Ragau. Parthian royal places with no Greek community; Ragau is unlocated.

left_out.name: Karina, Bazigraban and Adrapana (Isidore's road through Media)
left_out.reason: Stations on the road from Chala to Ecbatana in Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 4 and 6): a village, a customs post and a royal palace. Not Greek cities.

left_out.name: Talabroke, Samariane, Karta and Tape (Hyrcania)
left_out.reason: Hyrcanian towns and royal seats in Strabo (11.7.2); no Greek settlers or institutions attested.

left_out.name: Alexandria and Alexandropolis in Sakastane
left_out.reason: Named by Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 18) among the towns of Sakastane, which lies mostly in Afghanistan; nothing places them in Iranian Sistan. Alexandropolis is counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia (the Alexandria there is taken as a scribal repetition).

left_out.name: Corada (Phoenice Libanensis)
left_out.reason: A see under Damascus in the Notitia Antiochena, with bishops Peter (451, 458) and Theodore (553). Its site is unknown (the proposed Qara is Chonochora, counted separately), so it cannot be placed; it probably lay in present-day Syria, and could be added as a point for the region only.

left_out.name: Eragiza (Euphratensis)
left_out.reason: A town on the Euphrates in Ptolemy, placed by the Barrington Atlas north of Barbalissos (Pleiades 658461), and listed among the cities of Euphratensis by Hierocles. It is not among the sees of Hierapolis in the Notitia Antiochena and no bishop is known, so the rule for sees does not apply, and no Greek evidence of its own is known.

left_out.name: Gadara of Palaestina I (Gadora, Tell Jadur?)
left_out.reason: Hierocles lists a Gadara among the cities of Palaestina I, a see distinct from Gadara of the Decapolis, but its site has not been identified and the bishops of the two sees cannot be told apart. Gadora (Tell Jadur by as-Salt), the old chief town of Peraea, is the usual candidate; Gezer (Gazara) has also been suggested. A see known only through a doubtful identification is not counted.

left_out.name: Adora (Adoraim, Dura) / Diara
left_out.reason: An Idumaean town rebuilt by Gabinius. The see 'Diara' at the synod of Jerusalem in 536 has been read as Dora or as Adora; a see known only from a doubtful identification is not counted.

left_out.name: Gazara (Gezer)
left_out.reason: A see 'Gazara' at the synod of Jerusalem in 536 is known from one signature, and it is uncertain that it was Gezer, which Eusebius calls a village. A see known only from a doubtful identification is not counted.

left_out.name: Zabulon / Chabulon (Kabul), Galilee
left_out.reason: A bishop 'of Zabulon' appears only in some lists of Nicaea (325); the title may be the district of Zebulun rather than a town. A see known only from a doubtful title is not counted.

left_out.name: Sariphaea (Palaestina I)
left_out.reason: Known from one bishop, Stephen, at the synod of Jerusalem in 536. It is probably Diocletianopolis, which is counted (the Barrington Atlas marks 'Sapharea?' there); as a separate see it cannot be placed.

left_out.name: Agrippia and Orogizo (Ragizo, Orthalea), sees under Sergiopolis
left_out.reason: Sees under Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena, known only as names in the list, with no bishop known; unlocated, so they cannot be placed.

left_out.name: Seriane (Isriya)
left_out.reason: A road station and temple on the Strata Diocletiana. A see 'Serigene' under Sergiopolis is in the Notitia Antiochena, but its identification with Seriane is a proposal and no bishop is known, so the see rests on a doubtful identification.

left_out.name: Tell Mahre (Osrhoene)
left_out.reason: A see under Edessa in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570), with no bishop known before a Miaphysite one. It lay near the Balikh, but the site is not located: the Syriac sources put Tell Mahre near Callinicum (Syria), the titular see is placed in Turkey, and Vailhe took it for Macedonopolis (Birtha, in Turkey). It cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Chrysopolis, Eutyme and Neapolis in Arabia
left_out.reason: Sees of the province of Arabia known from church lists (Chrysopolis had a bishop, John, at Chalcedon 451). They are unlocated, and Arabia spans southern Syria and northern Jordan, so they cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Marcopolis and Himeria (Osrhoene)
left_out.reason: Sees of Osrhoene with bishops in the 4th-6th c. (Marcopolis: Cyrus at Ephesus 431, Caioumas at Chalcedon 451). Neither is located: Himeria lay near the Euphrates by Europos/Carchemish on the Syrian-Turkish border, and Marcopolis has been put at Batnae (Turkey) or Sinjar (Iraq). They cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Nea Valentia and Maratha (Osrhoene)
left_out.reason: Sees of Osrhoene in the Notitia Antiochena; unlocated, so they cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Arlane (Phoenice Libanensis)
left_out.reason: A see under Damascus with bishops at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) according to Le Quien. It is unlocated (Vailhe's Aracha north of Palmyra is a guess), so it cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Arbokadama (Syria Coele)
left_out.reason: Known only from the signature of its bishop Pegasius at Nicaea (325); unlocated, so it cannot be placed.

left_out.name: Damunda, Alamusa and Dorea (sees of Arabia)
left_out.reason: Sees of Arabia in versions of the Notitia Antiochena, known only by name and unlocated; they cannot be placed in a present-day country.

left_out.name: Maurikopolis, Stephanoupolis and Armenia (late sees under Emesa)
left_out.reason: Sees added under Emesa in revisions of the Notitia Antiochena (late 6th-early 7th c.); unidentified and possibly new names of towns already counted.

left_out.name: Onus (Palaestina I)
left_out.reason: A city of Palaestina I in Hierocles, but unlocated; its identification with biblical Ono (Kafr Ana near Lod) is a guess. A see known only from a doubtful identification is not counted.

left_out.name: Saltus sees: Gaulanitis, Gerariticus, Constantinianus, Hieraticus
left_out.reason: Sees of imperial estates and rural districts (saltus), not towns; not counted as towns.

left_out.name: Tricomias and Pentacomia (Palaestina I and III)
left_out.reason: Sees named after groups of villages ('three villages', 'five villages'), that is rural districts, not towns.

left_out.name: Parembolae (Palaestina I and Arabia) and the bishopric of the Saracens (Phoenice Libanensis)
left_out.reason: Sees of Arab tribal federates and their encampments, not of towns.

left_out.name: Iotabe (island in the Gulf of Aqaba)
left_out.reason: A see of Palaestina III on an island outside the Levant (Tiran in Saudi Arabia or Pharaoh's Island in Egypt). There the strict rule applies: Procopius calls its people Hebrews and no Greek-speaking residents are attested.

left_out.name: Mount Tabor
left_out.reason: A monastic sanctuary whose bishop is recorded only after the conquest (c. 808); a see of a monastery is not counted.

left_out.name: Ikaros (Failaka Island, Kuwait)
left_out.reason: A Seleucid settlement on Failaka with a fort and a temple; a stele carries Greek letters of the Seleucid officials Anaxarchos and Ikadion to 'the inhabitants of Ikaros' about the sanctuary and their privileges (c. 203 BC, Antiochus III). Greek-speaking settlers are attested, but no council, assembly or coinage: perhaps a garrison colony rather than a city. Abandoned after c. 100 BC.

left_out.name: Soteira (Parthia)
left_out.reason: Seleucus I's foundation in Parthia (Appian, Syr. 57); Ptolemy lists a Sotira in Areia, so it is counted in the companion set Greek Cities of Central and South Asia.

left_out.name: Dahan-i Ghulaman (Zranka?)
left_out.reason: Achaemenid planned town in Iranian Sistan, probably the provincial capital of Drangiana (Zranka), abandoned before Alexander; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Pura (Bampur), royal seat of Gedrosia
left_out.reason: The royal seat of the Gedrosians, reached by Alexander after the desert march (Arrian 6.24.1), usually placed at Bampur in Iranian Baluchistan; a native town with no Greek settlers or writing.

greek_communities_after_1800.start: 1897 (Cretan Muslim refugees settled by Abdülhamid II)
greek_communities_after_1800.peak: about 3,000-3,500 Greek-speaking Muslims before the war (Lasithiotaki; T-Vine 2018; WP: 3,000 = 60% of the town). WP 'Greeks in Syria' gives 8,000 citing Tsokalidou, which is more than the whole town (7,404 at the 2004 census) and probably conflates Hamidiye with Tripoli.
greek_communities_after_1800.today: Town of 7,404 at the 2004 Syrian census. Cretan Greek still spoken, but declining and kept mainly by older speakers in families (Shafaq News, July 2026). After 2011 some families moved to Crete (a community of about 500 in Chania by 2018, 'up to one in six' of the town by one informant) and to Cyprus (about 200 had residence rights there before the war).

sources.title: R. Tsokalidou, 'Oi ellinofonoi Kritikoi ston Livano kai ti Syria: i epiviosi mias idiaiteris ethnotikis taftotitas', in A.-F. Christidis et al. greek_communities_after_1800.today: Armenia's remaining Greeks (365 at the 2022 census) live mainly in Alaverdi and Yerevan, then Vanadzor, Gyumri, Stepanavan, Hankavan, Noyemberyan; Yaghdan described (2009) as the last Greek village in Armenia.
